articles.title: Experts Expect 'Security Reckoning' As AI Tools Find And Exploit Software Bugs
articles.body:
Experts Expect 'Security Reckoning' As AI Tools Find And Exploit Software Bugs (msn.com) 41
			
		 	
				The Washington Post reports:
Tens of thousands of South Koreans had their financial data exposed online in recent weeks after at least nine major banks there suffered cyberattacks that suggested a dark future for online security.  One man, a 26-year-old living in southern China, was allegedly behind the attacks, according to an investigation by cybersecurity company CrowdStrike. Traces left online and failure to secure his own systems allowed investigators to piece together the man's name, age, location and what he allegedly did. The clues revealed that the devastating assault on some of Asia's most sophisticated financial institutions was the work of an amateur. The attacks were launched with help from a few artificial intelligence chatbots, CrowdStrike found, before asking one to help sell the stolen data online and draft a fake résumé touting cybersecurity skills...
The hacker who broke into the South Korean banks had access to Anthropic's Claude, but because the U.S. firm's tools generally refuse to take illegal actions, free Chinese models were also used, including DeepSeek, CrowdStrike found.  "The models are interchangeable," said Meyers, the CrowdStrike executive. 
The Post calls it "part of a wave of AI-enabled hacking that is advancing across the world, triggering alarm inside national governments as well as multinational companies."
"Basically any pedestrian, non-hacker can take these frameworks and start leveraging them to go after different targets," said Adam Meyers, senior vice president of counter adversary operations at CrowdStrike. The company has tracked an increase in the speed with which cyberattacks can move once inside a target's networks, as seasoned hackers and rank amateurs alike get a boost from AI tools. "Anyone can be a super-hacker now," Meyers said...  Many cyber experts still expect the security reckoning to intensify as AI tools that can find and exploit software bugs become more widely distributed and understood.
[Last] Monday, The Post reported that cybersecurity researchers from the start-up Cathedral who set out to test Anthropic's security found that they could access internal messages and meeting transcripts. Cathedral reported its findings to Anthropic, which said it resolved the newly discovered problems... Security experts say it's unlikely that any hacker is forgoing the use of AI tools right now.  
Even in America, critical infrastructure like energy and water companies need to be "immediately and comprehensively" tested for exploitable bugs, according to Snehal Antani, chief executive of cybersecurity company Horizon3.  He tells the Post the government might need to fund that remediation, and even form "a public and private partnership to accelerate incident response."

articles.title: Supermarket freezers across Europe hit by second suspected cyber-attack
articles.body:
Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C (122F), echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France.
Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked.
The EU food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the repeated cyber-attacks were deeply concerning, calling them “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.
The incidents follow an attack in France last month in which hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets, raising their temperatures as high as 50C (122F) and causing fires and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros.
A growing range of devices, including refrigeration systems, can now be monitored and controlled remotely, leading authorities to particularly fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks in after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet that six of its shops had been hit, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.
An ICA shop at Sjöbo in southern Sweden posted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50C. Another in Stockholm said its freezers were broken “due to a 2am cyberattack” and that “everything was destroyed”.
The head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, said it was working on incidents around the country. It had established the country had “quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices” that needed updating or patching, he told Reuters.
The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last month reported a similar incident to police in the Netherlands, said fridges and freezers in dozens of its supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg had been hit.
It did not specify the cause, but reporters visiting a shop north-east of Brussels saw refrigerators and freezers empty and a sign reading: “Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products on the refrigerated or freezer shelves. We offer our sincere apologies.”
A company spokesperson, Sarah De Meester, said the range of fresh and frozen products was “temporarily somewhat limited” in affected shops, but that distribution centres were operating normally and there was no disruption to deliveries.
Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of shops and supermarkets had been affected, including five Spar outlets, Shop & Go convenience shops attached to Q8 service stations and some smaller Proxy Delhaize mini-markets.
“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s refrigeration systems, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations.”
He told the Belga news agency the incident had been a cyber-attack and that the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.
The Colruyt and Intermarché supermarket chains also said they had been hit by technical problems affecting fridges in five and 15 of their shops respectively, and Carrefour Belgium reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 shops.
“It’s a cyber-attack, there is no other reason,” said Mich Vergauwen, a Carrefour spokesperson. An Ikea Belgium spokesperson likewise told Agence France-Presse that a cyber-attack had caused the temperature of freezers in its Mons shop to rise suddenly.
Ikea, famous for its in-store Swedish meatballs, said it had had to remove some food products from refrigeration units as a precaution and expected some food waste as a result.
In Finland, the Helsingin Sanomat newspaper said shops operated by the Kesko supermarket chain were investigating similar problems, while the Dutch public radio NOS reported that the systems of at least 17 mainly small local shops had been affected.
At one Estonian supermarket chain, attackers accessed a computer controlling the refrigeration system and turned up the temperature to 50C, the refrigeration supply company Kitman Coldtech told the ERR broadcaster.
“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” its chief executive, Jann Mutso, said, adding that the attack was responded to within minutes and there had been no significant damage. The Selver supermarket chain said one of its outlets had been affected.
Ireland’s third-largest supermarket chain, SuperValu, said refrigeration systems limited to a specific model in 13 of its 223 shops had been affected by a cyber-incident, and that chilled and frozen products had been removed from sale.
Many cyber-attacks involve extortion or are politically motivated and are potentially carried out by state-level actors, said Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne. But the supermarket attacks, with no financial demands, point to sabotage, he said.
“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Hegel told Reuters.
Patrick Lamplmair of the cybersecurity firm Tributech said cyber-attackers would keep going “until it stops working” because the method was “cheap and the damage is immediate”. Many refrigeration systems had known and as yet unfixed flaws, he said.
“Thousands of these controllers were still reachable from the internet after the French attack,” he added. “A few commands to a temperature controller can destroy stock overnight and close stores.”
In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss, which said subsequently that it had identified some security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.
The hackers remotely overrode the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets at chains including Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C.
The shops had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products. Individual supermarkets reportedly suffered losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000).
The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigation into the French attack and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, Ansii, to investigate.
The agency subsequently reported that supermarkets using controllers from two other companies had also been targeted in the attack, but authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents. There have been no claims of responsibility.

articles.title: A fresh wave of cyberattacks has hit Europe’s supermarket refrigerators, destroying food across countries
articles.body:
A second wave of cyberattacks is suspected to have hit supermarket refrigerators across Europe, causing fridges to increase temperatures and spoil food at dozens of stores across Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden.
Supermarket giants Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt confirmed the hacks overnight, with one Belgian company that operates Delhaize’s systems saying that the hackers had changed the settings to defrost, per Reuters. Stores have experienced heavy food losses from the cyberattacks, forcing supermarkets to throw out goods that had defrosted or were otherwise no longer consumable.
The cyberattacks follow earlier refrigerator hacks in France last month that caused food spoilage at hundreds of supermarkets by deliberately raising the temperature on the units. Security researchers said that the cause of the hacks was internet-connected refrigerators made by Danish company Danfoss, which was no longer providing security updates. Security company Claroty warned back in August that those refrigerator units were at risk of remote hacks and outages.
The freezer hacks underscore how cyberattacks can have real-world effects, including on the food supply chain, often as a result of weak or overlooked cybersecurity practices. In 2025, a cyberattack on food distributor giant UNFI resulted in food shortages and empty shelves at grocery stores and supermarkets across the United States.
U.S. Department of Defense officials are reportedly investigating whether freezer units on military bases were hacked by Iran-backed hackers. Iranian hackers were also blamed for cyberattacks targeting U.S. water providers earlier this year.

articles.title: China's First Frontier AI Export Controls: Mofcom Announcement No. 48
articles.body:
Published: 2026-10-23
Categories: AI Governance and Regulation
China’s First Frontier AI Export Controls: MOFCOM Announcement No. 48
Key Takeaways
On October 16, 2026, China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) issued Announcement No. 48 of 2026. The announcement proposes adding 40 technologies to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export, 23 of them in artificial intelligence, and it imposes an interim pre-export registration requirement that is already in effect [1][2]. China’s catalogue has touched AI before: the 2020 revision added personalized recommendation and AI interaction interface technology [6]. Unlike those 2020 additions, the draft reaches frontier model weights, agent architectures, and AI-enabled offensive cyber capability, with explicit technical thresholds for each [1].
The announcement contains two instruments with different legal status. The catalogue additions are a draft open for comment until November 15, 2026, while the registration requirement applies now, including to exports that have started but are not yet complete [1][2]. Within the draft, model weights are restricted at frontier scale. Weights, key checkpoints, source code, architecture, and training and inference optimization know-how are restricted if a model meets any one of three tests: at least 10^26 FLOPs of training compute, at least 2 trillion parameters, or a global top-10 position on public evaluation rankings, global call volume, or comparable measures at the time of export [1][3]. Agents are controlled independently of the model. Planning, multi-agent coordination, tool use, and game-theoretic decision technologies are restricted above set benchmarks, and high-performance agents built for critical infrastructure, defense, or core government use are prohibited outright [1].
The line between service access and custody determines most enterprise exposure. MOFCOM says API, app, web, SaaS, and lightweight on-device use do not count as exporting a large model. Deploying a restricted model locally outside China does count, though automatic licensing may apply on a Chinese company’s own overseas cloud [2]. Multinationals also face exposure through licensing deals and changes of ownership or control, not only through product exports, and analysts read the registration form as potentially capturing intra-group code sharing as well [2][3][4]. Any transfer of ownership, licensing for overseas use, or shift of control to a foreign entity can trigger registration [2][4].
Background
China regulates outbound technology transfer under two overlapping regimes. The first is the technology-trade regime under the Foreign Trade Law and the Regulations on Technology Import and Export Administration, which governs the catalogue being revised here. The second is the dual-use export-control regime under the 2020 Export Control Law [5]. MOFCOM’s spokesperson described the revision as routine and grounded in Article 20 of the Foreign Trade Law. The spokesperson stressed that it “does not target any specific country, region, or entity” and that the aim is to prevent uncontrolled diffusion while protecting legitimate cooperation [2]. The catalogue has been revised several times since 2001. The August 2020 revision, which added recommendation-algorithm technology, coincided with the proposed sale of TikTok to a U.S. buyer and was reported as likely to complicate that deal [3][6].
Across all three sectors, Announcement No. 48 proposes 14 prohibited and 26 restricted items: 23 in AI, 5 in biomedicine, and 12 in photovoltaics [2]. In China’s technology-trade framework, prohibited technologies may not be exported at all, while restricted technologies require a license from commerce and science authorities. ChinaTalk notes that licensing is administered by provincial authorities, although central authorities have intervened in prominent cases [3]. The official annex groups the AI items into large models, agents, compute clusters, chip design, and information-processing technologies. It also excludes from management any technology that has already entered the public domain through open-source release or academic publication [1].
The interim registration requirement is the part that applies today. From the announcement date until the revised catalogue takes effect, exporters must register through MOFCOM’s unified business platform before exporting any listed technology. Registration covers four triggers: transfer of technology ownership abroad, licensing of domestic technology for overseas use, a change in ownership or control that makes a foreign entity the owner or controller, and other cases MOFCOM designates [2][4]. Exporters must decide for themselves whether a technology falls within scope. The registration form asks for recipient details, destination, technology description, end use, and estimated value [2][4].
The timing also matters for enterprises that already track U.S. controls. CSA’s prior research documented the first U.S. use of export-control authority to suspend a broadly deployed commercial frontier model [9]. Announcement No. 48 means frontier AI supply chains now face formal outbound controls from both of the largest AI-producing jurisdictions. ChinaTalk observes that the 10^26 FLOP threshold mirrors the figure used in the 2023 U.S. executive order and the since-rescinded 2025 U.S. AI Diffusion rule. The authors also estimate that no released Chinese model currently exceeds it [3].
Security Analysis
What the AI Annex Actually Controls
The annex is granular, and its structure matters for scoping. The table below summarizes the AI items drawn from the official draft annex [1], with interpretive notes from published analyses [3][4].
Three features of this structure deserve attention from security and compliance teams. First, the “global leading” test is dynamic. A model that falls below the compute and parameter thresholds can still become restricted if its public evaluation rank, global call volume, or similar measures place it in the top 10 when the export occurs [1]. ChinaTalk calls this criterion “by far the most up-for-interpretation,” noting that the rule names no ranking body [3], and it means the compliance status of a given model version can change after deployment. Second, the agent items are defined by system behavior rather than by the underlying model. An orchestration framework that integrates hundreds of tools could meet the tool-use threshold even when it runs on a model well below the frontier thresholds, an issue Ray Sun identifies as unresolved [5]. Third, the cyber items carry direct security consequences: Chinese-origin AI red-teaming, vulnerability-discovery, and detection tools that meet the thresholds would require a license to leave China, and offensive code-generation capability could not be exported at all.
Deployment Models and Where the Line Falls
MOFCOM’s spokesperson framed the central test as whether restricted technology moves from inside China to overseas [2]. That framing produces a clear distinction between consuming a model as a service and taking custody of it, as summarized below.
For enterprises, the practical consequence is that the deployment model the draft captures, local self-hosting, is also the one often chosen for data-protection reasons. Organizations that chose to self-host a Chinese frontier model in their own environment, rather than call a Chinese-hosted API, did so to keep sensitive data inside their own boundary. MOFCOM places local deployment outside China within export management, which means those self-hosting arrangements require the Chinese supplier to hold a license [2]. ChinaTalk reads this as also covering on-premises licensing deals and managed deployments in which a vendor runs an agent’s reasoning loop inside a customer environment [3]. Because licenses can be revoked or conditioned, ChinaTalk suggests this may lead some non-Chinese users to reconsider such dependencies [3]. The registration requirement already covers exports in progress, so ongoing weight-delivery or model-update arrangements may be affected now rather than after the catalogue is finalized [2].
The treatment of open weights depends on whether a model is already public. Weights that are already public are outside the controls [1]. Open-sourcing a new restricted model, however, falls under automatic licensing that still requires reporting [2]. Commentators note that “open source” is not defined, and that it is unclear how restricted-use licenses would be treated [3]. Organizations that depend on successive open-weight releases from Chinese labs should therefore treat future release cadence, not just current availability, as a variable outside their control.
Exposure Through Corporate Structure
The exposure most likely to surprise multinationals sits in their own organizational charts. Registration is triggered by licensing technology for overseas use and by changes of ownership or control, not only by sales to third parties [2][4]. A multinational with China-based R&D teams building agent frameworks, vulnerability-discovery tooling, or fine-tuned models may therefore need to register before sharing that work with affiliates outside China. ChinaTalk reads the registration form’s field on exports made outside formal contracts as potentially capturing intra-group code sharing and open-sourcing [3]. This reading is an inference from the form rather than an official statement, but it is a reasonable basis for conservative scoping.
The data-based items add a second pathway. A model fine-tuned in China on operational data that qualifies as “important data” under the Data Security Law would be restricted, unless the de minimis carve-out applies. A model trained on “core data” would be prohibited [1]. Organizations that classified China-resident data under the Data Security Law for cross-border data transfer purposes may not have applied the same classification to training and fine-tuning datasets, since those obligations previously governed data transfer rather than model transfer.
Finally, recent precedent suggests that redomiciling does not remove Chinese jurisdiction. In January 2026, MOFCOM announced an assessment of Meta’s acquisition of Manus, a Singapore-registered AI agent company whose products were developed in China. The assessment examined whether the relocation of staff and technology required export authorization [7]. Announcement No. 48 now gives that line of scrutiny explicit, agent-specific thresholds, which suggests M&A due diligence on AI targets with China-origin development history should include an export-control workstream.
Recommendations
Immediate Actions
Organizations should first inventory every Chinese-origin model, agent framework, and AI security tool in use and record how each is consumed: as an API or SaaS service, as a lightweight on-device component, or as locally deployed weights or code. The local-deployment category is the priority, because it is the one the draft places within export management [2]. For each locally deployed asset, teams should ask the supplier in writing whether it has registered the export under Announcement No. 48 and whether it expects to need a license once the catalogue is final.
Legal and engineering teams should jointly review technology flows out of China-based subsidiaries, joint ventures, and R&D centers since October 16. The goal is to identify transfers that may already require registration, including code repositories, model checkpoints, and agent frameworks shared with overseas affiliates [2][4]. Organizations with a material interest in the final scope should prepare comments before the November 15, 2026 deadline, through the email, fax, or postal channels published in the announcement [1][4].
Short-Term Mitigations
Over the next one to two quarters, organizations should treat restricted-category Chinese models as regulated dependencies with documented fallbacks. Vendor contracts for locally deployed models should allocate responsibility for Chinese export registration and licensing, specify notice obligations if a license is denied, conditioned, or revoked, and address whether updates and new checkpoints are covered by the same authorization. Because the “global leading” test depends on rankings at the time of export [1], teams should not assume that a model version cleared today will remain uncontrolled for later updates.
Security teams that rely on AI-assisted vulnerability discovery or deepfake detection tools developed in China should map those tools against the restricted thresholds and identify alternatives. A licensing interruption to a detection capability is a security-control gap, not only a procurement issue. Data governance teams should also extend Data Security Law classification work to cover training and fine-tuning datasets held in China, so that “important data” and “core data” exposure is known before models trained on them are shared abroad [1].
Strategic Considerations
Announcement No. 48, if finalized substantially as drafted, would mean that frontier AI is treated as controlled technology by both the United States and China, with each regime drawing its lines differently. Recent U.S. measures have emphasized compute and, in the Fable 5 case, access to a deployed model, although the since-rescinded 2025 AI Diffusion rule also reached model weights [3]. The Chinese draft centers on custody of weights, know-how, and agent architectures. Enterprise AI governance programs should model export-control disruption from either jurisdiction as a standing risk scenario and design architectures that can swap models without rebuilding agent workflows.
Organizations should also recognize that the draft treats agents as a distinct regulatory object. Defining controls by planning depth, concurrency, and tool count means that internal agent platforms, and not only foundation models, may be subject to cross-border technology rules. Agent inventories should record these characteristics alongside traditional security attributes. Finally, because the final catalogue may narrow, broaden, or shift after consultation [3], and because ChinaTalk notes the comment window closes shortly before an expected leaders’ meeting at APEC [3], a timing that could bear on the final scope, this analysis should be revisited once MOFCOM publishes the final text.
CSA Resource Alignment
CSA’s most directly relevant prior work is Frontier AI Export Controls: Enterprise Governance After Fable 5 [8]. That note argues for treating frontier model access as a contingent operational dependency that belongs in vendor management and business continuity planning. Announcement No. 48 extends that argument to a second jurisdiction and to a different control point. The U.S. action examined in that note interrupted service access, while the Chinese draft leaves service access untouched and instead governs weight custody and local deployment. Enterprises that built continuity plans around the U.S. scenario should check whether those plans also cover a supplier-side license failure for self-hosted models.
AI Model Export Controls: The Fable 5 Precedent [9] documented how a single regulatory directive can remove a widely deployed model with little notice. Its recommendation for multi-model fallback strategies applies directly to organizations that depend on Chinese frontier or open-weight models, particularly given the dynamic “global leading” threshold described above. Sovereign AI Access Controls and Enterprise Concentration Risk [10] provides the broader framing. It treats national control over AI capability as a source of concentration risk, and the Chinese draft is a concrete instance of that risk materializing on the supply side.
For control implementation, the AI Controls Matrix (AICM) v1.1 [11] provides the relevant control objectives in its supply chain management, transparency and accountability, and governance, risk and compliance domains, including supplier inventory, third-party assessment, and regulatory change management. For agent-specific exposure, MAESTRO [12] offers a layered threat model that can help teams document the agent capabilities, such as tool integration and multi-agent coordination, that now carry export-control significance.
References
[1] Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology of the PRC. “Announcement No. 48 of 2026 on Public Consultation on Revising the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export and Interim Registration of Related Technology Exports (商务部 科技部公告2026年第48号), with Annex 1 (Draft Scope of AI, Biomedicine, and Photovoltaic Technologies).” MOFCOM, October 16, 2026.
[2] Ministry of Commerce of the PRC. “MOFCOM Spokesperson Answers Questions on Revising the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export (商务部新闻发言人就修订《中国禁止出口限制出口技术目录》答记者问).” MOFCOM, October 16, 2026.
[3] Ennis, Q., Zhang, I., Ottinger, L., and Zakaria, A. “MOFCOM’s New Rules and the Future of Chinese AI.” ChinaTalk, October 21, 2026.
[4] Geopolitechs. “China Imposes Temporary Export Registration Requirements for AI, Biotech and Solar Technologies, Seeks Public Comment on Proposed Export Restrictions.” Geopolitechs, October 16, 2026.
[5] Sun, R. “China’s AI Export Control Announcement Raises More Questions Than It Answers.” Ctrl+AI+Reg, October 19, 2026.
[6] Center for Security and Emerging Technology (translation). “Revisions to the Content of the Catalog of Prohibited or Restricted Technology Exports.” CSET, Georgetown University, September 2, 2020.
[7] South China Morning Post. “China to Probe Meta’s Purchase of Manus Regarding Export Control and Tech Exports.” SCMP, January 2026.
[8] Cloud Security Alliance. “Frontier AI Export Controls: Enterprise Governance After Fable 5.” CSA AI Safety Initiative, June 2026.
[9] Cloud Security Alliance. “AI Model Export Controls: The Fable 5 Precedent.” CSA AI Safety Initiative, June 2026.
[10] Cloud Security Alliance. “Sovereign AI Access Controls and Enterprise Concentration Risk.” CSA AI Safety Initiative, June 2026.
[11] Cloud Security Alliance. “AI Controls Matrix (AICM) v1.1.” Cloud Security Alliance, 2025.
[12] Cloud Security Alliance. “MAESTRO: Agentic AI Threat Modeling Framework.” CSA Lab Space, 2025.

On October 16, 2026, China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) issued Announcement No. 48 of 2026. The announcement proposes adding 40 technologies to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export, 23 of them in artificial intelligence, and it imposes an interim pre-export registration requirement that is already in effect [1][2]. China’s catalogue has touched AI before: the 2020 revision added personalized recommendation and AI interaction interface technology [6]. Unlike those 2020 additions, the draft reaches frontier model weights, agent architectures, and AI-enabled offensive cyber capability, with explicit technical thresholds for each [1].
The announcement contains two instruments with different legal status. The catalogue additions are a draft open for comment until November 15, 2026, while the registration requirement applies now, including to exports that have started but are not yet complete [1][2]. Within the draft, model weights are restricted at frontier scale. Weights, key checkpoints, source code, architecture, and training and inference optimization know-how are restricted if a model meets any one of three tests: at least 10^26 FLOPs of training compute, at least 2 trillion parameters, or a global top-10 position on public evaluation rankings, global call volume, or comparable measures at the time of export [1][3]. Agents are controlled independently of the model. Planning, multi-agent coordination, tool use, and game-theoretic decision technologies are restricted above set benchmarks, and high-performance agents built for critical infrastructure, defense, or core government use are prohibited outright [1].
The line between service access and custody determines most enterprise exposure. MOFCOM says API, app, web, SaaS, and lightweight on-device use do not count as exporting a large model. Deploying a restricted model locally outside China does count, though automatic licensing may apply on a Chinese company’s own overseas cloud [2]. Multinationals also face exposure through licensing deals and changes of ownership or control, not only through product exports, and analysts read the registration form as potentially capturing intra-group code sharing as well [2][3][4]. Any transfer of ownership, licensing for overseas use, or shift of control to a foreign entity can trigger registration [2][4].
Background
China regulates outbound technology transfer under two overlapping regimes. The first is the technology-trade regime under the Foreign Trade Law and the Regulations on Technology Import and Export Administration, which governs the catalogue being revised here. The second is the dual-use export-control regime under the 2020 Export Control Law [5]. MOFCOM’s spokesperson described the revision as routine and grounded in Article 20 of the Foreign Trade Law. The spokesperson stressed that it “does not target any specific country, region, or entity” and that the aim is to prevent uncontrolled diffusion while protecting legitimate cooperation [2]. The catalogue has been revised several times since 2001. The August 2020 revision, which added recommendation-algorithm technology, coincided with the proposed sale of TikTok to a U.S. buyer and was reported as likely to complicate that deal [3][6].
Across all three sectors, Announcement No. 48 proposes 14 prohibited and 26 restricted items: 23 in AI, 5 in biomedicine, and 12 in photovoltaics [2]. In China’s technology-trade framework, prohibited technologies may not be exported at all, while restricted technologies require a license from commerce and science authorities. ChinaTalk notes that licensing is administered by provincial authorities, although central authorities have intervened in prominent cases [3]. The official annex groups the AI items into large models, agents, compute clusters, chip design, and information-processing technologies. It also excludes from management any technology that has already entered the public domain through open-source release or academic publication [1].
The interim registration requirement is the part that applies today. From the announcement date until the revised catalogue takes effect, exporters must register through MOFCOM’s unified business platform before exporting any listed technology. Registration covers four triggers: transfer of technology ownership abroad, licensing of domestic technology for overseas use, a change in ownership or control that makes a foreign entity the owner or controller, and other cases MOFCOM designates [2][4]. Exporters must decide for themselves whether a technology falls within scope. The registration form asks for recipient details, destination, technology description, end use, and estimated value [2][4].
The timing also matters for enterprises that already track U.S. controls. CSA’s prior research documented the first U.S. use of export-control authority to suspend a broadly deployed commercial frontier model [9]. Announcement No. 48 means frontier AI supply chains now face formal outbound controls from both of the largest AI-producing jurisdictions. ChinaTalk observes that the 10^26 FLOP threshold mirrors the figure used in the 2023 U.S. executive order and the since-rescinded 2025 U.S. AI Diffusion rule. The authors also estimate that no released Chinese model currently exceeds it [3].
Security Analysis
What the AI Annex Actually Controls
The annex is granular, and its structure matters for scoping. The table below summarizes the AI items drawn from the official draft annex [1], with interpretive notes from published analyses [3][4].
Three features of this structure deserve attention from security and compliance teams. First, the “global leading” test is dynamic. A model that falls below the compute and parameter thresholds can still become restricted if its public evaluation rank, global call volume, or similar measures place it in the top 10 when the export occurs [1]. ChinaTalk calls this criterion “by far the most up-for-interpretation,” noting that the rule names no ranking body [3], and it means the compliance status of a given model version can change after deployment. Second, the agent items are defined by system behavior rather than by the underlying model. An orchestration framework that integrates hundreds of tools could meet the tool-use threshold even when it runs on a model well below the frontier thresholds, an issue Ray Sun identifies as unresolved [5]. Third, the cyber items carry direct security consequences: Chinese-origin AI red-teaming, vulnerability-discovery, and detection tools that meet the thresholds would require a license to leave China, and offensive code-generation capability could not be exported at all.
Deployment Models and Where the Line Falls
MOFCOM’s spokesperson framed the central test as whether restricted technology moves from inside China to overseas [2]. That framing produces a clear distinction between consuming a model as a service and taking custody of it, as summarized below.
For enterprises, the practical consequence is that the deployment model the draft captures, local self-hosting, is also the one often chosen for data-protection reasons. Organizations that chose to self-host a Chinese frontier model in their own environment, rather than call a Chinese-hosted API, did so to keep sensitive data inside their own boundary. MOFCOM places local deployment outside China within export management, which means those self-hosting arrangements require the Chinese supplier to hold a license [2]. ChinaTalk reads this as also covering on-premises licensing deals and managed deployments in which a vendor runs an agent’s reasoning loop inside a customer environment [3]. Because licenses can be revoked or conditioned, ChinaTalk suggests this may lead some non-Chinese users to reconsider such dependencies [3]. The registration requirement already covers exports in progress, so ongoing weight-delivery or model-update arrangements may be affected now rather than after the catalogue is finalized [2].
The treatment of open weights depends on whether a model is already public. Weights that are already public are outside the controls [1]. Open-sourcing a new restricted model, however, falls under automatic licensing that still requires reporting [2]. Commentators note that “open source” is not defined, and that it is unclear how restricted-use licenses would be treated [3]. Organizations that depend on successive open-weight releases from Chinese labs should therefore treat future release cadence, not just current availability, as a variable outside their control.
Exposure Through Corporate Structure
The exposure most likely to surprise multinationals sits in their own organizational charts. Registration is triggered by licensing technology for overseas use and by changes of ownership or control, not only by sales to third parties [2][4]. A multinational with China-based R&D teams building agent frameworks, vulnerability-discovery tooling, or fine-tuned models may therefore need to register before sharing that work with affiliates outside China. ChinaTalk reads the registration form’s field on exports made outside formal contracts as potentially capturing intra-group code sharing and open-sourcing [3]. This reading is an inference from the form rather than an official statement, but it is a reasonable basis for conservative scoping.
The data-based items add a second pathway. A model fine-tuned in China on operational data that qualifies as “important data” under the Data Security Law would be restricted, unless the de minimis carve-out applies. A model trained on “core data” would be prohibited [1]. Organizations that classified China-resident data under the Data Security Law for cross-border data transfer purposes may not have applied the same classification to training and fine-tuning datasets, since those obligations previously governed data transfer rather than model transfer.
Finally, recent precedent suggests that redomiciling does not remove Chinese jurisdiction. In January 2026, MOFCOM announced an assessment of Meta’s acquisition of Manus, a Singapore-registered AI agent company whose products were developed in China. The assessment examined whether the relocation of staff and technology required export authorization [7]. Announcement No. 48 now gives that line of scrutiny explicit, agent-specific thresholds, which suggests M&A due diligence on AI targets with China-origin development history should include an export-control workstream.
Recommendations
Immediate Actions
Organizations should first inventory every Chinese-origin model, agent framework, and AI security tool in use and record how each is consumed: as an API or SaaS service, as a lightweight on-device component, or as locally deployed weights or code. The local-deployment category is the priority, because it is the one the draft places within export management [2]. For each locally deployed asset, teams should ask the supplier in writing whether it has registered the export under Announcement No. 48 and whether it expects to need a license once the catalogue is final.
Legal and engineering teams should jointly review technology flows out of China-based subsidiaries, joint ventures, and R&D centers since October 16. The goal is to identify transfers that may already require registration, including code repositories, model checkpoints, and agent frameworks shared with overseas affiliates [2][4]. Organizations with a material interest in the final scope should prepare comments before the November 15, 2026 deadline, through the email, fax, or postal channels published in the announcement [1][4].
Short-Term Mitigations
Over the next one to two quarters, organizations should treat restricted-category Chinese models as regulated dependencies with documented fallbacks. Vendor contracts for locally deployed models should allocate responsibility for Chinese export registration and licensing, specify notice obligations if a license is denied, conditioned, or revoked, and address whether updates and new checkpoints are covered by the same authorization. Because the “global leading” test depends on rankings at the time of export [1], teams should not assume that a model version cleared today will remain uncontrolled for later updates.
Security teams that rely on AI-assisted vulnerability discovery or deepfake detection tools developed in China should map those tools against the restricted thresholds and identify alternatives. A licensing interruption to a detection capability is a security-control gap, not only a procurement issue. Data governance teams should also extend Data Security Law classification work to cover training and fine-tuning datasets held in China, so that “important data” and “core data” exposure is known before models trained on them are shared abroad [1].
Strategic Considerations
Announcement No. 48, if finalized substantially as drafted, would mean that frontier AI is treated as controlled technology by both the United States and China, with each regime drawing its lines differently. Recent U.S. measures have emphasized compute and, in the Fable 5 case, access to a deployed model, although the since-rescinded 2025 AI Diffusion rule also reached model weights [3]. The Chinese draft centers on custody of weights, know-how, and agent architectures. Enterprise AI governance programs should model export-control disruption from either jurisdiction as a standing risk scenario and design architectures that can swap models without rebuilding agent workflows.
Organizations should also recognize that the draft treats agents as a distinct regulatory object. Defining controls by planning depth, concurrency, and tool count means that internal agent platforms, and not only foundation models, may be subject to cross-border technology rules. Agent inventories should record these characteristics alongside traditional security attributes. Finally, because the final catalogue may narrow, broaden, or shift after consultation [3], and because ChinaTalk notes the comment window closes shortly before an expected leaders’ meeting at APEC [3], a timing that could bear on the final scope, this analysis should be revisited once MOFCOM publishes the final text.
CSA Resource Alignment
CSA’s most directly relevant prior work is Frontier AI Export Controls: Enterprise Governance After Fable 5 [8]. That note argues for treating frontier model access as a contingent operational dependency that belongs in vendor management and business continuity planning. Announcement No. 48 extends that argument to a second jurisdiction and to a different control point. The U.S. action examined in that note interrupted service access, while the Chinese draft leaves service access untouched and instead governs weight custody and local deployment. Enterprises that built continuity plans around the U.S. scenario should check whether those plans also cover a supplier-side license failure for self-hosted models.
AI Model Export Controls: The Fable 5 Precedent [9] documented how a single regulatory directive can remove a widely deployed model with little notice. Its recommendation for multi-model fallback strategies applies directly to organizations that depend on Chinese frontier or open-weight models, particularly given the dynamic “global leading” threshold described above. Sovereign AI Access Controls and Enterprise Concentration Risk [10] provides the broader framing. It treats national control over AI capability as a source of concentration risk, and the Chinese draft is a concrete instance of that risk materializing on the supply side.
For control implementation, the AI Controls Matrix (AICM) v1.1 [11] provides the relevant control objectives in its supply chain management, transparency and accountability, and governance, risk and compliance domains, including supplier inventory, third-party assessment, and regulatory change management. For agent-specific exposure, MAESTRO [12] offers a layered threat model that can help teams document the agent capabilities, such as tool integration and multi-agent coordination, that now carry export-control significance.
References
[1] Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology of the PRC. “Announcement No. 48 of 2026 on Public Consultation on Revising the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export and Interim Registration of Related Technology Exports (商务部 科技部公告2026年第48号), with Annex 1 (Draft Scope of AI, Biomedicine, and Photovoltaic Technologies).” MOFCOM, October 16, 2026.
[2] Ministry of Commerce of the PRC. “MOFCOM Spokesperson Answers Questions on Revising the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export (商务部新闻发言人就修订《中国禁止出口限制出口技术目录》答记者问).” MOFCOM, October 16, 2026.
[3] Ennis, Q., Zhang, I., Ottinger, L., and Zakaria, A. “MOFCOM’s New Rules and the Future of Chinese AI.” ChinaTalk, October 21, 2026.
[4] Geopolitechs. “China Imposes Temporary Export Registration Requirements for AI, Biotech and Solar Technologies, Seeks Public Comment on Proposed Export Restrictions.” Geopolitechs, October 16, 2026.
[5] Sun, R. “China’s AI Export Control Announcement Raises More Questions Than It Answers.” Ctrl+AI+Reg, October 19, 2026.
[6] Center for Security and Emerging Technology (translation). “Revisions to the Content of the Catalog of Prohibited or Restricted Technology Exports.” CSET, Georgetown University, September 2, 2020.
[7] South China Morning Post. “China to Probe Meta’s Purchase of Manus Regarding Export Control and Tech Exports.” SCMP, January 2026.
[8] Cloud Security Alliance. “Frontier AI Export Controls: Enterprise Governance After Fable 5.” CSA AI Safety Initiative, June 2026.
[9] Cloud Security Alliance. “AI Model Export Controls: The Fable 5 Precedent.” CSA AI Safety Initiative, June 2026.
[10] Cloud Security Alliance. “Sovereign AI Access Controls and Enterprise Concentration Risk.” CSA AI Safety Initiative, June 2026.
[11] Cloud Security Alliance. “AI Controls Matrix (AICM) v1.1.” Cloud Security Alliance, 2025.
[12] Cloud Security Alliance. “MAESTRO: Agentic AI Threat Modeling Framework.” CSA Lab Space, 2025.

articles.title: Could data center backlash flip Florida?
articles.body:
Patti Zirhut, a lifelong Republican, has been studying her ballot for weeks. Zirhut eagerly voted for President Donald Trump in 2016, 2020, and 2024, but she isn’t toeing the party line this year. “My ballot is all mixed up,” she says. She’s voting for some Republicans, some independents, and even a few Democrats. Zirhut remains undecided on a few races, but of one thing she is absolutely certain: “I will not vote for Byron Donalds,” she tells me. “No way will I ever vote for him.”
Could data center backlash flip Florida?
Bipartisan outrage has been growing for months — but Republicans’ many advantages could still help them win.
Could data center backlash flip Florida?
Bipartisan outrage has been growing for months — but Republicans’ many advantages could still help them win.
Donalds, the Republican nominee in Florida’s gubernatorial election, has Trump’s endorsement, the party’s backing, and $148 million in campaign funds, much of it from the tech industry. It’s this latest point that particularly rankles Zirhut, an organizer with a group called No Data Center Hernando County, whose purpose is summed up in its name. Donalds has been a vocal supporter of the controversial developments — a fact that may now cost him votes, even among members of his own party.
I first met Zirhut in August at a small protest in the rural community of Spring Hill, Florida. Back then, Donalds was the front-runner in a crowded Republican primary, and Zirhut told me she wouldn’t vote for him if he won. Now Donalds is the nominee in a race that is much closer than anyone anticipated, and Zirhut is sticking to her word. “I’m disgusted with all these dirty politics,” she tells me. She’s thinking about voting for Donalds’ Democratic opponent, former Rep. David Jolly.
Jolly, a former Republican who left the party in 2018, is now hoping to win over newly disgruntled conservatives like Zirhut — and his stance on data centers may help him do it. In Florida, the opposition to data centers “is more intense among Republicans than it is among Democrats,” Jolly tells The Verge, “because it is a reflection of the outsized influence and control of Big Tech and Big Data in a world where people are worried about surveillance, whether it’s AI or development encroaching on their land and their freedom.”
When it comes to data centers, the differences between Donalds and Jolly couldn’t be more stark. Jolly has traveled to Virginia’s Loudoun County, also known as Data Center Alley, to “see what massive hyperscale data centers really do to a community.” Donalds has said he wants to “make Florida the financial capital of the world.” Jolly has promised to implement a one-year moratorium on data center developments. Donalds has said he wants to welcome the tech industry — including data center developers — to the Sunshine State. “There ain’t no bans coming,” Donalds said in August. “But it sounds good on TV, or it sounds good on social media.” Donalds has since moderated his stance on data centers, trying to appeal to the 68 percent of Floridians who say they oppose the developments in their communities.
“This is an opportunity you rarely see in politics for candidates to both lead and follow,” Jolly says. “If 70 percent of the state is saying ‘Don’t do it,’ the job is to listen to voters, not to tell voters they’re wrong. But there are policy reasons, as well, to lead in this moment.”
Jolly rattled off a litany of reasons to slow down, if not altogether halt, data center development in Florida: air and noise pollution; the public health effects on people who live near data centers’ on-site power plants; and environmental concerns including water use, an issue he acknowledged is partly mitigated by the move to closed-loop air cooling. He also pointed to the rapid development of AI technology, which is advancing so quickly that facilities built today “may well be functionally obsolete in the next 10 years.”
When it comes to data centers, the differences between Donalds and Jolly couldn’t be more stark.
Donalds is quick to point out that his running mate, state Sen. Bryan Ávila, sponsored a bill regulating new data center projects that requires them to pay their fair share for water and electricity. And he’s emphasized that these developments ultimately aren’t the governor’s purview. “When it comes to data centers and local control, local governments are going to have the final say,” Donalds recently told CBS News. “Governors don’t issue building permits; local governments do. So if a local community does not want a data center, then no data centers.” But Jolly has saddled his opponent with a nickname that sums up their differences on the issue: “Data Center Donalds.” Donalds’ campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
Raul Alfonso, the chair of Watchdogs of Fort Meade, a community group fighting a $2.6 billion hyperscale data center development in deep-red Polk County, said his group has reached out to candidates in the lead-up to the election. Earlier this year, Watchdogs of Fort Meade received what Alfonso describes as a “form letter” from both Donalds and from Ron DeSantis, Florida’s current Republican governor. “It was basically, ‘We have to trust that your local city commissioners and your local city representatives will do the right thing,’” he says. The group hasn’t heard back from Jolly — which doesn’t bother Alfonso much, given Jolly’s promised moratorium. James Fishback, the controversial Republican contender who ended up with 10 percent of the primary vote, was the first to respond. Bobby Williams, a Republican candidate who garnered just 4.1 percent of the vote, has attended several events. Angie Nixon, the Democrat running to unseat Sen. Ashley Moody, hosted a town hall in Fort Meade to discuss residents’ opposition to the data centers. For Alfonso, the difference comes down to a willingness to hear locals’ concerns. Nixon, a Democratic Socialist, has little in common with the far-right Fishback, but both have engaged with the locals fighting the Fort Meade data center in a way Donalds hasn’t.
“There are a lot of people that were deep-red individuals who voted party line all the way, who are looking at flopping over to somebody who will actually take the concerns of the citizens more seriously,” Alfonso says. Alfonso’s voting history skews conservative — he voted for Trump in 2016, 2020, and 2024 — but he was a registered independent until this year, when he switched his affiliation to Republican to vote for Williams in the primary.
Williams, a pastor who had not previously run for office, has since endorsed Jolly. “The Republican Party, they kind of selected their nominee. They had their guy from the get-go: Donalds,” Williams tells me. “Big corporations are obviously buying a lot of these seats. They’re buying the governor’s role.” For Williams, data center developers are the latest in a long list of outsiders that want to have their way with Florida.
If he wins, Jolly will be the first Democratic governor Florida has elected in 28 years. The polls are close. One recent survey conducted by the University of North Florida put Jolly just two points behind Donalds, within the 2.8 percent margin of error. Donalds has several advantages over Jolly, not least of which is money. Jolly has raised $22 million to Donalds’ $148 million. There’s also the fact that Florida, once a swing state, now has nearly 2 million more registered Republicans than Democrats, in part because of DeSantis’ response to the covid-19 pandemic. The fact that Republicans currently lead Democrats in early voting may suggest that the state is unlikely to flip. But some of those Republicans, including Zirhut, are wary of Donald’s support for — and from — the tech industry, and are voting accordingly. Donalds has received $5 million from Leading the Future, a pro-AI super PAC whose funders include executives of OpenAI, Palantir, and Andreessen Horowitz.
As vocal as data center opponents may be, these developments aren’t Florida voters’ main issue. Poll after poll has shown that in Florida and elsewhere, the cost of living is top of mind for voters of all political orientations. But Jolly says the mass opposition to data centers is a manifestation of voters’ broader concerns.
“It’s almost a physical metaphor for anxieties around, ‘What is the future of work? What’s the future of wages? What does this mean for security and privacy for myself and for my kids?’” Jolly says. The huge sums of money spent on the governor’s race, he adds, are a testament to economic inequality in a state with an ever-rising cost of living. “In a state like Florida with unlimited money, where people feel like they’ve lost their political and economic power and voice, the deepest-pocketed special interests — be it tech, data, utilities — are able to capture our politicians and decision-making.”

articles.title: Supermarket Freezers Across Europe Hit By Second Suspected Cyberattack
articles.body:
Supermarket Freezers Across Europe Hit By Second Suspected Cyberattack (theguardian.com) 67
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Guardian: Supermarket chains in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg have said the temperatures of their refrigerators and freezers in dozens of stores rose overnight, prompting fears of a cyber-attack similar to one that caused millions of euros of food losses in France. Sweden's Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet on Monday that six of its stores had been affected, while ICA said it was "aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems".
The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last month reported a cybersecurity incident to police in the Netherlands, said an "IT incident" had hit fridges and freezers in dozens of its supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg. A company spokesperson, Sarah De Meester, said the supermarket chain had established that temperatures in the cooling systems had increased, adding that the incident was being investigated. Belgium's Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of stores and supermarkets were affected, including five Spar outlets, multiple Shop & Go convenience stores attached to Q8 service stations, and a number of smaller Proxy Delhaize minimarkets. "We started mobilizing technicians at 1am," Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which specialises in refrigeration system installations, told the paper. "We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations from the grid."

articles.title: Egoless Mathematics in the AI Era
articles.body:
[This is a guest post by Karthik C. S., Amit Sahai, and Jie Xue. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]
This is a good time for mathematicians to think carefully about the purpose of their work. The development of artificial intelligence brings that question before us with unusual force. Much of the discussion concerns which tasks machines will perform and which abilities will remain distinctively human. But our response also depends on a prior question: what do we understand mathematical work to be, and what gives it its worth? If our answer has become inseparable from the production of results and the demonstration of individual ability, the present uncertainty may reveal a difficulty in our conception of the work itself.
There are broadly two perspectives on mathematics. According to one, we invent it as we construct it: we introduce concepts, choose axioms, and develop theories. According to the other, mathematics exists independently of these activities, and our task is to discover it. These perspectives need not disagree about every aspect of mathematical practice. We plainly develop formalism and arguments. The deeper question is whether the truths we come to understand owe their existence to these acts, or whether our constructions enable us to recognize something that does not depend on us.
While discovery of mathematical truth can sound passive, a paleontologist searching for fossils must decide where to excavate, develop techniques, and recognize the significance of incomplete remains. The fossils existed long before the investigation, but finding them may require extraordinary imagination. Their prior existence gives direction to the investigator’s activity. Similarly, a mathematical discovery may require the invention of an entire language and framework through which a previously unnoticed relationship becomes intelligible. The discovery may require great creativity, but that does not make the truth discovered a creation of the individual. We encounter this distinction whenever our constructions surprise us. A definition introduced for one purpose reveals an unexpected connection elsewhere. A conjecture that seemed to organize our examples admits a counterexample. Two theories developed through different questions turn out to express a common structure. In each case, our thought encounters something it did not freely determine. We can revise our definitions or abandon our conjecture, but we cannot make the original argument valid merely by wishing it so.
The Platonic perspective gives a natural account of this independence. On this view, there were infinitely many primes before anyone proved that fact. Mathematical truth neither waits for our recognition nor receives its authority from it. We may choose how to describe a structure, but we do not choose its properties in the same way. This perspective also changes the place of the mathematician. Our intelligence becomes a means through which an order independent of us can be understood. The significance of the work lies in its relation to that order.
The distinction between a correct derivation and an understanding of its significance is equally important. An axiomatic system permits indefinitely many deductions, but the ability to produce them does not by itself supply a worthy direction of inquiry. Mathematical statements may be formally correct without being enlightening. We can introduce countless definitions and prove countless statements about them. What makes one definition illuminating? Why does one theorem disclose something fundamental while another merely adds to the available material? These questions concern the relation of a particular investigation to the principles it brings into view. Mathematical taste has a place here, provided we understand it as more than individual preference. We value a theory when it reveals a unity among things previously understood separately, or enables us to recognize why a phenomenon occurs. Although mathematical truths may exist independently of us, their discovery can transform our understanding and enrich our experience of the world. The ability to carry out longer chains of reasoning does not by itself explain such understanding. Reasoning serves understanding by articulating relationships and making their justification explicit. However, the success of reasoning does not mean that all knowledge can be reduced to it. Nor does our ability to reason more extensively determine what is worth knowing or why we seek knowledge.
Mathematics is only one field of knowledge. Not everything can be understood mathematically, nor is mathematical achievement the ultimate purpose of intellectual life. Yet we increasingly measure intellectual life through publications, citations, awards, and other indicators of performance. While useful, these measures become problematic when they define the worth of the work itself. We begin to see mathematicians as collections of productive abilities, and mathematics as merely their output. From this perspective, anxiety about being replaced by AI is natural: a machine that performs these tasks better appears to threaten our worth. But the problem began before AI arrived. We had already come to understand ourselves in terms suited to machines. AI merely exposes the consequences of this view.
The response cannot simply be to seek refuge in distinctively human abilities such as creativity, intuition, or taste. If we value these abilities primarily because they give us an advantage over machines, we remain trapped in the same conception of intellectual worth. Why should the value of our pursuit depend on being better at it than someone or something else?
Mathematics offers an opportunity to reconsider this whole orientation. Its truths do not become more true through the distinction of the person who expresses them. In understanding a proof, we bring our thought into conformity with a relationship whose validity does not belong to us. The particular path by which we arrive may bear the marks of our individuality. What is understood is available beyond that individuality. We can allow this experience to loosen the belief that knowledge has its highest value as an achievement attributable to ourselves.
Egoless mathematics begins with taking that possibility seriously. Humility then reaches beyond modesty about our accomplishments or generosity in sharing credit. It concerns the place from which we pursue knowledge. We may seek truth to serve our existing purposes, or allow what we discover to change those purposes themselves. If we approach truth on the condition that its discovery must preserve our importance, we have already made it subordinate to ourselves. Accomplishing this reordering can be demanding, as intellectual sophistication can furnish elaborate defenses of the very attachments that prevent us from understanding. What matters is whether our abilities remain answerable to truth, including when it requires us to reconsider what we have been using those abilities for.
From this perspective, the possibility of mathematical discoveries through AI need not be a source of sadness about our purpose. A truth has become accessible; its worth is not diminished by the absence of our authorship. We need not immediately turn the event into a judgment about our relative importance. The search can continue without requiring every advance to vindicate the seeker. Indeed, the demand for such vindication has always burdened the pursuit, whether the competing claim came from another mathematician or from a machine.
The opportunity before us is therefore more substantial than a rearrangement of mathematical labor. It invites us to reconsider what gives an intellectual life its worth, and to let the pursuit of truth shape not only our work but also how we approach life.
This may sound like asking us all to become saints. Insofar as it asks us to grow in virtue and relinquish our attachment to our own importance, that impression is not far from the truth. But virtue is not something to cultivate for the admiration of others. It is necessary for genuine joy, even in our work. The satisfaction of solving a difficult problem or winning a prize can be fleeting when it rests on our standing relative to others. The joy of understanding is different. Something previously obscure becomes clear, and we recognize a beauty that does not diminish when someone else discovers it first. We can share this joy without depriving anyone of it. Growing in virtue allows us to experience it more fully, free from the need to establish our own importance.
This perspective may also help reconcile two positions within the mathematical community regarding AI. Some are comfortable with or even enthusiastic about using AI, but wish to develop appropriate processes and principles for its use. Others prefer not to use AI at all. Both positions have their merits. Egoless mathematics offers a way of reconciling them by introducing a higher consideration: both approaches can reflect the same underlying commitment to mathematical truth, regardless of how we choose to pursue it. Our aim here is not to settle particular questions of policy, but to develop a higher-level perspective that can guide our deliberations and ultimately our actions.
Seen in this light, we need not be afraid of what AI may achieve in mathematics. Mathematics was beautiful before any of us were born, and it will remain beautiful long after we are gone. Its worth does not depend on our accomplishments, nor does our joy in understanding it have to depend on being the ones who make the discoveries. Our purpose rests on our willingness to let truth govern what we seek and what we become.
We, the authors of this essay, are still far from having attained such egolessness. Nevertheless, we recognize it as an ideal toward which we wish to strive.
We conclude with a thought experiment. Ramanujan is reported to have said, “An equation has no meaning for me unless it expresses a thought of God” (Robert Kanigel, The Man Who Knew Infinity, 1992). If he were alive today, witnessing the advances of AI in mathematics, would he be perturbed by what they might mean for his purpose as a mathematician?

articles.title: Egoless Mathematics in the AI Era
articles.body:
[This is a guest post by Karthik C. S., Amit Sahai, and Jie Xue. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]
This is a good time for mathematicians to think carefully about the purpose of their work. The development of artificial intelligence brings that question before us with unusual force. Much of the discussion concerns which tasks machines will perform and which abilities will remain distinctively human. But our response also depends on a prior question: what do we understand mathematical work to be, and what gives it its worth? If our answer has become inseparable from the production of results and the demonstration of individual ability, the present uncertainty may reveal a difficulty in our conception of the work itself.
There are broadly two perspectives on mathematics. According to one, we invent it as we construct it: we introduce concepts, choose axioms, and develop theories. According to the other, mathematics exists independently of these activities, and our task is to discover it. These perspectives need not disagree about every aspect of mathematical practice. We plainly develop formalism and arguments. The deeper question is whether the truths we come to understand owe their existence to these acts, or whether our constructions enable us to recognize something that does not depend on us.
While discovery of mathematical truth can sound passive, a paleontologist searching for fossils must decide where to excavate, develop techniques, and recognize the significance of incomplete remains. The fossils existed long before the investigation, but finding them may require extraordinary imagination. Their prior existence gives direction to the investigator’s activity. Similarly, a mathematical discovery may require the invention of an entire language and framework through which a previously unnoticed relationship becomes intelligible. The discovery may require great creativity, but that does not make the truth discovered a creation of the individual. We encounter this distinction whenever our constructions surprise us. A definition introduced for one purpose reveals an unexpected connection elsewhere. A conjecture that seemed to organize our examples admits a counterexample. Two theories developed through different questions turn out to express a common structure. In each case, our thought encounters something it did not freely determine. We can revise our definitions or abandon our conjecture, but we cannot make the original argument valid merely by wishing it so.
The Platonic perspective gives a natural account of this independence. On this view, there were infinitely many primes before anyone proved that fact. Mathematical truth neither waits for our recognition nor receives its authority from it. We may choose how to describe a structure, but we do not choose its properties in the same way. This perspective also changes the place of the mathematician. Our intelligence becomes a means through which an order independent of us can be understood. The significance of the work lies in its relation to that order.
The distinction between a correct derivation and an understanding of its significance is equally important. An axiomatic system permits indefinitely many deductions, but the ability to produce them does not by itself supply a worthy direction of inquiry. Mathematical statements may be formally correct without being enlightening. We can introduce countless definitions and prove countless statements about them. What makes one definition illuminating? Why does one theorem disclose something fundamental while another merely adds to the available material? These questions concern the relation of a particular investigation to the principles it brings into view. Mathematical taste has a place here, provided we understand it as more than individual preference. We value a theory when it reveals a unity among things previously understood separately, or enables us to recognize why a phenomenon occurs. Although mathematical truths may exist independently of us, their discovery can transform our understanding and enrich our experience of the world. The ability to carry out longer chains of reasoning does not by itself explain such understanding. Reasoning serves understanding by articulating relationships and making their justification explicit. However, the success of reasoning does not mean that all knowledge can be reduced to it. Nor does our ability to reason more extensively determine what is worth knowing or why we seek knowledge.
Mathematics is only one field of knowledge. Not everything can be understood mathematically, nor is mathematical achievement the ultimate purpose of intellectual life. Yet we increasingly measure intellectual life through publications, citations, awards, and other indicators of performance. While useful, these measures become problematic when they define the worth of the work itself. We begin to see mathematicians as collections of productive abilities, and mathematics as merely their output. From this perspective, anxiety about being replaced by AI is natural: a machine that performs these tasks better appears to threaten our worth. But the problem began before AI arrived. We had already come to understand ourselves in terms suited to machines. AI merely exposes the consequences of this view.
The response cannot simply be to seek refuge in distinctively human abilities such as creativity, intuition, or taste. If we value these abilities primarily because they give us an advantage over machines, we remain trapped in the same conception of intellectual worth. Why should the value of our pursuit depend on being better at it than someone or something else?
Mathematics offers an opportunity to reconsider this whole orientation. Its truths do not become more true through the distinction of the person who expresses them. In understanding a proof, we bring our thought into conformity with a relationship whose validity does not belong to us. The particular path by which we arrive may bear the marks of our individuality. What is understood is available beyond that individuality. We can allow this experience to loosen the belief that knowledge has its highest value as an achievement attributable to ourselves.
Egoless mathematics begins with taking that possibility seriously. Humility then reaches beyond modesty about our accomplishments or generosity in sharing credit. It concerns the place from which we pursue knowledge. We may seek truth to serve our existing purposes, or allow what we discover to change those purposes themselves. If we approach truth on the condition that its discovery must preserve our importance, we have already made it subordinate to ourselves. Accomplishing this reordering can be demanding, as intellectual sophistication can furnish elaborate defenses of the very attachments that prevent us from understanding. What matters is whether our abilities remain answerable to truth, including when it requires us to reconsider what we have been using those abilities for.
From this perspective, the possibility of mathematical discoveries through AI need not be a source of sadness about our purpose. A truth has become accessible; its worth is not diminished by the absence of our authorship. We need not immediately turn the event into a judgment about our relative importance. The search can continue without requiring every advance to vindicate the seeker. Indeed, the demand for such vindication has always burdened the pursuit, whether the competing claim came from another mathematician or from a machine.
The opportunity before us is therefore more substantial than a rearrangement of mathematical labor. It invites us to reconsider what gives an intellectual life its worth, and to let the pursuit of truth shape not only our work but also how we approach life.
This may sound like asking us all to become saints. Insofar as it asks us to grow in virtue and relinquish our attachment to our own importance, that impression is not far from the truth. But virtue is not something to cultivate for the admiration of others. It is necessary for genuine joy, even in our work. The satisfaction of solving a difficult problem or winning a prize can be fleeting when it rests on our standing relative to others. The joy of understanding is different. Something previously obscure becomes clear, and we recognize a beauty that does not diminish when someone else discovers it first. We can share this joy without depriving anyone of it. Growing in virtue allows us to experience it more fully, free from the need to establish our own importance.
This perspective may also help reconcile two positions within the mathematical community regarding AI. Some are comfortable with or even enthusiastic about using AI, but wish to develop appropriate processes and principles for its use. Others prefer not to use AI at all. Both positions have their merits. Egoless mathematics offers a way of reconciling them by introducing a higher consideration: both approaches can reflect the same underlying commitment to mathematical truth, regardless of how we choose to pursue it. Our aim here is not to settle particular questions of policy, but to develop a higher-level perspective that can guide our deliberations and ultimately our actions.
Seen in this light, we need not be afraid of what AI may achieve in mathematics. Mathematics was beautiful before any of us were born, and it will remain beautiful long after we are gone. Its worth does not depend on our accomplishments, nor does our joy in understanding it have to depend on being the ones who make the discoveries. Our purpose rests on our willingness to let truth govern what we seek and what we become.
We, the authors of this essay, are still far from having attained such egolessness. Nevertheless, we recognize it as an ideal toward which we wish to strive.
We conclude with a thought experiment. Ramanujan is reported to have said, “An equation has no meaning for me unless it expresses a thought of God” (Robert Kanigel, The Man Who Knew Infinity, 1992).
