Together they run around the building, from the Große Johannisstraße side, along the Rathausmarkt, to the Alter Wall side.
The Hanseatic League, or simply the Hanse, was a network of merchant towns that worked together to protect their trade. From the 13th to the 17th century it connected around 200 towns, from the Netherlands to the Baltic, with Lübeck as its leading city. The Hanse is so interesting that it would need its own article, but you can still see its traces in Hamburg today. The city's official name is the Free and Hanseatic City of Hamburg, and that's why Hamburg's number plates start with HH, for Hansestadt Hamburg.
Two of the coats of arms are bigger than the others: Lübeck on the left side of the front and Bremen on the right. They sit below the two most important busts, the president of the city parliament and the mayor, and it's probably no accident. Lübeck was the leading city of the Hanse, and when the league slowly faded away, Lübeck, Bremen and Hamburg were the last three cities that kept its name. Like Hamburg, they still call themselves Hanseatic cities, and their number plates still start with HL and HB.
Not every city on the façade was a full member. Amsterdam and Utrecht, for example, were trading partners rather than members. Florence is far from the North Sea, but its bankers, like the Medici, had offices across Europe, including in Bruges, one of the Hanse's main trading posts. A few of the coats of arms are not fully confirmed, Florence among them.
Here are all 28, grouped by where the cities are:
- The German Baltic coast: Lübeck, Wismar, Rostock and Stralsund
- Lower Saxony and Bremen: Bremen, Lüneburg, Hannover, Braunschweig, Goslar and Osnabrück
- Saxony-Anhalt and Berlin: Salzwedel, Stendal, Magdeburg and Berlin
- Westphalia and the Rhineland: Münster, Soest, Cologne and Aachen
- The Netherlands: Kampen, Stavoren, Amsterdam and Utrecht
- Around the Baltic Sea: Danzig (Gdańsk, Poland), Toruń (Poland), Königsberg (Kaliningrad, Russia), Riga (Latvia) and Tallinn (Estonia)
- Italy: Florence
The senators' families
Below the balcony that runs under the emperors, above the arched ground-floor windows, there is another set of coats of arms carved into the stone. These belong to Hamburg's own families. Until 1919, Hamburg was run by a Senate made up of men from the city's richest and most powerful families. They were chosen for life, not by a public vote, and 29 of these families have their coats of arms here.
You might not know their faces, but you probably know their names, because many of them live on in the city's streets, squares and parks:
- Mönckeberg and Petersen: the two mayors we already met among the busts.
- Versmann: Mayor Johannes Versmann, who led the talks that brought Hamburg into the German customs union in 1888. The Versmannstraße in HafenCity is named after him.
- Hertz: Senator Gustav Ferdinand Hertz was the father of the scientist Heinrich Hertz, after whom Hamburg's TV tower, the Heinrich-Hertz-Turm, is named.
- Hachmann: Mayor Gerhard Hachmann, after whom the Hachmannplatz next to the main station is named.
- Burchard: Mayor Johann Heinrich Burchard, after whom the Burchardplatz next to the Chilehaus is named.
- Lappenberg: Johann Martin Lappenberg, who looked after the city's old records and wrote its history. The Lappenbergsallee in Eimsbüttel is named after him.
- Hayn: Mayor Max Theodor Hayn, whose summer garden is today's Hayns Park in Eppendorf, where about 130 Alster swans spend the winter.
- Gossler: A family of bankers connected to the Berenberg bank, one of the oldest banks in the world. Goßlers Park in Blankenese was once the family's land.
- Amsinck and Sillem: Two trading families from the Netherlands, remembered in the Amsinckstraße and the Sillemstraße.
The others are the Abendroth, Bartels, Chapeaurouge, Geffcken, Kähler, Kunhardt, Lehmann, Merck, Möring, Moller, O'Swald, Roosen, Roscher, Schemmann, Schröder, Stahmer and Stammann families.
Hayns Park is one of my favourite parks for a walk on a nice day. I usually go there after stopping by the French café Éclair au Café. I had always wondered where the park's name came from, and now I know.
The saints on the gables
Higher than anything else except the tower, nine saints stand on top of the large roof gables. Two of them hold the front corners facing the Rathausmarkt, St. Michael on the Große Johannisstraße side and St. Catherine on the Alter Wall side, and the others are spread around the sides and the courtyard. They are also the hardest figures on the building to see. From the ground they are just small shapes against the sky, and only at 8x zoom do they turn into figures with faces and the objects they hold.
Hamburg had been Protestant for more than 350 years when the Rathaus was built, so the saints aren't there to be prayed to. They stand for places. For centuries the city was divided into parishes, areas that each belonged to one church, and these parishes were also the basis of its politics: citizens met, voted and paid their taxes by parish. So the nine saints are really a map of old Hamburg.
Five of them stand for the city's five main churches, which you can still visit today: St. Peter for St. Petri, Hamburg's oldest parish church; St. Nicholas for St. Nikolai, the church of the merchants and sailors, whose ruined tower is now a memorial to the victims of war; St. Catherine for St. Katharinen by the harbour; St. James for St. Jacobi; and St. Michael for St. Michaelis, the "Michel", Hamburg's best-known church.
The one that surprised me most was St. Michael. I know the Michel well: I've passed it many times and even lived close by for more than a year. But I had never imagined the saint behind the name, an archangel with big wings.
Two more stand for the old suburbs outside the city walls, St. Pauli and St. Georg. Both are still districts today, and it's interesting how far they have moved from the saints who gave them their names. St. Pauli, named after the apostle Paul, is known for the Reeperbahn and its nightlife, and St. Georg, named after the knight who killed the dragon, is known as the heart of Hamburg's gay scene.
The last two stand for monasteries that are long gone: St. Mary Magdalene for the monastery that stood where the stock exchange is today, and St. John for the St. Johannis monastery near today's Rathaus, which still gives its name to the Große Johannisstraße.
The Orators and Justitia
The Rathaus is home to two different bodies: the Bürgerschaft, the city parliament, and the Senate, the city government. The parliament sits in the wing on the Große Johannisstraße side, and the Senate in the wing on the Alter Wall side. The figures on the two side façades show what each of them is about.
On the parliament side stand two orators, both made by the sculptor Friedrich Offermann. One is a young man in a Roman robe with the words "Plus ultra", meaning "More beyond". He stands for progress. The other is an old man with a book and a document and the words "Parta tueri", meaning "To protect what has been gained". He stands for conservatism. Together they show the two sides of every debate in a parliament: moving forward and keeping what already works.
On the Senate side sits Justitia, the figure of justice, also by Offermann. Today we would expect justice to sit with a court, not with the government. But until 1860, the Senate was not only Hamburg's government but also its highest court, so justice belonged right there.
The courtyard
Behind the Rathaus is a courtyard it shares with the stock exchange, open to everyone from the Große Johannisstraße and the Alter Wall. It's much quieter than the Rathausmarkt, and the figures here tell an older story.
In niches about 12 metres up stand six men who shaped Hamburg long before it became a free city: three archbishops, who made it a centre of the church, and three rulers, who helped it become a trading town. Some of them we already met through the emperors on the front.
- Ansgar (archbishop 831–865): The first archbishop of Hamburg, appointed under Ludwig the Pious and sent to bring Christianity to Denmark and Sweden. He is often called the "Apostle of the North".
- Adaldag (archbishop 936–988): He led the archbishopric of Hamburg and Bremen for over 50 years, with the protection of Otto I.
- Adalbert (archbishop 1043–1072): Heinrich III's close adviser, under whom Hamburg-Bremen became one of the most powerful church seats in the empire.
- Henry the Lion (Duke of Saxony 1142–1180): Hamburg lay in his duchy, and he helped the trading towns of the north grow, above all Lübeck.
- Adolf III of Holstein (count 1164–1203): Around 1188 he started a new settlement for merchants next to the old town, and he is the count who got Barbarossa's promise of free trade on the Elbe.
- Adolf IV of Holstein (count 1224–1239): He ended Danish rule over Hamburg at the Battle of Bornhöved in 1227 and founded the Maria-Magdalenen monastery, the one remembered by St. Mary Magdalene on the gables. Later he became a monk himself.
Higher up, on four smaller gables, stand bronze shield-bearers, most of them in 16th-century armour, each holding a halberd and a shield. The round medallions below them carry four names: Bruegge, Nowgorod, London and Bergen. These are not member cities but the Hanse's four big trading posts abroad, called Kontore. In each of them, Hanseatic merchants had their own rules and trading rights, and everywhere except Bruges, their own walled quarter with warehouses and living quarters.
- Bruges: The trading centre of Flanders, where the merchants bought Flemish cloth and met traders from France, Spain and Italy.
- London: The Steelyard on the Thames, where they traded English wool and cloth, until Queen Elizabeth I closed it in 1598.
- Bergen: Bryggen, the harbour quarter at the centre of the trade in dried cod from northern Norway. Its wooden buildings still stand today.
- Novgorod: The Peterhof, where they bought furs and wax from Russia, until Ivan III of Moscow closed it in 1494.
In the left corner of the courtyard is a doorway that was meant for weddings. Above it sits Hymen, the god of marriage, with two torches, and on either side stand Adam with a dog and Eve with an apple and the snake. The figures were made in 1896 for a wedding office that was supposed to move into the Rathaus, but it never did, so the gate has never been used for a single wedding. Couples can marry in the Rathaus today, in the Phoenix Hall once a month, just not through this door.
In the right corner, above the kitchen window, sits a small carved kitchen boy, licking a spoon and holding a fork. It's one of the smallest details on the whole building and very easy to walk past.
In the middle of the courtyard stands the Hygieia fountain. It was built in 1895–1896 to remember the cholera epidemic of 1892, when more than 8.000 people in Hamburg died, mostly because of unclean drinking water. The first plan was to show Mercury, the god of trade, but after the epidemic the city chose Hygieia, the Greek goddess of health, instead.
Hygieia stands at the top, holding a small bowl of clean water, with a dragon at her feet that stands for the defeated cholera. Around the basin below sit six bronze figures showing how people use water, such as a man with a ship for shipping, a man with a fish for fishing and a woman with a jug for drinking water.
The best detail is hidden in the base. Between the figures hang bronze faces, each above an arched opening with a grille. These openings are the air intakes of the Rathaus ventilation system: air was drawn in over the water, which helped cool the building. So the fountain is not only a memorial, but also part of the building's air conditioning.
Standing in the courtyard, I always imagine it busy with senators and merchants, talking next to the fountain between a meeting in the Rathaus and a deal at the stock exchange. You have to admire how transparent the city is: the government and the stock exchange share one courtyard, so at least nobody can say they didn't know whose interests the decisions were made for.
Still more to see
Even after all this, there are many details I haven't covered, and I haven't even gone inside: the Rathaus has 647 rooms, and its halls and staircases are full of paintings and carvings that would need an article of their own.
I'm not sure there is another town hall in Germany that tells the story of its city in this much detail, from the emperors and saints to the fishermen, bakers and a kitchen boy licking a spoon. Almost every figure was chosen for a reason, and many of them point to something you can still see in Hamburg today.
While researching this article, one book kept coming up again and again: Das Hamburger Rathaus by Heinz-Jürgen Brandt, from 1957, which describes the building's history, architecture and decoration in detail. When I tried to buy it, I found out it's no longer in print, and in the end I ordered a second-hand copy for a much higher price, which I'm really looking forward to reading. There is a newer book, Das Hamburger Rathaus: 125 Jahre – 125 Geschichten by Rita Bake and Michael Zapf, published for the building's 125th birthday in 2022, but I'm not sure it covers the façade in as much detail as the old one.
This wasn't the first time I've had this problem. Whenever I want to go deeper into a part of Hamburg's history, the best books are often out of print, and second-hand shops are the only way to find them. When I first wanted to learn about the city's history, I couldn't even find a single book written in English.
I'm not sure the city is aware of this, but I believe that if these stories aren't told, they will slowly get lost. And if people don't know the stories behind the places they pass every day, they probably won't feel as connected to their city. This article is my small attempt to keep some of them alive.

articles.title: Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise
articles.body:
Hi HN, we're Aarush and Arnav from The Subvocal Company (YC F26) (
https://subvocal.company/
). We’re building smart glasses that let you talk to your computer without talking out loud. You can mouth words silently and discreetly and the glasses decode them to text at the speed of speech.
Here's a video of Dave from YC trying it out: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9QdX1eObVYI
(Edit: you don't actually have to move your lips or even open your mouth for this to work! Since the RF can see inside your mouth the system can be fine tuned on "internal speech". This isn't the automatic tongue movements that occur when "thinking" words to yourself, but more like mouthing with your lips closed. It's a bit weird to do, but with practice, we have been able to get it down pretty well.)
Arnav and I were studying CS at Georgia Tech at the beginning of the year, with no experience in silent speech or sensing. We were both AI-native builders and power users of Wispr Flow. What bugged us was not being able to use these tools in the library (or an office) or in public. At Stanford’s TreeHacks in February, we decided to build the most technically ridiculous thing we could think of. We’d read about AlterEgo, a silent speech system out of MIT’s Media Lab, and wanted to recreate it in 36 hours. We built a crude prototype, sticking EMG electrodes onto my face:
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1mwhv5HZMz3UTevdrgwS5O7g2jWV...
We got it to kind of work at a letter level in a very janky way. It wasn’t good enough to win the hackathon, but convinced us to go all in. The first time I typed a sentence without anyone noticing, I felt the magic of the technology.
We quickly realized EMG (reading muscle electrical signals) wouldn’t work:
- Signal changes due to sweat
- Electrical interference
- Placement variability
- Most importantly, no one wants to stick electrodes onto their face!!
So we switched to RF and built the glasses you see now. They emit radio waves, similar to Bluetooth, that pass through your face. As they cross the tongue, lips and soft palate, they’re modulated by silent mouthing. We train foundation models on this data to decode these perturbations to text.
Despite prior academic research, getting this to work was a huge engineering challenge. First we built an extremely low noise RF sensing stack. Then we had to place antennas so their fields overlapped maximally with the articulators. Our first attempt on glasses failed completely, so we reverted to old habits and taped antennas on our face:
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ks0dS0eZiTV9EqSFsyB_w5BBjpc...
Since taping antennas consistently in the same spot and angle was hard, we created this weird but effective head rig to hold them in place:
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1rhzNFpdDzr7oHk0isFY70dkoV4C...
This worked, but obviously wasn’t a product yet. So we worked deep in simulations to design glasses that could hold the antennas.
That evolved into our design now, with antennas embedded within the frames. Once we established there was a signal, the next hurdle was cross-user generalization. Everyone’s facial anatomy, and hence RF signal patterns, are vastly different. We tried algorithmic workarounds but realized the only lever was to massively scale pretraining data.
So that’s what we did. We set up booths in our office and paid people to read prompts wearing our glasses, to pretrain our models on. This produced a beautiful scaling curve, with errors falling quickly as we scaled our dataset and cross-user performance becoming genuinely compelling (as you see in the video above; Dave only had a short 20-sentence calibration).
We always heard about building things from first principles but never understood it before this. We tried tackling it top down but completely failed. Only when we broke each component (the antenna, electronics, ML) down to its fundamentals to understand and optimize it did we get it to work really well.
Over the next few months we’re continuing R&D to turn our prototype glasses into the slick product on our website and ship in Q1 2027. We’re also scaling up our dataset to improve performance on edge cases.
For anyone who loves voice dictation but hates using it around people, we’ve opened preorders for our first batch of 500 units, with a $200 discount off the final price. Allocation is running out quickly, so get yours at https://subvocal.co/preorder!

articles.title: Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia
articles.body:
When I saw Grokipedia’s articles about me, the memories came rushing back: my 19 years in minor league baseball, including that impressive season with the Montgomery Rebels when I hit 20 home runs. I was lean back then — 6 feet tall and 168 pounds — and earned a career batting average just under .300. I became a minor league coach and managed the Chicago White Sox for a short stint in 1970, which Grokipedia said “highlighted [my] readiness for higher-level responsibilities.”
I then attended Arizona State University, switched to a career in journalism, created the fact-checking site PolitiFact, won a Pulitzer Prize, and now teach journalism at Duke University.
Ah, the memories!…except that I never played minor league baseball, never managed the White Sox, and can only dream about being 6 feet tall. (I’m 5’8″.) Grokipedia, the AI-written encyclopedia of Elon Musk, has confused me with Marion Danne “Bill” Adair, who died in 2002.
That article and another one about “Bill Adair (journalist)” — which really is me — illustrate the many flaws of Grokipedia, which launched a year ago. The articles are littered with mistakes and superfluous details. They are terribly written and ridiculously long. If Grok, the AI engine that wrote this turgid prose, were a student in one of my writing courses, I would give it a D.
Still, the articles provide valuable lessons for Wikipedia editors who are debating how and when to use AI. Grokipedia adds new content and context that Wikipedia often lacks. It shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet and summarizing them in sweeping prose. It can also provide balance to articles that need it.
Grok can’t write worth a lick, but it shows how Wikipedia can take advantage of AI at a time when overworked editors are trying to keep the encyclopedia alive.
Musk launched Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he said was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet.
With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a new version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.”
When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had big aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video.
Maybe someday.
For now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia shows edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make.
Last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk.
Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites.
Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.)
By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder.
Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times.
Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models.
In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race.
Five other errors showed Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok said I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor.
The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too quickly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a big scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.”
I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop.
Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s important and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important.
The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.”
Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter.
Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia.
The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches.
Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”)
Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia.
Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version.
Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty.
Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR.
My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles.
After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities.
Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

articles.title: The U.S. Census Bureau and "Super Intelligence"
articles.body:
The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
2nd November 2026
I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies, a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis, and then to experiment with Claude’s new Code Interpreter. I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434, aka the asinine Super Intelligence one.
First, the updated chart
Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total—the surveyed group (a “panel”) cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks.
The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am.
I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version (GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau:
For comparison, here’s that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version):
In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered “yes” around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in “producing goods or services”.
Under the new “any business function” wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered “yes” around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%.
The data in the above chart comes from the “Employment size class” XLSX file, available from here. Here’s a copy of the file I used.
You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses—here’s my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF.
The changing language of the questions
As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine):
In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)
On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here’s the replacement:
In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)
No more “producing goods or services”—now it’s “in any of its business functions”! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable.
From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence
When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn’t find it. I found this instead:
In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.)
The BTOS about page explains what happened:
Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434.
The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording—the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday.
Is this going to affect the survey?
The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results.
The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn’t going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out “formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI”.
I can’t help but laugh at the absurdity of “SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service” though.
More recent articles

articles.title: Moving our warehouse off DuckDB
articles.body:
Why we're moving our warehouse off DuckDB
Contents
Five months ago, we rebuilt our warehouse on DuckDB instead of ClickHouse. We did it because a shared ClickHouse cluster couldn't handle hours-long modeling queries, and it lacked a cost-based query optimizer. DuckDB gave every customer their own instance, and tools like dbt could connect over Postgres. We're still fans.
But we underestimated how big and complex our customers' workloads would get. We didn't want them to have just a good experience, we wanted the best experience you can get when you pay someone else to run your warehouse. It should work at any scale, at a fair price.
So we spent the last three months re-architecting it, this time without DuckDB.
DuckDB is brilliant on one machine
We love DuckDB. It's probably the best single-node tool for analyzing heaps of data, and that node can be your laptop. It's robust and reliable. It almost always finishes your query, and if it runs out of memory, it spills to disk.
The same features that are great locally gave us problems in the cloud. Customers ran more complex queries than we expected, so we had to add huge instances. Adding disks was an option, but queries would have been too slow and expensive to be viable.
To run a single-node engine safely in the cloud, we have to size the worker before the query arrives. The ergonomics here are wonky. We couldn't find a good way to tell customers what resources their queries would need. Predicting CPU and memory for a specific query was even harder.
Users shouldn't have to worry about this. They should be able to run whatever they need to get their work done. Our job is to handle the rest and make it as predictable as possible.
We hit other bottlenecks too, like fetching lots of data from S3 without async fetching. DuckDB only added that recently.
DuckLake is built for compatibility, not scale
To use DuckDB as a fully-fledged data warehouse, we installed the DuckLake extension by default. It is a new lakehouse format from the same creators and follows the same principles as DuckDB: keep things simple and run on almost any setup. That works well up to a point, but at PostHog's scale, we needed something designed for distributed scale from the start.
DuckLake's catalog schema has to stay portable across many SQL databases, which limits engine-specific optimizations. At our scale, a single-table write could take more than three minutes because every commit re-read the statistics for the entire catalog.
We tuned DuckLake with table indexes and similar tweaks. But to keep offering DuckLake, we had to stay 100% compatible with its existing, "official" schema. This left us with fewer optimization options.
Another problem is that over 99% of the catalog's statistics rows belonged to tables that no longer existed. Cleaning them up made writes 30 to 50 times faster, but the rows kept growing back.
We also spent a lot of time on the number of connections DuckLake opens to metadata databases. That hurts on shared Postgres instances, where every connection has a real cost.
1 trillion rows was a challenge
DuckLake at PostHog didn't start small and ramp up. We fully committed and put all of PostHog in a DuckLake to dogfood as the first customer.
When we moved off it, it held about 2 PB: roughly 1 trillion rows and 15.3 million snapshots. It broke in lots of ways that were hard to fix within DuckLake's scope.
We'd rather have contributed to the existing community and helped it grow. But we couldn't land changes as fast as we needed, so we ended up carrying patches in a fork which defeats one of the main benefits of using DuckLake: the community.
Speaking Postgres is harder than it sounds
Offering direct Postgres connections over port 5432 sounds like a great idea. In practice, it was much harder to scale than HTTP.
Missing reconnects and managing TTLs and idle connections at scale is hard, and long-running connections are expensive. There's also very little tooling for load balancing pgwire compared with HTTP. Compare the ergonomics of an AWS NLB with an ALB and you'll see what we mean. HTTP headers also make routing in Kubernetes much more flexible.
There's also an endless list of Postgres clients, and each expects its own niche Postgres behavior. Customers kept asking us to fix their client or library. We spent a lot of time shipping many of those fixes, but coverage never got good enough. We'd rather spend our time building an excellent warehouse than chasing the long tail of Postgres compatibility.
We're rebuilding on Trino with HogLake
We've learned not to hype the tech behind a warehouse so much. What counts is the experience it gives you.
Still, we're happy to share what we're cooking next. We rebuilt everything around our own flavor of Trino and created our own open table format, HogLake. And yes, we're testing it at PostHog's petabyte scale first. We made it solid before handing it to design partners.
If your current warehouse is slow or expensive, let's talk, especially if you have a lot of data to query. We're always looking for design partners.
PostHog is your product's context layer. With a full suite of developer tools – AI observability, product analytics, session replay, feature flags, experiments, error tracking, logs, and more – PostHog ingests and stores all the data agents need to diagnose problems, uncover opportunities, and ship fixes. A data warehouse and CDP tie it all together, unifying that context into one source agents can read across. You can steer it all from Slack, the web app, the desktop (PostHog Desktop), or your own editor via the MCP.

articles.title: Apple reports fourth quarter results
articles.body:
PRESS RELEASE
                    
                    
                        November 2, 2026
                    
                    
                
Apple reports fourth quarter results
                
                
                    September quarter records for total company revenue, iPhone revenue, and EPS 
Services revenue reaches new all-time high
                
            
CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced financial results for its fiscal 2026 fourth quarter ended September 26, 2026. The Company posted quarterly revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent year over year. Company gross margin was 47.9 percent, including a favorable impact of approximately 1 percentage point from tariff refunds. Diluted earnings per share was $2.10, up 14 percent year over year, and included a favorable impact of $0.05 from tariff refunds.
“Today, Apple is proud to report a September quarter revenue record of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent from a year ago, with iPhone reaching a September quarter record and Services reaching an all-time high, capping off our best fiscal year ever,” said John Ternus, Apple’s CEO. “We’re closing the year with our most ambitious lineup yet. That includes the iPhone Duo, the most transformational iPhone since the original, alongside iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, our most powerful iPhones yet. We also just introduced a whole new generation of hardware for the home and brought Touch to Mac for the first time. Together with the all-new Siri AI, it’s an incredible lineup to carry us into the holiday season.”
“Apple delivered September quarter records for net income and EPS. Our record September quarter capped off a strong fiscal 2026, with all-time record revenue of $479 billion and double-digit EPS growth,” said Kevan Parekh, Apple’s CFO. “We generated $28 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter, allowing us to return $28 billion to shareholders. Thanks to our very high levels of customer satisfaction and loyalty, our installed base of active devices reached a new all-time high across all major product categories and geographic segments.”
Apple’s board of directors has declared a cash dividend of $0.27 per share of the Company’s common stock. The dividend is payable on November 16, 2026, to shareholders of record as of the close of business on November 12, 2026.
Apple will provide live streaming of its Q4 2026 financial results conference call beginning at 2:00 p.m. PT on November 2, 2026, at apple.com/investor/earnings-call. The webcast will be available for replay for approximately two weeks thereafter.

articles.title: Ballot Rejections Have Soared in Rural Counties as USPS Reduces Mail Service
articles.body:
Reporting Highlights
- Rural Cuts: Delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas, a ProPublica analysis found.
- Rejected Ballots: The rates of ballots rejected for arriving late this year doubled or tripled in areas affected by the cuts compared to the 2022 primary. That wasn’t the case elsewhere.
- Extraordinary Measures: Postal Service leaders say special procedures in place for the Nov. 3 election should prevent similar delays, but experts warn that mistakes are likely.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
In early August, election workers north of Spokane, Washington, went across the street to the post office to check for late mail-in ballots. It was three days after the primary and they were expecting no more than a few dozen.
Instead, their mailbox was brimming with envelopes — more than 500 of them, each a vote that wouldn’t count. The sight was “jarring,” said Auditor Lori Larsen, a Republican who oversees voting in Stevens County.
Across the region, other election officials were getting similar jolts. In the 11 predominately rural counties in eastern Washington, nearly 2,000 ballots came in late, compared to about 600 in 2022, the previous midterm primary.
In recent weeks, concerns about mail-in voting disruptions have focused almost entirely on President Donald Trump’s now-shelved plan to sharply restrict who can vote by mail.
But a ProPublica data analysis shows that delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas, not only in Washington, but across the country.
Over the past three years, as mail volume continued to plummet and annual deficits ballooned, the Postal Service started consolidating the processing of first-class mail at larger regional plants instead of at smaller hubs closer to local post offices. Then, in a little-noted switch that mostly took effect after the 2024 election, the agency cut the frequency of mail pickups in half at many post offices 50 miles or more from these processing plants, from twice daily to once.
The changes often added a day or more to delivery time and, most importantly for ballots, pushed back postmarking, which doesn’t happen until mail reaches the regional centers.
In this year’s primary, the effects of the cuts were clearest in five states that make detailed data on mail-in ballots available: Washington, California, Ohio, North Carolina and Oregon. All have or recently had grace periods allowing ballots to count if they come in after Election Day as long as they’re postmarked by the deadline.
Help Us Report on Key Election Issues
ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something?
In these states, the number of ballots rejected for arriving late soared in counties affected by the service changes compared to 2022, ProPublica’s analysis showed.
Rejection rates in counties where services were cut doubled or tripled from what they were four years ago, dwarfing any increases in counties where postal pickups remained as they were, our analysis showed. In urban Spokane, for example, the number of ballots rejected for being late actually dropped this year.
Across the five states, the delays have had the most substantial effect in areas that voted for Trump in 2024, ProPublica’s analysis shows. In Washington, Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, a Democrat, said he sees the service changes directed by Republican appointees leading the Postal Service as a way to undermine mail-in voting.
“I don’t think they realized how much it was going to affect their voter base,” he said, adding that Washington has “a lot of rural Republican voters.”
Rates of Rejection Due to Late Ballots Were Higher in Counties with Reduced Mail Service
Postal Service leaders say such delays are less likely in the Nov. 3 general election because of “extraordinary measures” the agency puts into place for these votes, when there’s typically far more turnout. They have circulated a memo to the nation’s more than 30,000 post offices saying that for the 10 days before the election, managers should separate completed ballots from other first-class mail and deliver those intended for local election offices the day they come in.
At an Oct. 15 news conference, Postal Service leaders emphasized the agency’s longstanding recommendation that voters mail ballots back at least a week before their states’ deadlines, while defending the agency’s ability to fast-track ballots through the system.
“We work to identify and address issues quickly,” said Amber McReynolds, chair of the Postal Service board of governors, “so ballots can continue to move swiftly from election offices to voters and from voters back to election offices.”
Election consultants, researchers and former Postal Service officials told ProPublica that the guidance for the upcoming vote gave more detailed directions on how to expedite ballots. They said they hoped the agency’s special measures would limit delays, but some said mistakes were likely.
“I don’t think we can say with any kind of conviction that there will be no ballots rejected,” said Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer of the National Association of Election Officials. “It isn’t a question of ‘if,’ but a question of ‘how many.'”
A pilot program instituting the delivery changes in 18 regions before the 2024 election ran into problems. An audit by the Postal Service’s inspector general found that agency staff in these areas sometimes didn’t handle ballots correctly, mainly because instructions weren’t clearly communicated. (A Postal Service spokesperson said “learnings from the pilot” have been applied as the program has expanded.)
After this year’s primary, reports by media outlets noted that mail-in ballot rejection rates were higher than in the past, but ProPublica’s analysis shows these increases were directly connected to Postal Service changes. Research published in September by the Brookings Institution also found this connection, projecting that if the pattern held in the general election, tens of thousands of mail-in ballots could be rejected.
At least seven closely contested congressional districts — including Washington’s 3rd, California’s 22nd and North Carolina’s 11th — are in areas that were affected by service changes in the primary, ProPublica found.
Elena Patel, who conducted the Brookings analysis, said service changes may still imperil mail-in votes in the general election.
“I think there remain risks to ballots,” she said, adding that the Postal Service’s plan for the general election “depends on flawless execution.”
Mail-in voting has become more popular over the last decade, with many states broadening access to it during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Nearly 1 in 3 Americans voted this way in 2022 and 2024. Trump himself frequently votes by mail, and in recent weeks has started to encourage his supporters to do so as well, though he has claimed without evidence that the process is rife with fraud.
The Postal Service has mostly ensured the timely delivery of hundreds of millions of ballots, even as mail volume overall has dropped 50% from its high in 2006.
When Louis DeJoy was appointed postmaster general in spring 2020, he inherited an $81 billion operating deficit and rapidly took steps such as eliminating overtime to reduce costs, under pressure from Trump and others in his administration. (DeJoy did not respond to questions from ProPublica.)
The NAACP sued that August, alleging the measures could affect mail-in votes in that year’s general election. Courts ordered DeJoy to reverse some of the cuts and the Postal Service agreed to implement special procedures to ensure ballots weren’t delayed. The Postal Service has continued following those procedures since.
Still, DeJoy went forward with a 10-year restructuring plan designed to save the agency billions. It ended evening pickups from some post offices, often in rural areas. Trucks serving these places travel long distances and at times were mostly empty. This part of the plan — called regional transportation optimization, or RTO — was projected to eventually save the Postal Service $4 billion a year.
The agency announced the national rollout of the RTO plan in 2024, but DeJoy agreed to pause it leading up to that year’s November election, leaving only about 4,000 ZIP codes in the pilot project affected by the service changes.
Mail Services Have Been Cut in 16,000 More ZIP Codes Since the 2024 Election
A pilot program that reduced mail pickups to save money was paused in the lead-up to the 2024 election. The rollout has since resumed, and the changes have been made in five times as many ZIP codes for the 2026 midterms.
In January 2025, the Postal Regulatory Commission, which oversees the Postal Service, warned that moving forward with the plan would be disruptive to rural communities and might not save as much money as expected. The Postal Service rolled out the reductions anyway, extending the changes to almost 20,000 ZIP codes to date. Officials said they expect the system to be fully implemented within two years.
This January, the agency put out a statement saying the transportation cuts would mean it took longer for mail, including ballots, to be postmarked and delivered. But the Postal Service didn’t specify which voters would be affected by the slowdowns and which wouldn’t.
Though the delay from RTO is often only a day, mail can be delayed longer if it’s deposited in a mailbox after the daily pickup time, or just before Sunday or a holiday.
A Postal Service spokesperson said the agency told election officials that RTO would change schedules and reemphasized the need for voters to get their ballots in the mail at least a week ahead of time. Election officials in Washington said the Postal Service wasn’t direct enough about the fact that the changes would lead to delays in delivering and postmarking ballots.
“What they said was, ‘We are going to change the way we do postmarks,'” said Hobbs, Washington’s secretary of state. “That was it.”
Patel, the Brookings analyst and a former Postal Regulatory Commission employee, said that more direct communication to voters could have helped change their behavior. “That’s the part that I think has not been super transparent about the whole process,” she said.
Many of the areas that saw a spike in late ballots were in Western states, which were the earliest and most enthusiastic adopters of expanded mail-in voting.
In 2004, Washington became the second state to start conducting all-mail elections, in which every eligible voter automatically receives a mail-in ballot. Most residents vote by putting their ballots in drop boxes. Still, in 2024, about 33% put them in the mail.
In the 30 mostly rural Washington counties most affected by RTO, the percentage of ballots postmarked late more than tripled compared to the 2022 primary, ProPublica found.
Has Mail Service Been Reduced in Your ZIP Code?
If the frequency of mail pickups has been reduced in your area, mail may take longer to send and receive, and the date on the postmark could be later than the day you dropped it off, which may matter for mail like ballots that is subject to a deadline.
In Garfield County, in southeastern Washington, 19 ballots — nearly 1 in 10 cast — had late postmarks this year. In 2022, only a single ballot was postmarked late. In Pend Oreille County, in northeast Washington along the Idaho panhandle, 6% of ballots were rejected for arriving late, compared to 1% in the 2022 primary.
“It was pretty awful telling people we couldn’t count their votes,” said Marianne Nichols, Pend Oreille’s longtime auditor. “They were quite upset because they felt like, ‘Why? This was in the mailbox on election day, the post office picked it up and had it.’ They felt like it should have counted.”
In Stevens County, the percentage of ballots rejected for having a late postmark jumped to 8%, from 1% in 2022.
Steve Hutkins, a retired professor who analyzes the effect of Postal Service changes on Savethepostoffice.com, also found that places in Washington with RTO had more ballot rejections during local elections earlier this year for school board and other measures. The patterns “set off the alarm bells,” he said.
Stuart Holmes, the state’s director of elections, said he reached out to Postal Service officials to find out what had happened, but got few answers and no specifics on delays related to RTO, which were a “total surprise,” he said.
Election officials in California and Oregon also reported thousands more ballots rejected for arriving late during their primaries. Counties affected by RTO, including Kern County, California, had substantially higher rates of ballots rejected for mail-related reasons, ProPublica found.
Kern County’s assistant registrar of voters, Laura Cantu, said election officials are urging rural voters to use drop boxes to cast their ballots in the general election.
The expansion of RTO had a similar effect in North Carolina and Ohio, where the rates of late ballots were about twice as high in counties affected by the restructuring as rates in counties that weren’t. Since 2022, these states have also eliminated grace periods in which ballots postmarked by Election Day could count even if they arrived later. Voters unused to the tighter deadlines also could have contributed to an increase in late ballots.
ProPublica didn’t find any association between RTO and higher rates of late ballots in Wisconsin, even though clerks reported delays involving mail-in ballots cast in its state election, held this spring. (Other Postal Service changes may have contributed to the delays.)
Wisconsin’s data does not distinguish ballots sent by mail from those cast in drop boxes or in person, making it impossible to definitively measure rejection rates just for ballots returned by mail. Election researchers said Wisconsin’s deadline for mail ballots, which must come into election offices by 8 p.m. on Election Day, also probably had an effect.
“If you know that you don’t have a grace period, it probably affects voter behavior,” said Patel, the Brookings researcher.
Recent Postal Service audits have found that RTO-related changes had saved the agency about $2.8 billion by the end of fiscal year 2025 — less money than expected — and are slowing down all first-class mail, not just ballots. Residents of rural areas are waiting longer for everything from prescriptions to bills, a report published in September by the Postal Service’s inspector general said.
A Postal Service spokesperson still defended the plan, both for financial reasons and to adjust to the changing marketplace. “These savings are both significant and necessary,” he said.
In the lead-up to Nov. 3, the agency’s plan is to route ballots meant for local election offices to a nearby postal facility or directly to their destination. They shouldn’t go to regional plants, which the Postal Service says should minimize delays.
Larsen, the Stevens County auditor, is encouraging Washington voters to deposit their ballots in drop boxes rather than relying on the mail. Since the primary, she’s increased the number of red, white and blue drop boxes that sit outside government buildings from seven to 12. Near each box, there’s a large sign encouraging people to take selfies when they vote and send the photos to Larsen.
In prior years, Larsen said, she avoided telling voters how or when to vote, concerned they might regret choices they made if critical information later emerged about the candidates. That’s no longer uppermost in her mind.
“Now we are more concerned that we get your ballot,” she said.
