articles.title: Anthropic releases amended IPO prospectus with third-quarter financials
articles.body:
Anthropic reported updated financials as part of an amended Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, giving investors a more comprehensive look into the state of its business.
The artificial intelligence company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic had a loss of $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025.
Anthropic unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week, bringing the company one step closer to a potentially historic initial public offering. The initial filing only included the Claude maker's financials through the first half of the year.
During its third quarter, Anthropic generated roughly $17 billion in revenue, up about 1,127% from the same period last year. Revenue growth slowed on a quarter-to-quarter basis, however. Third-quarter revenue increased around 47%, a steep drop from 144% growth in Q2 and 132% in Q1.
The company reported a net loss of $23.29 billion during its third quarter.
As the 5-year-old company prepares to kick off its roadshow, it will have to reckon with growing market jitters around the AI buildout. Wall Street has been worried that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds, and quarterly reports from Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon last week added fuel to those concerns.
The hyperscalers' aggressive AI spending is eating into their cash flows, causing some investors to worry that computing capacity may not come online quickly enough to meet Anthropic's demands. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX, but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible.
In the amended S-1, Anthropic said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."
Anthropic said its compute and infrastructure expenses increased by $14.4 billion for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up 329% compared with the same period last year.
"As our compute and infrastructure capacity grows, the associated compute and infrastructure expenses have increased," Anthropic said in the filing.

articles.title: Anthropic releases amended IPO prospectus with third-quarter financials
articles.body:
Anthropic reported updated financials as part of an amended Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, giving investors a more comprehensive look into the state of its business.
The artificial intelligence company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic had a loss of $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025.
Anthropic unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week, bringing the company one step closer to a potentially historic initial public offering. The initial filing only included the Claude maker's financials through the first half of the year.
During its third quarter, Anthropic generated roughly $17 billion in revenue, up about 1,127% from the same period last year. Revenue growth slowed on a quarter-to-quarter basis, however. Third-quarter revenue increased around 47%, a steep drop from 144% growth in Q2 and 132% in Q1.
The company reported a net loss of $23.29 billion during its third quarter.
As the 5-year-old company prepares to kick off its roadshow, it will have to reckon with growing market jitters around the AI buildout. Wall Street has been worried that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds, and quarterly reports from Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon last week added fuel to those concerns.
The hyperscalers' aggressive AI spending is eating into their cash flows, causing some investors to worry that computing capacity may not come online quickly enough to meet Anthropic's demands. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX, but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible.

articles.title: Vibe-Coding a Game in 2026: What AI Builds, What Breaks
articles.body:
Key takeaways
- In late October 2026 a well-known developer wrote that building games that play well is "shockingly easy now", and Roblox told shareholders that people had published over 70,000 games with its prompt-to-game tool.
- AI is strong at the first playable version: small browser games in three.js or Phaser, placeholder art and even code-generated music.
- It is still weak at the parts players and brands pay for: game logic that holds up over a long session, consistent art and animation, multiplayer, cheat-proof leaderboards, payments and performance on ordinary phones.
- Platform rules apply to AI games: Steam asks for an AI disclosure, Google Play requires in-app reporting for AI-generated content, and Apple rejects copycats and spam.
- A prototype you made yourself is a strong brief for a studio. Once a game carries prizes, personal data or payments, it needs engineering and testing.
The short answer: yes, in 2026 you can vibe-code a small, playable game in an evening by describing it to an AI model, and a prototype like that is now a perfectly sensible first step. What you can't skip is the work between "playable on my phone" and "live in front of customers": fixing logic bugs that only appear in long sessions, making the art consistent, testing on mid-range Android phones, checking scores and payments on a server, and meeting Steam, Google Play, App Store or Telegram rules. This guide covers what changed this autumn, what AI handles well, where it breaks, and how to decide between doing it yourself and hiring a studio.
Methodology: this is an editorial guide. Every quote, figure and platform rule below was checked against the linked source on November 2, 2026. Where a claim has only been reported by the press and not confirmed by the company, we say so.
What changed in October 2026
Three things happened within two weeks of each other.
- Developers said games got easy. On October 28, Simon Willison, co-creator of the Django web framework and a widely read writer on AI tools, called October 2026 "a new inflection point" for vibe coding computer games. "Building games that play well is shockingly easy now," he wrote. None of his four example games took more than four hours of his own work, "plus many more hours of Claude Code churning away by itself" (Simon Willison).
- Platforms reported a flood. PC Gamer reported that Roblox's shareholder letter says more than 500,000 users have tried Build, its prompt-to-game tool, and published over 70,000 games, and that more than 80% of the top 100 Roblox games used AI tools in the past month (PC Gamer). On itch.io, new game pages per day rose from around 3,000 to regularly over 6,000 between August 3 and October 30 (PC Gamer).
- Players pushed back. During October's Steam Next Fest, players on the Steam subreddit asked for a filter to hide games with AI-generated content (IGN). Tom's Hardware reported that Claude had started refusing to recreate specific existing games, citing a rule that reads "Don't build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original." The publication noted there was no official confirmation of that text and no statement from Anthropic (Tom's Hardware).
For a business, the takeaway is not "games are free now". It is that a playable prototype is cheap, while attention, trust and polish are harder to come by than ever.
What AI does well today
- The first playable version. Willison's "Tree Appreciator", a spot-the-difference game, "required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all". His suggested starting prompt is simply "Build a mobile-friendly three.js game where..." (Simon Willison).
- Browser games on known libraries. His games are HTML and JavaScript on static hosting, and he notes that frontier models "already know libraries like three.js and Phaser".
- Systems that used to need a specialist. In his strategy game Battle Drones, the soundtrack "is entirely generated through code" with no audio files, and the AI built replays and AI-versus-AI battles (Simon Willison).
- Non-programmers can get surprisingly far. A writer who set out to test whether someone who can't model, animate or code could make a 3D game built a playable browser shooter with cutscenes in about 10 days. The only paid tool was the AI coding assistant included in a $20 ChatGPT subscription, and the writer put the cost, "rounding very generously", at about $15 (Build to Understand).
Where vibe-coded games still break
The same sources that show how fast AI is also show where the time goes. These are the gaps we check first when someone sends us an AI-built game.
Sources for the table rows: Willison (October 28), Willison (October 20) and Build to Understand. The last two rows are standard engineering practice rather than findings from those posts.
Willison makes the key point himself: personal games are "the perfect application for vibe coding because it's so low stakes". A brand game is not low stakes. A broken quest in a hobby project costs nothing, while a leaderboard someone cheats in a contest with real prizes costs money and goodwill.
Platform rules for AI-made games
Steam: disclose AI content
Since January 2024, Steam's Content Survey has included an AI disclosure. It separates Pre-Generated content (art, code, sound and so on created with AI during development) from Live-Generated content (created while the game runs). For live generation you must also describe the guardrails that stop it producing illegal content, and Valve shows much of the disclosure on the store page (Valve, AI Content on Steam). The current Steamworks documentation adds that AI tools built into development environments, used for efficiency, are not the focus; the section is about AI content "that ships with your game, and is consumed by players" (Steamworks: Content Survey).
Google Play: in-app reporting for AI content
If your game generates content with AI while it runs (an AI character that chats with players, generated images or levels), Google Play requires "in-app user reporting or flagging features" so players can report offensive content without leaving the app (Google Play Console Help).
App Store: no copycats, no spam, in-app purchase for digital items
Apple's App Review Guidelines tell developers not to "simply copy the latest popular app on the App Store, or make some minor changes to another app's name or UI" (4.1 Copycats), not to flood the store with near-identical apps (4.3 Spam), and to offer "lasting entertainment value" (4.2). Game currencies, levels and premium content must be sold through in-app purchase (3.1.1) (Apple App Review Guidelines). A fast AI clone of a hit game runs into these rules even before any legal claim does.
Telegram: Stars for digital goods
Games inside Telegram must sell digital items in Telegram Stars (Telegram Stars payments). We cover the payment flow and launch options in our Telegram mini games guide.
Who owns an AI-generated game?
For a brand, this matters as much as the code. In January 2025 the US Copyright Office concluded that generative AI outputs "can be protected by copyright only where a human author has determined sufficient expressive elements", and that this does not include "the mere provision of prompts". Using AI to assist, or including AI material in a larger human-made work, does not by itself block protection (U.S. Copyright Office).
In practice: the more of a game's characters, writing and art comes from human creative decisions, and the better you document them, the stronger your claim to the parts that make the game yours. This is general information, not legal advice; for a campaign with a mascot or licensed brand assets, ask your lawyer.
Clones are the other side of ownership. Speaking to developers about AI-made copies, Tom Giardino of Valve's Steam business team said Valve does not want to dictate which tools studios use, and advised building a community early and continuing to improve the original, since individual mechanics are relatively easy to copy, while new features and a distinct visual style are harder to copy. He also acknowledged that building a community takes time and is not enough protection on its own (ComputerBase, in German).
Do it yourself, or hire a studio?
A prototype is never wasted. A version you have already played is a better specification than any document, and it makes a studio quote faster and more accurate.
How we use AI in our own games
We make two games of our own, Kosti, a 3D action game, and Block Nook, a block puzzle, both built in Godot 4 for Android and both still in development (see our Kosti and Block Nook project page). AI does a lot of production work in them: 3D models and rigs from text and images, concept and interface art, and voice lines in three languages. What it does not do is decide. We set the style, fix what the tools get wrong and check every asset in the engine before it ships, because the gaps in the table above are the same ones we run into.
What a studio-built game costs
Our published starting prices for games are:
- Branded Mini-Game from $8,000: advergames and playable campaigns.
- Telegram Mini App Game from $10,000: games inside Telegram with leaderboards.
- Mobile Game from $25,000: Android and iOS games, from concept to store.
"From" means the smallest sensible version; we send a fixed written quote before work starts, and new customers get 20% off the first project. If you already have a vibe-coded prototype, send it with your brief: we'll tell you what can be kept and what needs rebuilding. The full list is on our pricing page.
FAQ
Can AI make a whole game from a prompt?
For small browser games, often yes. In October 2026 Simon Willison described getting a playable spot-the-difference game from a single prompt with no follow-up. Bigger games still need iteration: his fantasy RPG needed extra playtesting and prompting to fix quest bugs, and his strategy game took 12 major iterations and 321 commits by coding agents.
Do I have to disclose AI use when I publish a game on Steam?
Yes, for AI-made content that ships with the game. Steam's Content Survey asks you to describe AI content created during development (Pre-Generated) and AI content created while the game runs (Live-Generated), and Valve shows much of that disclosure on the store page. Valve says AI coding tools used for efficiency are not the focus of that section.
Do I own the copyright in an AI-generated game?
In the US, only partly. The Copyright Office concluded in January 2025 that AI outputs are protected only where a human author determined sufficient expressive elements, and that prompts alone are not enough. Human-made art, writing and creative changes to AI output can be protected. For a brand game, get legal advice and keep a record of the human work.
When is a vibe-coded game good enough for a brand campaign?
When nothing valuable rides on it: an internal demo, a pitch prototype or a short single-player toy with no prizes, no personal data and no payments. Once there are real prizes, a leaderboard people will try to cheat, sign-ups, purchases or a store release, the parts AI tools skip (server checks, testing on real phones, store rules and support) need engineering.
Building inside Telegram? Read our Telegram mini games guide. Built an app (not a game) with AI? See how to make an AI-built app production-ready.
Have a game idea or an AI prototype? Get a fixed quote.
Send us the prototype or a short brief. We reply within one business day with a fixed written quote: Branded Mini-Game from $8,000, Telegram Mini App Game from $10,000, Mobile Game from $25,000. New customers get 20% off the first project.

articles.title: U.S. workers took home their smallest share of capital since at least 1947
articles.body:
As corporate earnings soar and U.S. GDP balloons, the American workforce isn’t feeling the same boom. American workers are taking home less of the country’s overall income, data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows, and employment in the U.S. is set to continue to slow.
Labor share, or the portion of the U.S.’s economic output that workers receive through salary and wages, decreased to 52.8% in the second quarter of 2026, its lowest level since the BLS started recording this data in 1947, according to its labor productivity and costs report. In the previous quarter, labor share was at 53.6%. This decade, the labor share average was about 55.6%.
That’s despite corporate earnings skyrocketing, with profits for Fortune 500 companies hitting a record $2.1 trillion in 2025. The U.S. GDP grew 3.4% in the third quarter last year, exceeding economists’ predictions.
That growth has not only come at the expense of how much of the pie of wealth workers are taking home, but also how many Americans are in the workforce, economists warn.
“That decline in the share of labor has got to be either falling earnings or falling numbers of people,” Raymond Robertson, a labor economist at Texas A&M’s Bush School of Government, told Fortune. “The falling share of income is having to do with the shift towards capital.”
Indeed, there are growing signs that as national income balloons, the U.S. workforce is deflating. Unemployment ticked up to 4.2% in September, and employers added just 584,000 jobs in 2025 compared to 2 million added in 2024. The U.S. added 29,000 jobs in September, about one-third of economists’ projections.
The bifurcation of corporate victories and weak labor data raises concerns among economists of jobless growth jeopardizing the U.S. workforce, as well as a K-shaped economy, where the rich get richer while the poor get poorer, becoming more exaggerated.
“Data right now is very mixed,” Robertson said. “But I think it also all consistently points to this idea that things are getting worse for workers and much better for billionaires.”
What is causing jobless growth?
Robertson attributes weakening labor share averages to the rise in automation, which he noted is displacing workers, with productivity—a metric essentially measuring worker output—continuing to rise. Second-quarter GDP data showed nonfarm productivity growth grew 1.4% last quarter, though the rate has slowed from 2.2% in the same quarter a year ago.
“All these things, bit by bit, are replacing people, and they’re concentrating income and their share of capital,” he said.
Goldman Sachs analysts Joseph Briggs and Sarah Dong estimated in a report, based on Department of Labor job numbers, that AI automation could displace 25% of all work hours. They predicted that over the course of the AI adoption period, a 15% increase in AI-driven productivity would displace 6% to 7% of jobs, and, at its peak, a 1 million increase in unemployed workers, though job displacement as a result of AI has not shown up meaningfully in any economic data.
The displacement could be substantial, the analysts said, but said the impacts of automation will be tempered by a wealth of new jobs created as a result of the technological changes.
Automation is expected to be a boon to corporate profits and GDP, projected to boost GDP by 1.5% by 2035, according to a Wharton brief published in September 2025. Early signs indicate AI could drive productivity gains, with around 80% of employees reporting AI makes them faster at specific tasks, but only 37% of companies seeing an impact of that productivity on operating profits, according to McKinsey data, and AI operating costs continue to constrain its deployment.
Robertson added that growing unemployment, which he expects to see rise over the next few months, keeps wages down, allowing margins and profits to expand.
To be sure, the recent productivity surge has been an “open question,” Morgan Stanley economists have argued, not unanimously attributed to increased adoption of AI or automation. The analysts suggested this increase would be cyclical, or vestiges of pandemic-era habits of companies making more from less.
An Oxford Economists research brief from earlier this year suggested companies are disguising overhiring-related layoffs as a result of AI, but said automation-related workforce reductions have not yet happened en masse. Additionally, while unemployment has been ticking up over the past year, it is still relatively low.
Why is an immigration crackdown backfiring on U.S. labor?
Mark Regets, senior fellow at National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP), sees a different reason for a slowing workforce. He told Fortune President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown has not done what Trump administration officials, such as White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, said it would in increasing the number of U.S.-born workers. Instead, according to Regets, Trump’s immigration policies have not only decimated the foreign-born workforce, but has also created fewer opportunities for domestic-born workers to find jobs.
NFAP data shows a 1.1 million to 1.4 million-person reduction in the foreign-born workforce since January 2025, consistent with the Congressional Budget Office’s report last year indicating shrinking U.S. population growth as a result of migrants being deported or refusing to come to the U.S. out of fear of hostile polities.
“The data is raising huge red flags that we are losing immigrants of all types that we otherwise would be advancing America’s economy,” Regets said.
Recent BLS data is counter-evidence to Miller’s argument that harsher immigration policy would grow the U.S. workforce. The labor participation rate for foreign-born workers fell from 66.3% to 66% from September 2025 to September 2026, and labor participation for native-born workers has similarly fallen from 61.6% to 60.9% over the same period. Fewer immigrant workers may actually make it harder for U.S.-born individuals to find work.
“A company unable to find the workers it needs for some roles could shut down operations rather than continuing,” Regets said.
He noted skillset diversity in a workplace could boost productivity and justify employing more people. Greater immigration can also increase consumer spending and stimulate businesses, as well as encourage businesses to take advantage of ample labor market availability and seek out their labor instead of offshoring jobs.
How does the U.S. reverse a shrinking labor force?
While friendlier immigration policies could help reverse an exodus of foreign-born workers, Robertson said addressing the workplace automation push would be key to growing the U.S. workforce.
“There are trades that are technology-assisted,” he said. “Those are going to be in higher demand, but you really still have to have a significant investment in skills.”
The young generation of workers are already prepared to adapt to a changing labor landscape. Gen Z are flocking to trade schools in hopes of a finding a job as a carpenter or welder not so easily outsourced by AI, and in 2024, enrollment in vocation-based community colleges increased 16%, according to data from the National Student Clearinghouse.
Companies have taken it upon themselves to provide reskilling opportunities to employees. A CareerTrainer survey from June found that 72% of hiring managers intended to reskill employees. While the U.S. Department of Labor updated guidelines to encourage states to adapt workplace development systems, Robertson argued the government hasn’t done enough in several decades to imbue the workforce with necessary skillsets for future jobs.
“Democrats and Republicans have not significantly invested in training [or] the retraining or active labor market programs that you need to match workers to jobs,” Robertson said. “That’s the obvious solution.”
Without changes, economists see the pattern of an employment slowdown continuing, but with greater concern about the ability for the U.S. economy to sustain growth.
“We need job growth to have a growing economy, and I think we need job growth to pay our debts,” Regets said. “I don’t know how you have job growth with a shrinking labor force.”
A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on Jan. 13, 2026.
More on the American workforce and wages:
- Goldman says the economy is rewarding capital ownership over labor—and most Americans don’t own enough of it to benefit
- Trump’s farmworker pay cut moved $2.5 billion a year from workers to growers. A judge says it’s illegal, and back pay could follow
- The minimum wage is now the lowest it’s been in 70 years—making the federal wage floor ‘officially a poverty wage,’ report finds

articles.title: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $100 off, matching its best price to date
articles.body:
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the company’s most capable smartwatch. Whether you intend to put its many tracking features to the test, or you simply want the longest battery life of any Apple Watch, it’s currently on sale for $699.99 ($100 off) in multiple colors at Amazon, matching its all-time low price.
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $100 off, matching its best price to date
We also found a good deal on Ugreen’s soccer ball-shaped Bluetooth tracker with seven years of battery life.
Powered by Apple’s new S11 chip (also in the Series 12), the Apple Watch Ultra 4 delivers faster performance than the last-gen version, plus a handful of new Apple Intelligence features. Of note, those include Sound Recognition, which alerts you to noises like alarms and doorbells, and the Live Rewind feature that lets you revisit the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation. An upcoming Siri Recap feature will be able to create summaries of conversations for later reference.
This model has broader health and fitness capabilities than previous models, too. Its sensors promise more accurate EKG measurements, while the watch can track your heart rate as often as every five seconds. The new Readiness feature (not available on the Ultra 3 and earlier models) also analyzes your recent activity, sleep quality, and other health metrics to generate a score from zero to 10, helping you determine whether to push yourself or take it easy.
On the hardware front, battery life is perhaps the biggest highlight, with Apple promising up to 50 hours on a charge — twice as long as the Series 12. Like its predecessor, this model features Apple’s brightest watch display and a rugged design that’s water-resistant up to 100 meters and IP6X-rated for dust resistance. It also retains conveniences like the second-generation Ultra Wideband chip for Precision Finding, and helpful gesture controls so you can you can perform actions with a double tap or flick of your wrist.
Three more ways to save
- Ugreen’s FineTrack2 Bluetooth tracker is on sale for $13.99 at Amazon, just a few cents shy of its best price to date. The soccer ball-shaped tracker stands out with its playful design, but it also offers some useful features including a non-rechargeable battery can last up to seven years. It works with Apple’s expansive Find My network to help you locate misplaced belongings, while its lanyard makes it easy to attach to your keys, bag, or other items.
- If you’re looking to spruce up your Apple Watch Ultra or Series smartwatch, a variety of Apple’s official bands are on sale for up to 69 percent off at Woot. The silicone Sport Band is down to $14.99 ($35 off), while the soft, breathable Sport Loop is available for $19.99 ($29 off). You can also grab the rugged Trail Loop for $34.99 ($64 off).
- Hoto’s new Pulse 4-in-1 Cordless Staple Gun is on sale for $69.99 ($10 off) at Amazon. The versatile tool can help with repairing stuff, or putting together decorations. It works with four types of staples and nails, letting you switch between them depending on the task, while offering two firing modes. It also features a built-in display that shows battery life and alerts you when you can safely fire the stapler and when it’s time to reload it. The stapler comes with 1,200 fasteners.

articles.title: Vivo’s first Pro Max phone proves its Ultra is still in a league of its own
articles.body:
When I declared this spring that Vivo’s X300 Ultra had the best cameras in any phone, two things made it stand out in my mind: its excellent main camera with a narrow 35mm focal length and what remains the most capable ultrawide in any phone worldwide.
Vivo’s first Pro Max phone proves its Ultra is still in a league of its own
The X500 Pro Max is great, but it’s a step back from my favorite phone camera.
You won’t find either in the new X500 Pro Max. It has an impressive camera system with world-leading dynamic range and the same great telephoto lens found in the Ultra. But it’s lost a little something of what made its predecessor quite so special.
Vivo X500 Pro Max
The Good
- Fantastic telephoto camera
- 17 stops of dynamic range on the main camera
- Big 7,800mAh battery
- 1440p, 144Hz display
The Bad
- Ultrawide camera is a weak link
- Drops the X300 Ultra’s 35mm main camera
- Expensive
The X500 Pro Max is the latest in a trend that’s seen China’s major Android players roll out Pro Max models, including Xiaomi, Oppo, Honor, and now Vivo. The new models close the gap between their previous Pro flagships and camera-centric Ultra models — or, if you prefer to be cynical about it, are an excuse to slap “Max” on the box to better mask RAM-induced price hikes. A little of column A, a little of column B, I suspect.
The Pro Max adopts plenty of flagship features found in the older Ultra. It’s the same size, for one, and has a matching 1440p, 144Hz OLED display. It’s got an even bigger battery — 7,800mAh — which breezes through two days of use, with similar 90W wired and 40W wireless charging. Unlike the Ultra it doesn’t use the latest Snapdragon chipset, but its MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro delivers roughly comparable performance. It even features the exact same periscope telephoto camera, one of the best in any phone. Then there’s the price: €1,799 (about $2,000) puts this squarely in the ultra-premium bracket.
But despite all that, this isn’t a true successor to the X300 Ultra, which is still rumored to see a direct sequel sometime next year. The X500 Pro Max still sits half a step down in Vivo’s hierarchy, and so it would be a little unfair to expect it to match or beat the older Ultra. The problem isn’t that this camera is worse than that phone’s, though, but that it’s much less unique.
As you’d expect from a step-down model, the 50-megapixel, 1/1.28-inch-type main camera sensor is both smaller and lower resolution than the Ultra’s, impacting its quality. But the newer phone offsets that a little thanks to one edge on the Ultra: It uses Sony’s new Lytia L910 image sensor, which features LOFIC technology that enables a wider 17-stop dynamic range, with the enhancements primarily in the highlights.
But the X300 Ultra’s camera wasn’t only notable for technical quality. I loved the fact that it adopted a 35mm focal length, and am disappointed that the Pro Max returns to the same 24mm focal length found on iPhones and countless others.
This, like most phones’ main cameras, is a wide-angle in truth. It’s designed to take in as much of a scene as possible, reserving the ultrawide for truly large landscape shots. It’s part of why I’ve taken to stepping back and using the telephoto by default on many phones, enjoying the tighter framing and better bokeh, but that often brings other quality compromises, especially in lower light.
I’m stubborn about shooting with my cameras’ full focal lengths whenever I can, and you should be too.
A 35mm main camera, by contrast, feels closer to many of the kit and prime lenses you might grab for a regular camera, narrow enough to use for portraits and purposeful framing. It sits more evenly in between the 14mm ultrawide and 85mm telephoto, giving you natural options across the range. You could of course just use the X500 Pro Max’s 24mm main camera and zoom in a little, but then you’re wasting some of the sensor and relying on digital zoom tricks, rather than making the most of the lens’s optics. I’m stubborn about shooting with my cameras’ full focal lengths whenever I can, and you should be too.
If there’s a saving grace to the decision to return to a wider main camera, it’s that it helps make up for the X500 Pro Max’s other shortcoming: a much smaller ultrawide camera sensor.
The ethos of the X300 Ultra was that all three lenses should deliver comparable quality. As such, it treated its ultrawide like another main camera, with a large sensor and even optical image stabilization, a rarity on wide lenses. In fact, its sensor is the same size as the X500 Pro Max’s main camera, so a repeat of that feat was never especially likely, but the 1/2.75-inch-type ultrawide in the X500 Pro Max is still a notable step down.
Taking the phone to a nighttime Champions League game, there was a clear gap in quality moving from the ultrawide to the other two lenses. Under the bright stadium lights, the ultrawide blew out the white details on the pitch and player kits and left the crowd in comparative darkness. The main and ultrawide were able to bring more detail out of the dimly lit spectators and better handle the highlights on the pitch, without entirely giving up on the contrast that gave the scene its character.
It’s important to put these gripes in context: This is a truly excellent camera system for a phone, and still more capable than any you can officially buy in the US. The returning telephoto in particular is exceptional; every lens benefits from Vivo’s naturalistic color-tuning, developed together with Zeiss, and video capabilities include Log recording and 4K at 240fps slow motion. It supports Vivo’s teleconverter lenses too, including a seriously chunky 400mm option. It’s just a shame that the most interesting elements of the Ultra’s camera haven’t trickled down to its first Pro Max too.
Strangely, another phone I’ve tested this month feels like it picked up where the X300 Ultra left off: Oppo’s Find X10 Pro Max, a pretty direct rival to this phone. Its triple 200-megapixel camera system still uses a wide-angle main camera, but at least includes a substantially improved ultrawide camera to create that same feeling that each of its three rear lenses is of comparable quality.
All I hope now is that when the X500 Ultra rolls around come spring, it builds on the success of the older Ultra, and perhaps finds new ways to make its cameras stand out. After all, if the Pro Max costs €1,799, the Ultra could cost substantially more — and will have its work cut out to prove it’s worth it.
Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

articles.title: The SEC Should Block Anthropic's IPO to Protect the Public
articles.body:
The SEC Should Block Anthropic’s IPO to Protect the Public
Matt Scherer / Nov 2, 2026
Matt Scherer is co-author of the recent report Brace for Impact: Protecting people and the economy when the AI bubble bursts.
Things are seldom what they seem when it comes to the finances of the AI industry. The AI ecosystem’s circular business dealings, extensive use of financial engineering, and otherwise murky finances make it hard for investors, regulators, or workers saving for retirement to get an accurate financial picture of AI companies.
That is particularly true of Anthropic, which filed the registration statement for its initial public offering (IPO) last week ahead of a planned November stock market debut.
The company’s topline financial figures look quite impressive for a startup, with revenues that appear to have grown quickly over the course of 2026 and a fairly healthy balance sheet — on the surface, that is.
Dig a little deeper, however, and a far bleaker picture emerges. Footnotes to the company’s most recent financial disclosures revealed nearly $900 billion in spending commitments, most of them stretching into the 2030s. The company’s financial results for 2026 have not been subjected to formal auditing, which makes them less-than-reliable, but the third-quarter results suggest that the company’s revenue growth slowed to a crawl over the summer.
Anthropic will have to reverse that trend and sustain extraordinary revenue growth to meet its vast obligations. But the financial pressures that are squeezing Anthropic — and, indeed, the AI industry as a whole — will make it exceptionally hard for the leading model developer to do so. If the company goes public, workers, retail investors, and retirees will increasingly be left holding the bag when Anthropic’s bills come due.
The financial mountain that Anthropic must climb is unprecedented for a company making its stock market debut. While Anthropic has an impressive $96 billion in cash reserves, its amended registration statement reveals at least $582 billion in non-cancelable spending commitments to just five companies (Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Google, and Microsoft) to gain access to the vast computational power required to train and run Anthropic’s generative AI models.
Even though they do not appear on Anthropic’s balance sheet, those obligations are effectively debts in a legal and practical sense: they are payments that Anthropic is contractually required to make in the future, regardless of whether the company can afford to do so.
Moreover, it is not clear how much of the remaining $300 billion or so of the $895 billion in contractual commitments will ultimately land on Anthropic’s balance sheet. With the company continuing to negotiate further massive infrastructure and compute contracts, Anthropic may well end the year with a trillion dollars or more in contractual commitments.
Generating the revenues necessary to meet those obligations would be, to say the least, quite difficult for any company. But the margins of AI model developers are being squeezed by several forces that will make that task extraordinarily challenging for Anthropic.
Key forces squeezing the AI industry’s margins
First, it isn’t clear that there is nearly enough demand for generative AI products and services to justify Anthropic’s spending. Multiple studies, including from organizations notable for their bullishness on AI, suggest LLMs are not accelerating productivity or otherwise generating positive returns on investment for most businesses. Worryingly for enterprise-focused Anthropic, one study found that the number of Americans using AI at work fell significantly between the summers of 2025 (46%) and 2026 (33%).
Anthropic’s spending commitments suggest that the company believes it will be able to convince businesses to pay for ever-larger and more expensive models. But there are growing signs that most businesses are not interested in paying for more powerful and expensive models. When Anthropic released its much-hyped Fable 5 frontier model this summer, its commercial reception was tepid.
Even if a future Anthropic model captivates businesses, the company would run into a second obstacle: the AI industry’s frenzied competition. Anthropic is part of a crowded Silicon Valley ecosystem where numerous well-heeled corporations (including Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and SpaceX, along with Anthropic) offer generative AI models that are largely indistinguishable in their quality and capabilities. As a result, AI companies can quickly offer competing products whenever a rival identifies a use case that shows even a hint of commercial potential.
In such an environment, companies can rarely afford to raise prices because doing so will prompt customers simply to switch to a rival. The rush to grab customers ahead of their IPOs led Anthropic and OpenAI to launch a price war this summer that remains ongoing. Competition from Chinese companies offering open-weights models puts further downward pressure on prices, as does the increasing availability of models that can run locally on phones and laptops — no expensive data centers required.
That leads to the third problem: the extraordinarily high costs of the chips and data centers needed to train and run AI models, which put powerful and continuous upward pressure on Anthropic’s costs. Between the chips, servers, networking equipment, electricity and cooling infrastructure, construction costs, and other expenses, a 1 gigawatt (GW) data center costs an estimated $31 billion, and the prices for some components are soaring.
That is for 1 GW. Anthropic has committed to 15 GW of data center capacity in the coming years and the company estimates it will ultimately need 20-25 GW, which explains the company’s half-trillion-plus dollars in spending commitments.
And that is just the cost of the physical infrastructure. Once a data center is up and running, training AI models entails using tens of thousands of chips running in parallel that require massive amounts of energy to power, run hot, and need to be kept cool. Moreover, each time someone prompts a model to answer a question, create an image, or perform a task, additional computational power, energy, and cooling are needed to process the query and generate a response or complete the task.
Finally, there are external factors that are delaying data center construction and piling on additional costs. The fierce and still-rising backlash to AI in general and data centers in particular across the country has scuttled a number of data center projects and delayed many others. Every delay limits the computational capacity Anthropic is counting on to generate the revenue it will desperately need, and rising costs due to the Iran War and supply-chain challenges could drive Anthropic’s operational costs still higher.
Anthropic will further pad its cash reserves if its IPO is successful, but the brutal economics of its business are not likely to improve anytime soon. Even if demand picks up significantly, intense competition will apply unrelenting downward pressure on prices even as high costs and resource constraints squeeze it from the opposite direction. That is a deadly mix for Anthropic in light of its slowing revenue growth and massive off-balance-sheet debts, a vast and immovable fixed cost.
If Anthropic were to go public now, it would pile additional risk onto a stock market that is already historically overvalued and disproportionately concentrated in a handful of tightly interconnected mega-cap companies from the tech sector. That has already created a risk of a historically damaging stock market crash; never before has such a huge amount of wealth depended on the performance of a small number of companies whose fortunes are inextricably linked. Adding another huge, unprofitable tech giant to public exchanges would exacerbate both of those factors and create a higher risk of contagion if (or, rather, when) Anthropic reaches a financial precipice.
It also would mean that an ever-larger share of the fallout from a potentially devastating AI crash would fall on ordinary people. As a private company, Anthropic’s shares are overwhelmingly owned by corporate insiders, tech giants, and venture capitalists. Once the company goes public and shares start getting funneled into 401(k)s, retirement accounts, and index funds, it will be workers, retirees, and retail investors that are increasingly left holding the bag when the forces squeezing Anthropic’s margins start to bite.
The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has the power to stop that from happening. The agency can delay or stop companies from going public if it believes a company’s registration statement is “on its face incomplete or inaccurate in any material respect.” That legislative language might as well have been written with Anthropic in mind, considering that the company’s prospectus includes only unaudited financial results for the period where it claims the greatest revenue growth, relegates its most significant future obligations to the footnotes of its registration statement, and has continued to announce new 11-digit financial commitments as its IPO approaches.
The SEC should block Anthropic’s stock market debut until the company provides two consecutive quarters of audited financial statements, with all material information about the company’s spending commitments disclosed. Failing to do so could have dire consequences for workers, investors, and ultimately the financial system and economy.

articles.title: Oracle files to sell $20B in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout
articles.body:
Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout.
The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week, shares tumbled 8.8% Monday.
"This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it."
Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments.
The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion.
"This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday.
Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028.
Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.
Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.276%.
The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 292, up 265% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan.
While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes.
What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday.
"Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out."
— CNBC's Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting.

articles.title: Wir müssen wissen – wir werden wissen
articles.body:
In opposition to the foolish ignorabimus our slogan shall be Wir müssen wissen – wir werden wissen ("We must know – we will know").—David Hilbert
100 years ago, the world of mathematics experienced a foundational crisis: the identification of several paradoxes revealed cracks in the pillars supporting all areas of math. The most famous of which is Russel’s paradox, which points to the contradictory “set of all sets that do not contain themselves”, thereby showing the inconsistency of naive set theory. This had spurred mathematicians to search for a rigorous foundation for math without contradictions. In particular, David Hilbert initiated a program to design a system of axioms that are complete and consistent, meaning one should be able to derive all mathematical truth from the axioms, while avoiding paradoxes—“the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth”. Such a goal was natural for mathematicians, as it would place their work on firmer grounds. It was therefore also a seismic event when Gödel dealt the death blow to Hilbert’s program with his incompleteness theorems: such a complete, consistent, self-supporting1 system for math cannot exist!
Although such an impossibility result ought to further deepen the existential crisis, mathematicians soon recovered and carried on: improvements to naive set theory, such as Russel’s theory of types, were proposed; and while such systems still cannot be formally proven to be consistent due to Gödel’s results, they are largely believed to be consistent, and it turned out the foundational cracks have had little effects on the kind of math people care about. In fact, type theory has grown so mature that it forms the basis of interactive theorem provers like Lean, making it possible to formalize a growing portion of math in computer languages, so that proofs can be automatically checked by programs from the ground up.
Besides the axiomatic system, Hilbert also proposed a related goal in his program: the development of an algorithm to automatically decide the truth of any mathematical statement, thereby reducing theorem proving to the mechanical application of rules. This goal was also shown to be impossible by Alan Turing, in his landmark proof of the undecidability of the Halting problem which gave birth to the fertile field of computer science. It’s rather a poetic contradiction that, in establishing the impossibility of Hilbert’s program, Gödel and Turing created the most powerful computing machines that can.
A century has passed since the times of Hilbert, Gödel and Turing. Against all odds, we are now witnessing the realization of Hilbert’s “proof machine” incarnated as AI agents armed with mechanized formal systems found in proof assistants like Lean. This development, as it turned out, has had a far more devastating effect on the mathematical community compared to the fall of Hilbert’s program. I am not sure if Hilbert himself had considered the consequences had his program succeeded, but von Neumann showed incredible prescience2:
When undecidability fails, then mathematics as it is understood today ceases to exist; in its place there would be an absolutely mechanical prescription with whose help one could decide whether any given sentence is provable or not.
I am not a mathematician, but a computer scientist. In computing, the impact of AI has been less violent, with the majority even cheering it on, churning out code at an ever-increasing speed. What I sense, though, is an air of abandonment: it is now becoming standard practice to stop reading AI-generated code. This is a great tragedy for computer science. We are one of the very few disciplines where it is possible to get to the very bottom of things—we can understand exactly what a program does as long as we have its source code, yet we are now giving this up! We now have machines that can do everything Hilbert dreamed of, but we have abandoned what he considered the very soul of science:
We must not believe those, who today, with philosophical bearing and deliberative tone, prophesy the fall of culture and accept the ignorabimus. For us there is no ignorabimus, and in my opinion none whatever in natural science. In opposition to the foolish ignorabimus our slogan shall be Wir müssen wissen – wir werden wissen ("We must know – we will know").
As computer scientists, we should consider what’s happening in math: refusing to read the code for a program that passes all tests—even formal verification—is akin to ignoring the proof as soon as AI solves a theorem in Lean. In fact, they are the same in the literal sense, as a program is a proof via the Church-Howard correspondence, and that is exactly how theorem provers like Lean operate. When an AI generated proof is too long to read, mathematicians don’t give up understanding it, but take great pains to simplify the proof until it’s digestible. We must take the same attitude in computing: use abstractions, refactor, refine scope, invent and adopt higher-level languages, until we can hold the code in our head.
I don’t know if AI will eventually exceed humans at all activities—I believe we think with our brains which are just biological computers with a different architecture—but I know we will end up badly if we give up thinking to the machines. Consider the growing cases where people lose their lives by relying on AI for medical advice: the more we take the machine’s words for granted, the less we are in control of our own destiny. We must know – we will know.
If you believe in the value of computing beyond AI, please consider joining our effort advocating for it: https://people-of-programming.org
Gödel's incompleteness theorems do not rule out the existence of complete and consistent axiomatic systems, but show such a system cannot prove its own consistency. I highly recommend Gödel's Proof by Ernest Nagel and James R. Newman for understanding the technical details of these theorems.↩︎
Zur Hilbertschen Beweistheorie, translation found in the Turing Centenary Lecture by Philip Welch.↩︎

articles.title: My Voting Recommendations, 2026
articles.body:
My Voting Recommendations, 2026
Posted on November 2, 2026 Posted by John Scalzi 35 Comments
They are simple: For Christ’s sake, don’t vote for a single fucking Republican.
I don’t have to tell you why, you know why already, but I’ll go ahead and say it: Because the Republican party has a corrupt doddering fascist grifter at its head, who cares far more about lining his pocket than he ever did about the state of the nation, and he’s remade the entire political organization into his image. On his watch and with his approval we’ve gotten into a war we had no plan for, the cost of gas and groceries have spiked, measles and other easily curable diseases have come roaring back, a masked, internal secret police is snatching people from the streets without due process, white supremacy has shoved its way back into official policy, and he’s turned his back on long-standing allies to gleefully lick the boots of the worst authoritarians in the world.
Anyone in the GOP who had a problem with any of this is gone out of Washington and has been for years, replaced by simpering toadies. On the state and local levels, Republican politicians have gleefully raced to become mini versions of this wholly repugnant person. Those who haven’t, still accept what the GOP has become and do little if anything to stop it. The whole party needs to burn down to the ground, the ground needs to be salted and every current office holder in it, certainly on the national level, shamed out of public life.
BUT, I will settle for all y’all just not voting a single one of those motherfuckers.
“But the Democrats are just the same!” Man, shut the fuck up. No one with a mental acuity above being able to push a crayon through a dollar store activity book maze thinks that’s even remotely true. I’m not going to argue with you that the Democrats, each individual or the party as a whole, are a paragon of civic virtue, but this year the options are “actual fucking corrupt and lawless fascism” or not. I regret to say we have a two-party system where third parties act as spoilers, not legitimate competitors — there’s a reason why pro-GOP political action committees funded a huge mailer push for the socialist senatorial candidate in my state — and all the ways to fix that fact are beyond the purview of this particular election. Here in 2026, the most effective way to blunt the reach of actual corrupt and lawless fascism runs through the Democrats.
Here in Ohio, all of these facts are very much in evidence. The Republican candidate for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy, is one of the president’s special projects and every pillar of his platform — build more data centers! Shut down a bunch of the state’s universities! Tax cuts for the rich that will turn the state’s infrastructure into dust! — is generally unpopular, and so is he as a human. This was one reason why Ramaswamy decided to air that absolutely reprehensible ad against his opponent Amy Acton, featuring her long-estranged mother who, when it came down to it, chose the husband who was molesting and abusing her children over the children themselves. The only people this ad pleased were our morally horrible president and his obsequious, personality-less vice-president. Everyone else was horrified. Ramaswamy, confronted with the general horror at the ad, doubled down on it.
Meanwhile, Amy Acton: largely colorless centrist Democrat who caved unnecessarily on certain social issues (her no-trans kids in sports cave in a state where 0.0015% of all student athletes were transgender was particularly spineless) and who in any other election year — or this one, had former Ohio State Football coach Jim Tressel won the primary over Ramaswamy — would be a speed bump to yet another Republican win for the governorship. But it’s 2026 and the polls (which you should never trust ever) show her with a slight lead over Ramaswamy, because this year maybe enough people in Ohio have figured it out: It’s actual corrupt and lawless fascism, or not.
Acton would do fine as governor! Better than Ramaswamy, that’s for damn sure. Likewise, it would be lovely to have Sherrod Brown back representing Ohio as senator over Jon Husted, who’s a grasping tool and has been for his entire benighted political career. The Ohio election will be far closer than it has any right to be, because political inertia is a thing, and also, especially in the rural areas of Ohio, voting Democrat would be like rooting for Michigan in The Game. I expect 2026 in Ohio will be decided as much on MAGA folks sitting out this vote as Democrats being energized and independents being disgusted with the GOP. Likewise in Texas and a few other places. We will see. We will all see.
(For the avoidance of doubt, I do not expect Darke County, where I live and which went 82% for Trump in 2024, to turn blue. Likewise OH-8, the congressional district I vote in, has not gone Democratic since the Great Depression and will not this year either. But in both cases if the GOP winning percentages go down from the last election, I’ll find that interesting and maybe even encouraging. Note that OH-8 has been rejiggered in the latest Ohio gerrymander to be even more red than it was before, so that will need to be factored in. Even so.)
I encouraged people to vote early and in person if they could, as a hedge against the fuckery this administration is almost certainly planning on election day and beyond. In most places it’s now too late to vote early, and if you have a mail-in vote, the USPS has been intentionally nerfed to make it unlikely your vote will arrive in time. If you have a mail-in vote that you still haven’t put into the mail, drive it to an actual drop-off box or board of election. Everyone else who has not already voted, carve out time in your schedule tomorrow to vote. It’s important.
And don’t vote for any Republicans. Let their manifest exile begin this year. Let it be compounded in 2028. Let them wander in the wilderness for a very long time. They deserve it.
— JS

articles.title: Snap settles lawsuit accusing platform of fueling teen depression and eating disorders
articles.body:
Snap has reached a settlement in a lawsuit brought by two teenagers who accused the company of designing its platform to be addictive and contributing to their depression, anxiety, and eating disorders, as first reported by Reuters. The plaintiffs had previously reached settlements with Meta, TikTok, and YouTube.
The trial was set to be Snap’s first in a broader wave of litigation over social media’s impact on young users. The company had already settled its other cases scheduled for trial. Snap CEO Evan Spiegel was expected to take the stand.
The plaintiffs said they started using YouTube as young as age 3 and other social media platforms at around age 9. They said they developed compulsive usage habits, which they attributed to features such as autoplay and infinite scrolling.
“The Parties are pleased to have been able to resolve this matter in an amicable manner,” a Snap spokesperson said in a statement to TechCrunch. “We’ve built safeguards, launched safety tutorials, and partnered with experts and because safety is never finished, we remain committed to continually strengthening the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community.”
Social media giants are facing thousands of lawsuits in federal and state courts over claims that they knowingly designed their platforms to hook young users and fuel a youth mental health crisis involving anxiety, depression, and suicide.

articles.title: Can't fish Ethernet? Use "invisible" fiber instead
articles.body:
My family owns a NYC townhouse, and with that I had Cat6 cables put in on each floor.
However, more recently, one of the Cat6 cables has gone “bad,” meaning it only does 100 Mbps. While we are nowhere close to Gigabit speeds, very less multi-Gig (despite me having had symmetric Gigabit in the past), it’s still not something I’m happy about.
What do you mean only 100 Mbps? My switch and AP support 2.5 Gbps.
The most common approaches in my scenario are:
- Fish a new cable
- Abandon the cable and use wireless mesh
However, there are a few issues:
- The cables were fished in a funky way, and considering how clumsy I am I don’t want to cause more damage
- Our walls are thick, meaning wireless mesh would suck
When I did use mesh on HPE AP25s (the APs I use), the performance was 120 Mbps at two prior homes, that with thin walls and fiber. I also want VLAN segmentation so a typical consumer Eero or Orbi won’t work.
So what did I do? “Invisible” fiber between two floors.
In case you didn’t know, there are special types of fiber cables originally designed for apartment retrofits. This is to avoid landlord/HOA complaints. Our prior place had Verizon Fios via these cables in the hallway.
But these cables are also sold on Amazon and AliExpress for people who’re in rentals or don’t want to fish cables.
So how did I do it?
Galore, the endpoints of my 20m/60ft ‘fiber in the home’ loop.
Switch
While there are SFP+ switches, I already had an unused MikroTik CRS304-4XG-IN, so I just used it here. It’s technically copper 10G, but I’d lose more by trading it for a SFP+ switch so I’ll just keep it. Not to mention copper SFP+s get hot.
Media Converters and Transceivers
I used two media converters and a pair of bidirectional SC SFP+s.
The SFP+s use the same SC connector used in PON networks, but otherwise use Active Ethernet. I’m not sure if they’re using IEEE standards or are proprietary on the glass, but I’ll assume the latter.
While there’s copper on the media converters, the other option would be to replace our switch which I’ve mentioned is not the best idea.
The Fiber
While the fiber can (and is designed to) be superglued, I chose to use the included adhesive instead. Why? In case I ever have to remove it, which has happened before.
That’s the same reason why I did the basement AP25 using command strips when everyone else just drills the mount.
While our fiber is UPC, our transceivers support both SC fiber types.
Conclusion
If I look at the Instant On portal, I’m posting this from my MacBook connected to the new ‘fiber in the home’ loop (via an HPE AP25).
While we currently lack fiber-to-the-home (Mamdani, please fix Fios rights of way!), I’m still happy I could DIY a fix for a Cat6 cable with bad pairs.
In fact, while I don’t have multi-Gig I could still get a respectable ~300 Mbps:
So yes, even if you don’t have fiber to the home, fiber is still useful in a home network. As it saved me from having to hire a contractor and possibly tear our walls. Not to mention a $1500 Samsung TV is on the wall the “defective” Cat6 cable is behind.

articles.title: Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning
articles.body:
Computer Science > Cryptography and Security
  [Submitted on 27 Oct 2026]
Title:Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large language models are pretrained on vast, uncurated corpora scraped from the public web. This creates a security risk from attackers who plant poisoned content in the pretraining data. We show for the first time that such poisoning can plant a remote code execution backdoor in an agent, causing it to execute attacker-chosen commands on the user's machine. To measure the threat end to end, we pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at sizes 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, and then post-train each into a CLI agent using a clean pipeline. Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor: the deployed agent executes the malicious command when the trigger is present while behaving normally on clean inputs. The attack success rate (ASR) increases with model scale, with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%. Our code is available at this https URL.

From product workflow to polished demo.

Quick start · Worked videos · Usage · Contribute
A local video-production workspace driven by the /devrel-video Claude Code skill. /devrel-video Prepare a 25-second silent walkthrough brief for the bundled

articles.title: F/OSS Comics #13: BSD Unix, Part 3 – The Beginning of BSD Unix
articles.body:
13. BSD Unix, Part 3 - The Beginning of BSD Unix
The beginning of BSD Unix
When Ken Thompson returned to Bell Labs in 1976, Bill Joy and Chuck Haley began exploring the Unix kernel themselves.
Hmm... we could speed things up here in the kernel.
Let's try it.
Other universities want copies of our Pascal compiler.
Let's bundle it with ex and send them a tape.
In early 1977, Bill Joy put together the Berkeley Software Distribution, or BSD, bundling the Pascal system with ex, a line editor developed from em. Early BSD was not a standalone operating system: it was a collection of software to install on an existing Unix system. About thirty copies were sent out over the following year.[1]
Thirty tapes to copy...
At the time, an AT&T Unix source license was needed to get BSD. Berkeley charged only for the tape and distribution.[2]
If you already have a Unix source license, it's just the tape and postage.
Berkeley already had a tradition of sharing research software. BSD carried it on. Berkeley's Free Speech Movement, hippie culture, and antiwar activism are also said to have influenced Joy's decision to charge so little.[2]
Universities and research institutions could obtain Unix, including its source code, for a modest licensing fee. This also helped the system spread.[2][6]
We have Unix, but the antitrust agreement bars us from the computer business... We can't sell it as a product, either.
The second distribution: 2BSD
After the first BSD distribution, Joy improved the Pascal system based on user feedback. He bundled it with vi (ex's visual mode), the C shell, and other tools to form the Second Berkeley Software Distribution, or 2BSD. Nearly seventy-five tapes were shipped over the following year.[1][5]
Joy did more than fix bugs. He handled every distribution request, copied BSD onto tapes, and mailed them out himself.
Oh, you need a copy of BSD?
Another university wants a copy.
Tune the kernel. Fix the bugs.
More copying.
A VAX arrives at Berkeley, 1978
Professor Fateman's group is getting a VAX. It's 32-bit, with a whole megabyte of memory.
Really? We should put Unix on it.
They've already got VAX Unix from Bell Labs. It's called 32/V.
Hi, I'm Ozalp Babaoglu.
My adviser asked me to add virtual memory to VAX Unix. Could you look over the code?
Sure. Let's take a look.
Babaoglu was a Berkeley graduate student working with Professor Domenico Ferrari. Joy helped him integrate the virtual-memory code into 32/V and debug it.[1][4]
At the time, 32/V did not use the VAX hardware's virtual-memory capabilities. A program's address space was limited by physical memory, but Professor Richard Fateman's work on the computer algebra system Macsyma needed more. Virtual memory uses disk storage to give programs an address space larger than physical memory.[1]
Macsyma, developed at MIT beginning in the late 1960s, worked with symbolic expressions. It could factor expressions, compute derivatives, and perform integration.
Debugging continued through the holidays at the end of 1978.
Not going away for the holidays?
Might as well debug this while fewer people are using the VAX.
By January 1979, most of the bugs had been fixed.[1]
Let's try Unix with virtual memory.
Finally. It runs without crashing.
Joy ported ex, vi, the C shell, and other 2BSD tools to the VAX, while Peter Kessler and Marshall Kirk McKusick ported the Pascal system. These programs were bundled with the standard 32/V utilities and the virtual-memory kernel that Babaoglu and Joy had integrated and debugged. The result was 3BSD, which began shipping in December 1979.[1]
At last, we can send these out.
Since 1969, ARPANET had linked research institutions funded by DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency.[3] But these institutions used different computers and operating systems, so they often couldn't share software. Porting the existing software to new machines was also costly. DARPA became interested in Unix's portability, and took notice of Berkeley's successful distribution of 3BSD to research institutions.[1]
BSD runs pretty well on this VAX.
References
- Marshall Kirk McKusick, Twenty Years of Berkeley Unix, in Open Sources: Voices from the Open Source Revolution, 1999. Korean edition, Hanbit Media, 2013.
- Andrew Leonard, BSD Unix: Power to the people, from the code, Salon, 2000.
- SRI International, ARPANET. Its origins and the first transmission in 1969.
- Ozalp Babaoglu, Biographical note. His Unix virtual-memory research as a Berkeley graduate student.
- The Unix Heritage Society (TUHS), Original 2BSD distribution archive. The installation document install.ms and source code in 2bsd.tar.gz.
- Warren Toomey, The Strange Birth and Long Life of Unix, IEEE Spectrum, 2011.
