articles.title: One of Google’s Android partners turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet
articles.body:
Google says one of its Android manufacturing partners secretly built a backdoor in 1.3 million devices and turned them into a botnet. The company says it has now dismantled the backdoor and “cut ties” with the manufacturer, the Shenzhen, China-based Videostrong Technology Co., which has been banned from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software for them.
One of Google’s Android partners turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet
Google says a manufacturer ‘intentionally’ hijacked its devices with malware.
The infected devices were used without owners’ knowledge for “malicious activity,” like ad fraud, data exfiltration, and routing unauthorized network traffic. Google claims the “backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain,” saying:
Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.
It wasn’t just one device that was impacted, either — the malware was found “built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years.” Most of those were Android TV set-top boxes, but the botnet also infected other “Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.”
Google says Videostrong used “obfuscation techniques” to load the malware onto users’ devices after they booted up the hardware for the first time. Google also says it made changes to its review process for device manufacturers after this incident.

articles.title: Three Dots
articles.body:
Last Friday, Reddit had its worst day since its IPO, with a drop of almost 30%1. It didn’t matter that they beat their third-quarter estimates; what mattered most was a weak Q4 forecast and the quote from Reddit CEO Steve Huffman, “Our search referral traffic was down meaningfully in Q3, with the decline accelerating later in the quarter.” He also wrote, “During October, we have seen that search traffic has dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week.”
There’s no baseline to understand whether 1 million referrals is a lot or a little, but there is no doubt a stock dropping 30% in a day is a lot.
Reddit, which I am certain looks at the data daily, has seen this coming for years; hence their other announcements that shape a larger strategy:
- Testing a logged-in-only experience outside the U.S.
- Shutting down RSS feeds
- Shutting down the public API
- Moving data access to its Developer Platform, which makes all Reddit data access paid only.
The Three Dots Are Pretty Easy to Connect
Dot #1: Traditional Google search: you search for X, Google searches for X and provides a list of high-quality X links, which — if the links are high quality — means you click on X, which is a Reddit post about X.
Google would greatly prefer if you didn’t click on X because the moment you do, you’ve left Google and they’ve mostly lost their ability to present you with advertising. You read that right: the reason you go to Google is to find other high-quality stuff that they don’t want you to actually see. My favorite attempt was AMP, Accelerated Mobile Pages, where publishers built lightweight copies of their content, and Google served them from their own servers. Yes, you were promised a traffic advantage, but you lose control over design, ads, and analytics.
Google dropped AMP’s search perks in 2021 in the face of continued criticism, but all they really had to do was wait a few years because a vastly better solution would present itself.
Dot #2: I’m guessing sometime in 2022, all the AI players started sucking down all the data in order to train ever-improving models. The more data? The better the models. It’s vastly more complicated than that, but alarms at Reddit apparently started going off in April of 2023, when they moved to charge for API access. The CEO quote: “… [w]e don’t need to give all of that value to some of the largest companies in the world for free.”
While content producers perhaps saw a massive theft of intellectual property, content consumers did not. What they eventually saw was the eerily accurate answer to the dumb throwaway question they typed into their first chatbot. They thought, “Golly, that’s cool.”2 Sub-dot thought: Like Google, AI players have paradoxical motivations: the goal is to get you to use the services so they can help, but helping doesn’t pay the bills. Using more tokens is the business, which means that, like Google, the gig is to keep helping whether you want the help or not.
Dot #3: Present day. Google has a feature called AI Overviews, which you’ve already seen. It’s a human-sounding summary that attempts to answer your questions. There is no way to turn it off — it exists to keep you on Google. The research shows that when an AI Overview shows, clicks on the first result drop 58%. More than half the folks who would have clicked that top result are no longer leaving, which means more sweet, sweet ad revenue.
That’s Not the Dot
I’ve spent the past decade watching the blogging community vanish. There are the stalwarts, but the vast majority of bloggers either stopped or left for lighter-weight walled gardens. Sure, blogging was a fad. Writing, however, is not. I get it — it’s easier to write a pithy one-line Reddit post than a fully fleshed-out thought. Guilty as charged.
I giggle when folks mention Google is in trouble because of declining search usage. First, decades of search habits will take time to disassemble and reassemble. Second, if you are using Google Search less, I’m guessing you’re still using Gmail and similar Google services. If you’re like me and have wired the robots into Gmail, you’re using Gmail significantly more. Yes, I’ve turned off every switch that says “don’t train on me,” but go throw those switches yourself and report on how confident you are that you flipped them all successfully.
I started this piece with Reddit because the company provides a service that creates tremendous value, and I’m not talking about the monetary value; I’m talking about the social value. Early on in my robot journeys, I asked Claude to source any fact it shared with me. I skimmed the sources and was surprised to see how often a random Reddit post was the source of the robot’s thoughts.
Yes, the robot sucked down all the books (including all of mine). Yes, they did the same with countless images, as well. I feel we haven’t yet seen the full set of legal consequences, but that’s not the dot: it’s the value of humans talking with other humans, building things for each other — often simple, frequently hilarious, and doing the work to document why they did what they did… because they want to help.
This was supposed to be a brief introduction to a new feature I’m launching on Rands on Tuesday, but it turned into a whole bunch of dots explaining the disproportionate value of what happens when humans hang with other humans.
See you Tuesday.

articles.title: More European supermarkets are getting their freezers hacked
articles.body:
Grocery stores across Europe have been hit by another wave of suspected cyberattacks, reporting sudden changes in the temperatures of their fridges and freezers. Major supermarket chains across Belgium, Sweden, Luxembourg, and Estonia were affected, according to local reports shared by Bloomberg and Reuters.
More European supermarkets are getting their freezers hacked
Stores in Belgium, Sweden, Luxembourg, and Estonia have had their cooling systems tampered with.
One Ica Kvantum store in Sweden said on its Facebook page that its fridges and freezers had been hacked overnight, with temperatures remotely raised to 50 degrees Celsius (122 Fahrenheit). In a statement to Business Insider, a spokesperson at Swedish supermarket chain Coop also confirmed that “unauthorized actors were able to access and tamper with the cooling systems at a small fraction of our stores.” Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize said an “IT incident” was responsible for adjusting the temperature of refrigeration units in dozens of its supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg. The full scale of the incident has yet to be confirmed.
Many modern supermarket fridges and freezers are connected to the internet to support remote maintenance and system failure alerts, but the increasing number of these suspected hacks is raising concerns around how security flaws can impact food supply chains. This latest incident follows an apparent cyberattack that targeted hundreds of French supermarket refrigerators last month, with the resulting food spoilage estimated to be worth millions of euros, along with a string of US military base freezer malfunctions also suspected to be the result of a cyberattack.

articles.title: The Big Idea: Nancy Kress
articles.body:
The Big Idea: Nancy Kress
Posted on November 2, 2026 Posted by Athena Scalzi Leave a Comment
Spooky season may be over, but you can still be in the spirit with author Nancy Kress’s newest novel, The Queen’s Witch. Take a peek through the veil of magic and into the Big Idea to see some historical truths about these “witches.”
NANCY KRESS:
Forget Halloween witches, pock-marked and flying on broomsticks. Forget Shakespeare’s weird sisters, boiling and toiling and bubbling. Forget even modern Wicca. Think pagan worshippers who throughout medieval and Renaissance eras performed both healing with plants and minor magic—or so everyone believed. In England, they were called “cunning women,” and they predated Christianity. They also co-existed with it, especially in East Anglia and the North. Until Henry VIII decided otherwise, England was Catholic, and Catholicism was already comfortable with mysteries, miracles, and special people set aside from the ordinary. Even today in England you can see old churches whose beams are still carved with both angels and pagan symbols like the Green Man or the dagaz rune.
Cunning women persisted for centuries. 1863, The Prince of Wales, who would become Edward VII, bought Sandringham in Norfolk and evicted all its tenants—except one. The prince’s agent believed her to be a witch and was too frightened to evict her. When the prince fell ill, she was one of the healers summoned to cure him. And as late as 1968, a Norfolk newspaper reported that the local weekly livestock sale sold more than cows; people came to consult “white witches.”
Anne Boleyn, Henry VIII’s second queen (of six; he was hard on wives) has always fascinated me—a woman who gambled everything and lost. Many in Tudor England believed Queen Anne to be a witch. After her beheading, a strange legend grew up around her: that her body was taken from its hasty grave in unhallowed ground inside the Tower of London and was moved to the Church of St. Peter and St. Paul at Salle, in Norfolk. Anne’s ancestors were buried there, and she had been baptized in that church. We know that her cousin Thomas Wyatt, the poet, was in love with Anne, and he later wrote she had received “sacred burial…in consecrated ground.” Not in the Tower of London.
Anne was not a cunning woman. To tell her story, and that of the Sisterhood of witches, I invented my protagonist Alysoun Rowe. Alysoun’s paths and Anne’s become inextricably tangled together, an uneasy but necessary alliance. They need each other to achieve their very different goals. That alliance ultimately affects not only the two women but also the other huge forces sweeping through England: Lutherism, arriving from the continent. Catholicism as Henry VIII tries to redefine it. Papism, of old-style Catholics still loyal to the pope. Also, unknown to those other three groups, a secret Sisterhood of witches who manipulate events behind the scenes to try to stave off the mass persecutions they fear are coming.
Witches are also symbols of something else: female power. There existed in Tudor England some cunning men, but not many and with lesser abilities than the women. The Physicians and Surgeons Act of 1512 was passed to restrict the practice of medicine to only those licensed by the government. The licensees were all men. The Act was in part an effort to keep healing arts away from cunning women, who “boldly and consistently take upon them great cures and things of great difficulty in which they partly use sorcery.” Women are dangerous.
In addition to Alysoun Rowe and Anne Boleyn, this novel let me write about a vivid ruler who is egotistical, vengeful, allows no challenge to his power, and seeks to remake the foundations of the nation he rules. Witches are not the only type of people whose existence persists.
The Queen’s Witch: Amazon

articles.title: Microsoft's Canada Timezone Troubles Leave Admins Fixing Calendars, Pretending They're In Bogota
articles.body:
Microsoft's Canada Timezone Troubles Leave Admins Fixing Calendars, Pretending They're In Bogota (theregister.com) 56
			
		 	
				Microsoft is scrambling to fix time-zone problems across Outlook, Power Automate, Fabric, SharePoint and other products after parts of Canada stopped observing seasonal clock changes on November 1. "The company has confirmed problems across a chunk of its software estate, leaving some customers facing incorrect times, broken schedules and a collection of workarounds while Redmond catches up," reports The Register. From the report:  Outlook users have been left with the most homework. Switching to the new Canadian time zones won't automatically update existing calendar entries, meaning that meetings scheduled after November 1 are potentially an hour out of whack. Microsoft advises users to change their Outlook calendar time zone, then update upcoming events and meetings to use it. For meetings involving other people, only the organizer can make the change.
Recurring meetings come with an additional treat: changing the time zone resets any previously moved occurrences, which then have to be recreated. Anyone with a calendar full of recurring meetings may wish to put the kettle on first. Microsoft is working on an Exchange Online PowerShell cmdlet to remediate non-recurring meetings, but according to its guidance, that's not due until later this week. A fix for recurring meetings remains "in development," with an ETA yet to be confirmed.
Things get stranger with Power Automate and Fabric, where Microsoft's temporary fix involves pretending you're somewhere else entirely. Depending on the product and province, that could mean Saskatchewan, Arizona or, for Manitobans, Bogota. Because apparently time zones weren't confusing enough already. SharePoint On-Prem customers, meanwhile, have to wait until November 10 for the correct time zones to arrive, while Power Pages users could see server-formatted dates appear an hour out until a service fix lands. Microsoft's current milestone for that is December 12.

articles.title: Chicken Corn Chowder
articles.body:
This Chicken Corn Chowder is thick, creamy, a little smoky, and full of tender chicken, sweet corn, and soft potatoes. I skip adding milk and cream to help keep costs down, but the chowder still turns out beautifully rich and creamy! There’s just something about a big pot of soup that feels like home, especially on a chilly day, and this one is cozy and comforting without feeling too heavy. It’s ready in about 50 minutes and makes eight generous servings for only $1.49 each. I love that there’s plenty to feed the family, with enough left over for a few easy lunches later in the week, too!
All recipes are rigorously tested in our Nashville Test Kitchen to ensure they are easy, affordable, and delicious.
A Creamy Chicken Corn Chowder Without Cream!
The bacon does a lot of the flavor-building in this chicken corn chowder, and I’m not just talking about the crispy bits sprinkled on top! Cooking the vegetables in the bacon drippings gives the whole pot a deliciously smoky, savory flavor. And instead of adding milk or cream, I use a little flour and purée some of the cooked vegetables and corn to make the broth wonderfully thick and silky. The rest stays chunky, so you still get plenty of tender chicken, sweet corn, and soft potatoes in each spoonful.
I also love using frozen corn here because it’s already prepped, budget-friendly, and means I can make this chowder any time of year without hunting down fresh corn on the cob. Between the chicken and all those vegetables, you get a hearty, satisfying meal made with familiar, inexpensive ingredients that my whole family will happily eat up (and ask for seconds!). What more could you ask for in a bowl of chowder?! If you love this sweet corn and potato combination, our potato corn chowder is another delicious one to try!
Recipe Success Tips
- Keep the potatoes evenly diced. Cut them into similar-sized, bite-sized pieces so they cook at the same rate. They should be tender enough for a fork to slide through easily before you move on to blending.
- Cook the flour and add the broth slowly. I cook the flour with the vegetables for 1-2 minutes to get rid of the raw, floury taste (because nobody wants that in their chowder!). Don’t skip this step! Once the flour has cooked, slowly whisk in the chicken broth, a little at a time, so everything combines smoothly without any lumps.
- Be careful when blending hot soup! I recommend letting the portion you’re puréeing cool slightly first. If using a countertop blender, work in small batches, fill it no more than halfway, vent the lid to avoid steam buildup, and start on low speed to avoid hot splashes. You can also use a handheld immersion blender in a separate, deep heatproof bowl.
- Don’t blend everything. I only purée about half of the cooked vegetables and broth with ½ cup of corn. This gives the chowder its creamy, velvety consistency while leaving plenty of vegetables and corn whole for texture. Just make sure you’ve removed the chicken before blending!
- Check the chicken AND the potatoes. They won’t necessarily finish cooking at the same time, especially if your potatoes are larger than the ones shown in my step photos below. The chicken should reach an internal temperature of 165°F, while the potatoes should be fork-tender. If the chicken is done first, I recommend taking it out to shred while the potatoes finish simmering. This helps prevent the lean chicken breast from becoming dry and tough.
- Don’t skip the apple cider vinegar! I know a teaspoon of vinegar might sound strange in a creamy chicken corn chowder, but that little splash makes a big difference. I add it right at the end to brighten up the flavors and balance the sweetness of the corn. It won’t make your chowder taste vinegary, but it helps bring all those delicious flavors together.
Chicken Corn Chowder
Cost $11.89 recipe / $1.49 serving
Ingredients
- 5 slices (110 g) bacon (diced, (4 oz.) $1.41)
- 1 medium (200 g) onion (diced, (2 cups) $0.66)
- 2 garlic cloves (minced, $0.12)
- 2 medium (140 g) carrots (diced, (1 cup) $0.30)
- 2 ribs (115 g) celery (diced, (1 cup) $0.25)
- 1 (200 g) red bell pepper (diced, (1½ cup) $1.48)
- ¼ cup (30 g) all-purpose flour ($0.03)
- 1 lb. chicken breast (boneless & skinless, $4.64*)
- 6 cups chicken broth ($0.71**)
- 1 lb. (450 g) Yukon gold potatoes (diced, (about 2 potatoes, 3½ cups) $0.96***)
- ½ tsp smoked paprika ($0.08)
- ½ tsp dried thyme ($0.05)
- ½ tsp salt ($0.04)
- ¼ tsp black pepper (freshly cracked, $0.04)
- 12 oz. frozen corn (1½ cups, $0.98****)
- 1 tsp apple cider vinegar ($0.02)
- 2 Tbsp fresh parsley (chopped, $0.12)
- green onions (optional)
Instructions
- Gather and prep all ingredients.
- In a large pot or Dutch oven, cook bacon over medium heat until crisp. Transfer to a paper towel-lined plate and leave the rendered fat in the pot.
- Add onion, garlic, carrots, celery, and red bell pepper to the bacon fat. Cook for 5-6 minutes until softened.
- Sprinkle flour over the vegetables and cook, stirring constantly for 1-2 minutes to remove the raw flour taste.
- Slowly whisk in the chicken broth. Stir in diced potatoes, chicken breasts, smoked paprika, thyme, salt, and pepper. Bring to a simmer, cover, and cook for 15-20 minutes, until potatoes are tender and chicken is cooked through.
- Remove chicken from the pot, shred with two forks, and set aside.
- Carefully remove about half of the vegetables and broth, add ½ cup of corn, and puree until smooth. Return the puree to the pot.
- Add shredded chicken, the remaining corn, apple cider vinegar, and chopped parsley. Taste and adjust seasonings as needed.
- Garnish with crumbled bacon and optional green onions. Serve warm with crusty bread.
See how we calculate recipe costs here.
Notes
Nutrition Information
how to make Chicken Corn Chowder Step-by-Step Photos
Gather and prep your ingredients: Dice 5 slices of bacon, 1 onion, 2 carrots, 2 celery ribs, 1 red bell pepper, and 1 lb. of Yukon Gold potatoes. Mince 2 garlic cloves and chop 2 Tbsp of fresh parsley. Try to keep the potatoes similar in size so they cook evenly. If you’re using Better Than Bouillon like I am, mix up 6 cups of chicken broth according to the package directions so it’s ready when you need it.
Cook the bacon until crispy: Add the 5 slices of diced bacon to a large pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Cook until browned and crispy, stirring occasionally so it cooks evenly. Transfer the bacon to a paper towel-lined plate, but leave the rendered fat in the pot. We’ll use those flavorful drippings to cook the vegetables!
Soften the vegetables: Add 1 diced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, 2 diced carrots, 2 diced celery ribs, and 1 diced red bell pepper to the bacon fat. Cook for 5-6 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the vegetables begin to soften and the onions look translucent.
Cook the flour: Sprinkle ¼ cup of all-purpose flour over the softened vegetables. Stir constantly for 1-2 minutes, until the flour is evenly mixed in. This cooks out the raw flour taste and helps create a thick, creamy broth later on.
Add the broth, chicken, and potatoes: Slowly whisk in 6 cups of chicken broth, a little at a time, until the flour is smoothly incorporated. Add 1 lb. of boneless, skinless chicken breasts, the diced potatoes, ½ tsp smoked paprika, ½ tsp dried thyme, ½ tsp salt, and ¼ tsp freshly cracked black pepper. Stir gently, bring to a simmer, then cover and cook for 15-20 minutes, or until the potatoes are fork-tender and the chicken reaches an internal temperature of 165°F.
Carefully lift the chicken breasts out of the pot and transfer them to a plate or cutting board. If the chicken reaches 165°F before the potatoes are tender, remove it anyway and let the potatoes continue simmering. This helps keep the chicken from becoming dry and tough.
Shred the chicken: Once the chicken is cool enough to handle, use two forks to pull the meat apart into bite-sized shreds. Set it aside while you thicken the chowder.
Blend part of the chowder: Carefully transfer about half of the cooked vegetables and broth to a blender, along with ½ cup of frozen corn. Let the mixture cool slightly, then blend until smooth.
Safety tip: Hot soup can build up steam and pressure in a blender, so let it cool for about 5 minutes before blending (the frozen corn will also help cool it down). Work in small batches, fill it no more than halfway, vent the lid, and start on low speed. You can also use an immersion blender in a separate heatproof bowl (use a deep one).
Finish the chowder: Return the smooth purée to the pot and stir to combine. Now add the shredded chicken, remaining frozen corn, 1 tsp apple cider vinegar, and 2 Tbsp chopped fresh parsley to the pot. Stir everything together and continue heating gently until the corn is thoroughly cooked and the chicken is hot. Taste the broth and adjust the salt and pepper if needed.
Garnish and serve: Ladle the finished chicken corn chowder into bowls and top with the reserved crispy bacon, extra parsley, or optional sliced green onions, if desired. The broth should be thick and creamy, with tender chicken, potatoes, and sweet corn throughout. Serve warm with some crusty bread for dipping!
What to Serve with Chicken Corn Chowder
While the chowder is simmering, there’s time to make a little something on the side, and warm bread is usually where my mind goes first. A slice of our homemade cornbread is delicious with the smoky bacon and sweet corn, and it only takes 30 minutes to make. Homemade garlic bread, crusty bread, or soft dinner rolls are also great for soaking up every last drop of that creamy broth. If you want something a little lighter, try a simple side salad for some fresh crunch. It takes just 5 minutes to throw together, or you could add a side of roasted vegetables.
And don’t forget the toppings! I save the crispy bacon from the beginning of the recipe to crumble over each bowl, along with some fresh parsley or sliced green onions. A little shredded cheddar or Parmesan is also delicious, as are some ranch oyster crackers, and you can even add a dollop of sour cream or a swirl of heavy cream if you want to make your chowder extra rich. For bigger appetites, try stirring a little cooked rice, pasta, or quinoa into individual bowls to make it even more filling.
Storage & Reheating
This chicken and corn chowder makes 8 generous servings, so it’s a great recipe for meal prepping lunches throughout the week. Let any leftovers cool slightly, then divide them into airtight containers and refrigerate for up to 3 days. I recommend keeping any extra bacon and toppings separate, so they stay fresh and crispy.
Reheating
I prefer reheating this chowder in a saucepan over medium-low heat, stirring occasionally until heated thoroughly to 165°F. The broth does thicken in the fridge, so add a splash of chicken broth to loosen it up if needed. You can also microwave individual servings, stirring between short intervals so everything heats evenly. I recommend only reheating what you plan to eat to help keep the chicken tender.
Freezing
You can freeze this chicken corn chowder for up to 2 months. Once cooled, portion it into freezer-safe containers or heavy-duty freezer bags, leaving about an inch of space at the top for expansion.
Thaw overnight in the fridge before reheating on the stovetop or in the microwave. Because this chowder doesn’t use milk or cream in the base, there’s less concern about dairy separating, although the potatoes may soften a little after freezing. Add a splash of broth if it needs thinning out.
Try These Creamy Potato Soup Recipes Next
- When I want a simple, classic potato soup, I make my Classic Potato Soup. It uses russet potatoes and a little milk to create a thick, creamy broth, with plenty of tender potato chunks.
- Leftover holiday ham is a delicious excuse to make our Ham and Potato Soup. The salty ham adds plenty of savory flavor to the creamy potatoes and vegetables, and it makes eight servings in about an hour.
- For those days when you’d rather let the slow cooker handle dinner, try our extra-rich, creamy, EASY Slow Cooker Potato Soup too!

articles.title: Bad Flock Info Leads Police To Tow Wrong Car, Then Towing Company Totals It
articles.body:
Bad Flock Info Leads Police To Tow Wrong Car, Then Towing Company Totals It (jalopnik.com) 102
			
		 	
				"Police continue to blindly trust Flock cameras above and beyond the evidence in front of their own eyes," reports Jalopnik.com.
"After incorrectly connecting Rosalyn Crump's car to a shooting that had occurred the previous day, police had her car towed and impounded as evidence, reports Moneywise..."
According to WWBT 12 On Your Side, Richmond, Virginia, police didn't have a license plate number for the suspect's car, making it impossible to search Flock's records for that plate. Flock cameras collect more than just license plate information, so police searched for a make, model, color, and approximate model year.    Based on this extremely vague description, police zeroed in on Crump's 2012 Hyundai Elantra. Around 2 a.m. they started looking through the windows with flashlights to see what was in plain sight, which isn't technically a "search" — at least, not one that would require a warrant...   [Crump was asleep, but left her home to speak to the police officers to tell them they had the wrong car. But they didn't believe her.]
Other body cam footage shows an officer expressing doubt that Crump's car is the right one, since child seats and other items inside seem inconsistent with a shooting. Another officer replies, "Don't be surprised if they would have set that up like that." Instead of believing the evidence, or Crump, or interviewing witnesses who could have corroborated her story, police called Seibert's Towing to impound the car...
[Later] Police identified a similar-looking car that seemed to be actually connected to the shooting, and released Crump's Elantra. Nobody actually told Crump this until four days later. Seibert's told Moneywise that police didn't actually release the car until then. Either way, they didn't tell her that Seibert's had ripped the front bumper off during the towing process — leaving the car undrivable — until she arrived to pick it up. Seibert's took responsibility for causing the cosmetic damage, and was willing to cover the $2,212.30 bill to paint and replace the bumper cover, fog lights, and wheel liners. Then Crump asked for a full mechanical inspection, which revealed damaged tie rods and ball joints, jacking the bill beyond $6,000. Seibert's says it didn't cause this damage. Regardless of how it occurred, Seibert's insurer and Crump agree that her Hyundai is now a total loss due to the cost of the repairs it needs. It had been drivable, if mechanically worn, before police ordered it towed, damaging it for nothing more than a case of mistaken identity. 
The president of Seibert's towing told Moneywise that while they'd originally offered $2,200 to repair the bumper damage, Crump must now negotiate with their insurance company.   Crump has now resorted to a GoFundMe campaign to attempt to raise $17,100 for rental car expenses, a new car, and the expenses of moving to a different neighborhood.  130 donors have already contributed $7,431.
Reached for comment, the Richmond Police Department told local newscasters they "understand that Ms. Crump did not ask to become part of this investigation," and that they recognize the "frustration of having a vehicle towed and subsequently damaged."  But they also said they were following a "credible" lead, which is their responsibility.  The department "appreciates Ms. Crump's cooperation" (and "sincerely hopes the remaining concerns about her vehicle can be resolved.")
The city of Richmond has "already started backing away from Flock before Crump's story aired," reports Moneywise.  "Mayor Danny Avula has decided not to renew Richmond's license plate reader deal with Flock, which ends June 30, 2027. As of September, the city had 99 Flock readers on its streets."
They note that the Institute for Justice, a public interest law firm in Arlington, Virginia, "has tallied at least 27 cases since 2018" of similar police errors. "In each case, a license plate reader mistake led police to stop, jail or point guns at drivers who'd done nothing wrong. More than half came in 2023 or later."

articles.title: Polyend releases the Tracker firmware source code
articles.body:
Tracker. The biggest update yet.
Polyend releases the Tracker firmware source code
Today we’re publishing the firmware source code for the original Tracker, Tracker+ and Tracker Mini on GitHub. We’re also releasing Tracker Community Edition 1.0 with tons of new features and improvements. You can install it on any of the three instruments, modify the firmware yourself and share your own version. We’ve built in a recovery system to keep a faulty firmware build from bricking your Tracker.Explore the Tracker Community Edition repository on GitHub
Here at Polyend, creativity is what we value most. We’ve seen it firsthand in the unofficial Tracker mods you’ve built, and we’re sharing the firmware source code to support that work. Maybe you want to build an entirely new instrument on the Tracker hardware. Or maybe there’s just one thing you wish your Tracker did differently. Either way, you can now try it on the unit you already own. I bet some of you already have ideas for the original Tracker that never crossed our minds.Piotr Raczyński, CEO of Polyend
What’s new in Community Edition 1.0
- Stream long samples from the SD card. Bring full-length stems, loops and field recordings into a project using a fraction of the sample memory they’d normally need. This works even on the original Tracker.
- Record timing and velocity while keeping both step FX slots free. Micro-move and Volume now have dedicated fields on every step. New Chance conditions let you bring in a snare fill every fourth pass.
- Load plugins in the Sample Editor. Six effects and generators are included, from an analog-style kick generator to a stereo delay. The plugin SDK lets you build, share and sell your own.
- Play two new synths on Tracker+ and Tracker Mini. CHIP and DIRT join the synth lineup. A new SDK lets you build your own synth engines.
All three models also get wavetable envelopes and LFOs, faster project loading and saving, and tighter MIDI clock timing. You can design custom Tracker themes and fonts in your browser.

articles.title: BioWare co-founder: game execs "have never made a game" and don't get it
articles.body:
'None of these people have ever made a game,' BioWare co-founder Greg Zeschuk says of game industry executives: 'They just don't know how it works'
In a rare interview, Zeschuk said the closure of BioWare is sad, but his greater concern is for the people put out of work.
It's been almost 15 years since BioWare co-founders Greg Zeschuk and Ray Muzyka announced their retirements from the videogame industry, and they've been resolute about staying out of it ever since: Muzyka continues to head up the ThresholdImpact investment firm he founded in 2012 and holds multiple roles at the University of Alberta, while Zeschuk owns Blind Enthusiasm Brewing Company, also based in Alberta, where he works with a small handful of other BioWare veterans.
But Zeschuk stepped back into the videogame spotlight, briefly, following last week's closure of BioWare by parent company Electronic Arts, telling 80lv that he got the news hours after it happened because he was on a fishing trip, and by the time he flew home a couple days later, he'd "already shelved it away."
"I wasn't there to share in the moment, which in some ways was nice because I was able to kind of just take my time with it," Zeschuk said. "I’m not saying it doesn't hurt and doesn't suck. And I think it's kind of sad. It's actually, in some ways, saddest for the city of Edmonton, where we're from, because we were kind of this beacon of hope and excitement and possibility. We showed you could do something really special in a place that was not known for doing things like that."
Zeschuk said he had his own "emotional moment" about BioWare years ago, when he left the company; his real concern now is for the people at the studio who now find themselves out of work: "Anyone getting put into the job hunt is a sort of terrifying endeavor and super sad."
He also said he has no regrets about the EA acquisition, saying it offered "stability" as the studio continued to grow and that "we saw there'd be value in being part of something bigger rather than going our own way and taking all the risks." At the same time, he had a feeling when EA was acquired by Saudi Arabia's PIF that it probably wouldn't go well for BioWare, because it doesn't fit into the guns-and-sports model: "BioWare makes these kind of unusual games that take a long time and they're complicated and so it's easier just to pump out sports games every year and that's a better business model in some ways."
Zeschuk was also critical of the idea, seen in the recent wave of studio mergers and AI-powered cutbacks, "that you can just kind of recreate great games with random people and AI. It doesn't work," Zeschuk said.
"The other harsh reality of almost all these companies, the people that go down the business track never really come from the development track. Because none of these people have ever made a game, like, never really sat and made one, like, from start to finish, even a small thing, they just don't know how it works."
From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews
Zeschuk does know how it works, and he was clear that he's not interested in going back. "For me it was time to go, and I kind of walked out of the games business without any intention of ever returning. I'm happy being a consumer and playing games," he said. "I have my opinions on how to make stuff, but as enticing as it would be, it's just not [worth] the personal struggle and cost and effort required to make a great game. Having gone through the crucible of game development, I'm not going back in there."

Andy has been gaming on PCs from the very beginning, starting as a youngster with text adventures and primitive action games on a cassette-based TRS80. From there he graduated to the glory days of Sierra Online adventures and Microprose sims, ran a local BBS, learned how to build PCs, and developed a longstanding love of RPGs, immersive sims, and shooters. He began writing videogame news in 2007 for The Escapist and somehow managed to avoid getting fired until 2014, when he joined the storied ranks of PC Gamer. He covers all aspects of the industry, from new game announcements and patch notes to legal disputes, Twitch beefs, esports, and Henry Cavill. Lots of Henry Cavill.

In a rare interview, Zeschuk said the closure of BioWare is sad, but his greater concern is for the people put out of work.
It's been almost 15 years since BioWare co-founders Greg Zeschuk and Ray Muzyka announced their retirements from the videogame industry, and they've been resolute about staying out of it ever since: Muzyka continues to head up the ThresholdImpact investment firm he founded in 2012 and holds multiple roles at the University of Alberta, while Zeschuk owns Blind Enthusiasm Brewing Company, also based in Alberta, where he works with a small handful of other BioWare veterans.
But Zeschuk stepped back into the videogame spotlight, briefly, following last week's closure of BioWare by parent company Electronic Arts, telling 80lv that he got the news hours after it happened because he was on a fishing trip, and by the time he flew home a couple days later, he'd "already shelved it away."
"I wasn't there to share in the moment, which in some ways was nice because I was able to kind of just take my time with it," Zeschuk said. "I’m not saying it doesn't hurt and doesn't suck. And I think it's kind of sad. It's actually, in some ways, saddest for the city of Edmonton, where we're from, because we were kind of this beacon of hope and excitement and possibility. We showed you could do something really special in a place that was not known for doing things like that."
Zeschuk said he had his own "emotional moment" about BioWare years ago, when he left the company; his real concern now is for the people at the studio who now find themselves out of work: "Anyone getting put into the job hunt is a sort of terrifying endeavor and super sad."
He also said he has no regrets about the EA acquisition, saying it offered "stability" as the studio continued to grow and that "we saw there'd be value in being part of something bigger rather than going our own way and taking all the risks." At the same time, he had a feeling when EA was acquired by Saudi Arabia's PIF that it probably wouldn't go well for BioWare, because it doesn't fit into the guns-and-sports model: "BioWare makes these kind of unusual games that take a long time and they're complicated and so it's easier just to pump out sports games every year and that's a better business model in some ways."
Zeschuk was also critical of the idea, seen in the recent wave of studio mergers and AI-powered cutbacks, "that you can just kind of recreate great games with random people and AI. It doesn't work," Zeschuk said.
"The other harsh reality of almost all these companies, the people that go down the business track never really come from the development track. Because none of these people have ever made a game, like, never really sat and made one, like, from start to finish, even a small thing, they just don't know how it works."
From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews
Zeschuk does know how it works, and he was clear that he's not interested in going back. "For me it was time to go, and I kind of walked out of the games business without any intention of ever returning. I'm happy being a consumer and playing games," he said. "I have my opinions on how to make stuff, but as enticing as it would be, it's just not [worth] the personal struggle and cost and effort required to make a great game. Having gone through the crucible of game development, I'm not going back in there."

Best PC games: Our all-time favorites

Best FPS games: Finest gunplay
Best RPGs: Grand adventures
Best co-op games: Better together
Andy has been gaming on PCs from the very beginning, starting as a youngster with text adventures and primitive action games on a cassette-based TRS80. From there he graduated to the glory days of Sierra Online adventures and Microprose sims, ran a local BBS, learned how to build PCs, and developed a longstanding love of RPGs, immersive sims, and shooters. He began writing videogame news in 2007 for The Escapist and somehow managed to avoid getting fired until 2014, when he joined the storied ranks of PC Gamer. He covers all aspects of the industry, from new game announcements and patch notes to legal disputes, Twitch beefs, esports, and Henry Cavill. Lots of Henry Cavill.

articles.title: Anthropic warns that it’s very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI
articles.body:
While much attention has focused on the updated financials Anthropic revealed in its revised S-1A on Monday, (revenue is soaring, but so are expenses), the AI lab dropped another little bombshell in the fine print.
The filing seems to warn that the company is on the cusp of creating a model capable of recursive self-improvement (RSI).
RSI is the point at which AI grows so good at training itself that it spawns a dramatic acceleration of AI capabilities. To the AI doomers, RSI represents the cataclysm from which there is no return, in which AI builds itself into something powerful enough that it slips beyond human control and may be indifferent to the damage it causes while achieving its goals.
To AI enthusiasts, RSI, or some version of AI reliably using itself to improve, represents the technology’s promise, where it becomes a tool of unimaginable productivity, scientific discovery, and more.
Anthropic seems to believe that RSI is both a promise and a peril. It says in the S-1 that it uses AI in its R&D, but it cautions: “Using AI to help build more capable AI could also pose a considerable safety risk, particularly if it sharply accelerates the pace of progress. This is one of the areas covered by our Responsible Scaling Policy, which sets out our plans to monitor and mitigate the risks as we approach what has been termed ‘recursive self-improvement.’”
When the term RSI became popular earlier this year, many believed it was a buzzword or, at best, a goal too hard to achieve, define, or prove.
But on Monday, Anthropic added new statements to its Risk Factors section, saying 1) it has already used AI to develop new models whose leaps in capability it didn’t recognize at the time, and 2) it may soon meet its own internal definition of RSI (bold emphasis ours, below):
In addition, our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures. As a result, we have in the past not identified, and may in the future not identify, a significant acceleration in our rate of development until after it has occurred.
For example, our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.” We have not designated any of our current models as exceeding this threshold, and we continue to assess the underlying data.
However, Anthropic also said in the filing that none of its models have crossed this RSI threshold yet and that it is promising to keep humans in the R&D process for the foreseeable future. “We do not anticipate being able to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding, if and when that becomes technically possible. Accordingly, we are considering updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development at Anthropic.”
Skeptics might point out that an S-1 functions as both disclosure and marketing, and that claims of being close to a model so powerful that it can build itself could fall into the latter category.
Nevertheless, there’s no question that Claude’s capabilities, especially in terms of coding, math, and cybersecurity, have grow in leaps and bounds this year. If Anthropic thinks the possibility of RSI is close, maybe we should believe it and act — perhaps govern — accordingly.

articles.title: The New York Times sues Brave web browser for AI scraping and bypassing paywalls
articles.body:
The New York Times and a group of other publications have filed lawsuits against the company that makes the Brave web browser over alleged unlawful scraping to train AI and also letting users bypass their paywalls, as reported by Reuters.
The New York Times sues Brave web browser for AI scraping and bypassing paywalls
Brave has allegedly provided ‘stolen copyrighted content’ to many AI companies.
According to a complaint filed by the New York Daily News, the Chicago Tribune, and the Orlando Sentinel, Brave Software has monetized its index of scraped websites by, in part, providing AI companies with paid access to “real-time online content from the Brave Index.” The AI companies then use that index to train their models, access content to “respond to specific user queries,” or both. Brave has allegedly provided “stolen copyrighted content” to “many” AI companies including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere.
Brave also promotes “hundreds of top publishers” as being accessible through its “Paywall blocker” feature in its browser.
“Brave has never asked for the Publishers’ permission to access their websites, much less to copy the material and provide it to users or other AI companies,” the complaint says. “On the contrary, as noted above, Brave allows its users to bypass the Publishers’ paywalls without their consent, and has taken other steps that prevent the Publishers from blocking Brave’s access to the Publishers’ websites. Brave has never compensated the Publishers for the unlawful use, copying, and distribution of the Publishers’ copyrighted content.”
“While we believe in the ethical and responsible use and development of AI, Brave has flouted established copyright law and ignored repeated requests by The Times to stop its infringing conduct,” Graham James, an NYT spokesperson, says in a statement to The Verge. “We filed this lawsuit to hold Brave accountable for stealing our content to power its own products and to provide it to some of the most prominent and well resourced generative AI companies in the world.”
“AI giants are now desperate to avoid getting caught red-handed stealing news from publishers, so Brave Software is selling them a back door to the journalism they know they have no right to,” says Steven Lieberman, the attorney who filed the lawsuit on behalf of the other three publications. “Buying stolen goods secondhand doesn’t make them legitimate. Brave must be held responsible for laundering pirated reporting for the AI industry.”
Brave, Anthropic, Mistral, SpaceXSI, and Cohere, didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. “The New York Times is overpaying its attorneys and underpaying its journalists. (Who could’ve easily identified the disinformation in this suit.)” says Jesse Dwyer, Perplexity’s chief communications officer.
Update, November 2nd: Clarified that one lawsuit was filed by New York Daily News, the Chicago Tribune, and the Orlando Sentinel, not the companies that run them. Also added a statement from the attorney that filed the lawsuit on behalf of those publications.

articles.title: WTF Ubuntu?
articles.body:
WTF Ubuntu?
2026-11-02
What the fuck, Ubuntu?
In case you missed it: CVE-2026-98432 is a critical (CVSS 9.8) bug in the Linux kernel's TCP code. It's been there since 2016, so virtually every Linux server on the planet has it, and it can be hit remotely. Anthropic says it built a working exploit that gets root on a server. A total takeover.
Debian patched it on October 16. Ubuntu still doesn't have a patch more than two weeks later. Every supported release, LTS included, is listed as "Vulnerable".
Ubuntu's website promises "timely patches for critical vulnerabilities." Ubuntu hasn't shipped the patch nine days after it was rated 9.8 and six days after a working root exploit. Very fucking timely indeed.
Software is full of this blabber where words mean nothing. Ubuntu uses words like these: "Timely." "Enterprise-grade." "Production grade." "Enterprise resilience. Developer velocity. Build with confidence on Ubuntu."
Somebody, or perhaps worse, some special team at Canonical is dedicated to writing these........
So I'm asking again... What the fuck, Ubuntu?
I'm moving all my servers off Ubuntu. I've completely lost trust in it. On the desktop I always hated it anyway. On servers I mostly used it because it's the default on most VPS providers, and I considered it the solid, no-drama LTS distro. Fuck that now.
I can't express how crazy this is. I didn't have time to migrate my services and data when I learned about this, so I had to take all my servers that run Ubuntu offline.
Oh and btw, distros run by volunteers (Debian, Arch, Alpine...) hve shipped the fix. Meanwhile Ubuntu, made by a company that sells security subscriptions, hasn't. This is true as of 2026-11-02 14:48 UTC.

articles.title: Pray for Chaos
articles.body:
Pray for Chaos
There’s two basic ways AI can play out, one is order, the other is chaos.
Order is the very dangerous one. If it turns out that models are actually capable of patching all the exploits, it’s hard to imagine what will disrupt the status quo. Fortunately, this seems unlikely, but that doesn’t mean order won’t prevail in the short term. At the end of my Yudkowsky debate we found a tangible point of disagreement. He thinks AI will be able to find a solution to the Prisoner’s dilemma. I know there already is a solution (it’s defect), EA people just aren’t happy about it.
If it won’t be order (and you better pray it won’t be order) that leaves chaos. AI that can play a whole society in hours can manufacture entire histories, years of archives of daily newspapers, and an Internet that never happened. The dead Internet theory is coming true before our eyes. Now I can still see the bots, soon I won’t be able to. Scratch that, I probably already often can’t.
Gwern wrote about this, it’s hard to imagine a vision of humans as prompters or enter pressers in 2030. The US AI companies don’t believe they have to offer any solution to this, why would they have to justify in any way that their products are good for society? Anthropic cannot wait until they have the leverage to ban all their users. Why would you keep around the middle man?
Here’s the most positive vision I can come up with. If it turns out things can’t be secured, we enter an era of increased decentralization. Think everyone running their own custom different OS, not everyone running the same version of Linux on a computer they can touch. Because the centralized homogeneous systems are too vulnerable. Cyber attacks flying in every direction, nobody capable of keeping infrastructure up, cars sitting in driveways as bricks (or worse, rooted to steer you off a cliff).
Self replicating AI hiding out in every corner of every hard drive. How powerful of a model do you need for it to stand a chance of reproduction in today’s cyberworld? GLM-5.2 and up?
A media landscape that is botted and microtargeted to all hell, nonsensical elections where the only thing people agree on is the names of candidates. Massive dumps of corporate slacks and intranets. (come on Russian kids, grab an abliterated AI and do a hacking!)
Whatever you hold dear the chaos army will come for too. The Internet era is over. Your life will never be the same. The chaos will come for the resistance as well as the fascists; it’s unclear who it will hurt more. Your life plan is probably already nonsense in the face of AI. Mine sort of is. What economic value you think you will have in 10 years? Who will be around for you to have that value to? Do you think you’ll be able to make any sense of the world?
And remember, chaos is the good outcome. The alternative is that you are a dancing monkey in a cage you won’t be smart enough to see.

articles.title: AI Can Write More of the Code. We Still Have to Engineer the System
articles.body:
Software engineering · AI-assisted development
AI Can Write More of the Code. We Still Have to Engineer the System.
Durable decisions, relevant context and verifiable increments: a pragmatic perspective on keeping engineering judgment in AI-assisted development.
When people say AI has transformed software development, I want to know which part they mean. Producing an implementation? Exploring a design? Deciding whether a system solves the right problem?
Those activities are connected, but automating one does not settle the others. My argument is that agents can take on more implementation work, and assist with analysis, design, and testing, while engineers remain responsible for deciding what to build and what evidence is sufficient to accept it.
That changes the work. It does not make the responsibilities disappear.
I am wary of describing this as replacing the person who churns out code. It reduces developers to typing, understates what agents can assist with, and turns task automation into a claim about jobs. Claims about workforce replacement require evidence beyond an impressive demonstration.
The practical question interests me more: how do we use these tools while keeping our decisions visible and our feedback useful?
Give decisions somewhere to live
A conversation is convenient for exploring options. It is a fragile place to keep the only record of an architectural decision.
Model context is bounded. A long session may be summarized, compacted, or resumed with selected information. The summary can preserve the conclusion and lose the condition that made it reasonable. “Use a local cache” is different from “use a local cache because this screen must remain usable without connectivity.”
Anthropic's account of long-running agents describes continuity problems across context windows and an approach using incremental work and persistent progress artifacts. It also reports that compaction can leave unclear instructions. This is a vendor engineering report about a particular setup, rather than a universal comparison of development workflows.
My preference is to give durable decisions a small, reviewable home. A PROJECT_GUIDE.md might contain:
- The product's purpose and current scope, including explicit exclusions.
- The important system boundaries and the reasons behind architectural choices.
- Quality expectations and the commands used to check them.
- Links to deeper decisions when those decisions need more space.
The filename has no special power. An agent will not necessarily load it automatically. I would connect it through the tool's supported project instructions or explicitly include it in the task, then check the agent's interpretation.
For each increment, I would supply the relevant files and ask for a brief account of the intended change, constraints, and acceptance cases. A paraphrase is an early opportunity to catch misunderstanding; the implementation still has to demonstrate compliance.
Simon Willison's June 2025 discussion of context engineering helps frame the problem of choosing information for the next model step. My narrower recommendation is to make that selection deliberate and inspect its consequences.
Markdown alone guarantees neither retrieval nor obedience. Sending every document on every task can increase context and cost. Selective retrieval may reduce input, but maintaining documents, retrieving them, and correcting mistakes also consume resources. Any claim of savings needs a measurement of the complete task.
Specify the next behavior
Consider a hypothetical mobile search screen. This is an illustration, not a report from a completed project.
The story could be: “As a user, I want to search saved items so that I can find an item without scrolling through the entire collection.” For the first increment, the scope is local search over existing items. Remote search and changes to persistence are excluded.
Before implementation, I would make these acceptance cases explicit:
- A matching query displays the expected items.
- A query with no matches displays an empty result state.
- Clearing the query restores the complete collection.
- If filtering is asynchronous, an older result cannot overwrite a newer query's results.
These cases expose a technical question: does filtering need asynchronous work at all? The agent can help assess that decision. We should resolve it against the expected data size and responsiveness requirements, rather than introducing concurrency because a template expects it.
For this example, I might choose unidirectional data flow, explicit UI states, and a separation between filtering logic and rendering. That makes state transitions easier to inspect. Another system may justify a different structure; this is an engineering choice with a purpose.
The project guide should preserve that purpose. Feature-level notes should explain the behavior and any new decision. They do not need to reproduce the entire architecture.
After the increment, I would inspect the diff, run the relevant checks, and exercise the screen. If the agent rewrote persistence despite the scope restriction, passing tests would not make that expansion acceptable. If the empty state looks correct but the search matches the wrong field, a screenshot would not establish correctness either.
Make generation answer to verification
Agent output is probabilistic. Acceptance should depend on evidence that we can inspect and, where practical, reproduce.
A local verification command can run formatting checks, static analysis, compilation, and focused tests. These checks answer different questions. A formatter checks conventions; a compiler checks language and type rules; tests evaluate selected behavior under selected conditions. None establishes that we chose the right product behavior.
Controlled verification also needs controlled inputs. Tool versions, fixtures, and execution conditions matter. Tests involving timing, devices, networks, or external services may be flaky. Calling a test suite deterministic does not make it so.
Even a perfectly repeatable check can verify the wrong thing. A search test might assert that some result appears without checking which result it is. A generated test can faithfully encode the same misunderstanding as the generated implementation. I would review the assertion against the acceptance case and use deliberately chosen examples, including a failure case.
Running the app adds another kind of evidence: whether the behavior makes sense through the actual interface. When performance matters, define the measurement before declaring success—device, dataset, scenario, and threshold. A quick impression of responsiveness is useful feedback, but it is not a latency result.
Hooks can make local checks convenient and catch mistakes earlier. Their coverage depends on what triggers them and whether they can be bypassed. Where a team requires enforcement, server-side checks and repository protections need their own configuration. A local hook is not equivalent to an enforced remote policy.
The engineer still decides whether the evidence supports acceptance, revision, or rejection. An agent can help gather that evidence; it cannot make an incomplete test suite complete by announcing success.
Documentation has to earn its maintenance
I become skeptical when a small change requires a long chain of generated documents before anyone can see working behavior. Each document becomes something to review, reconcile, and keep current. Producing text cheaply does not make understanding it cheap.
That is a criticism of proportionality and feedback cadence. Spec-driven development has multiple meanings. Birgitta Böckeler's 2025 examination of Kiro, spec-kit, and Tessl distinguishes approaches that write specifications first, retain them during maintenance, or treat them as the primary source. Those differences matter when discussing costs and control.
François Zaninotto's critique of document-heavy workflows raises concerns about review overhead and instruction following through reported examples. Those cases are useful prompts for investigation. They do not establish that specifications generally cause worse outcomes.
An incremental specification can support rapid feedback. Agile does not mean avoiding documentation: its principles emphasize frequent working software, technical excellence, and adaptation. A short acceptance case can serve those aims; so can a detailed design when the risk warrants it.
Stronger specifications can be valuable for safety constraints, regulated work, public interfaces, migration compatibility, and coordination across teams. In those settings, a concise guide is an entry point to the necessary detail. It cannot replace that detail.
My test for a document is practical: what decision, implementation, or verification does it support, and who will maintain it? I would keep the explanation of a compatibility constraint even if it takes several pages. I would remove repeated prose that neither changes a decision nor helps someone evaluate the work.
Matt Pocock's collection of engineering skills offers another example of packaging guidance into adaptable, composable pieces. I find that direction useful. Its stated design goals are not evidence that a collection of skills outperforms another workflow.
Keep the acceptance decision explicit
A small increment can still contain a bad assumption. Its advantage is that it gives us an earlier, more bounded opportunity to discover one.
The loop I would advocate is straightforward: define the next behavior, supply the context it needs, check the interpretation, inspect the change, collect evidence, and decide whether to accept it. Update durable guidance when a decision changes. If review becomes unmanageable, reduce the increment or improve the checks before asking the agent to produce more.
This approach has limits. It depends on the engineer's understanding, the quality of the evidence, and the cost of keeping guidance current. This article presents a working position, not a controlled study or a demonstrated productivity gain. Establishing such a gain would require comparable tasks and accounting for review, rework, defects, and maintenance—not just generation time.
I am comfortable delegating more of the work when I can explain what was requested, what changed, and why the evidence supports accepting it. That is the engineering standard I want to carry into AI-assisted development.
Which decisions in your workflow remain visible after the conversation ends—and what evidence tells you that the agent respected them?
Authorship note: The initial draft was generated with AI assistance from Armando Picón's arguments and a source review. Armando reviewed the article and approved publication. The Spanish translation was produced with AI assistance. The mobile example is hypothetical.

articles.title: OccupySaaS
articles.body:
Every hire, every intern, every contractor — another line item. Infrastructure shouldn't charge rent by the head.
They laid us off. We're rebuilding their SaaS.
OccupySaaS is a protest movement written in code. Laid-off engineers, armed with AI and public documentation, are building clean-room, open-source, drop-in replacements for the platforms that rent our own industry back to us — one seat at a time.
1,000,000
The software built
by the 99% belongs
to the 99%.
In 2011, Occupy Wall Street asked who the economy was really working for. In 2026 we're asking the same question about the cloud. The tools every company runs on are now toll booths — and the people who built them were shown the door.
Proprietary APIs, export walls and surprise price hikes keep customers captive. Compatible open alternatives set them free.
A million engineers were let go while the platforms kept growing. We still know how to ship. Now we ship it in the open.
Clean room.
AI rebuild.
Drop-in.
We don't leak, decompile or copy anyone's code. Every project is rebuilt from public documentation and open standards, with AI doing the heavy lifting on the build side of a strict firewall — then proven compatible against the vendors' own public SDKs.
- Read the public record Public API references, open standards (OAuth 2.0, OIDC, REST) and published SDK behaviour become a written specification. Nothing confidential, nothing leaked, nothing from former employers.
- Raise the firewall Spec writers and builders stay separated. Each repo carries a CLEAN_ROOM.md policy, and provenance is recorded for every fixture and reference.
- Rebuild with AI AI agents implement from the spec alone — contracts first (openapi.yaml), then code, then tests — under human review at every merge.
- Prove compatibility A compatibility laboratory runs the vendors' own public client SDKs against our server. If your existing code doesn't work unchanged, it isn't done.
- Release it to everyone Apache-2.0. Self-hostable. Pluggable storage. No telemetry you didn't ask for, and no seat counter.
Allowed in →
- Public API docs
- Open standards & RFCs
- Public SDK behaviour
- Black-box test results
× Never allowed
- Leaked or proprietary source
- Decompiled binaries
- Former-employer confidential info
- Copied UI assets or trademarks
Two towers
occupied.
Identity and CRM: the two subscriptions almost every company pays for and almost nobody loves. Both are early, both are public, and both welcome contributors today.
ZeroAuthy
Auth0
A self-hostable identity server that speaks the Auth0 Authentication API. Point an existing Auth0 SDK at a ZeroAuthy tenant domain and it works with no code changes.
- OIDC discovery, JWKS & multi-tenant domains
- Hosted login, authorization code + PKCE
- client_credentials, rotating refresh tokens, revoke & logout
- Verified with auth0-spa-js, auth0-react & nextjs-auth0
# build & run
$ go build -o bin/zeroauthy ./cmd/zeroauthy
$ ./bin/zeroauthy serve --config config.yaml
$ curl https://localhost:8443/.well-known/openid-configuration
SalesCompel
Salesforce
A free, open-source Salesforce replacement with a tenant-isolated Go/PostgreSQL core, a Vue record editor, and a compatibility laboratory that checks behaviour against Salesforce's public API contract.
- Persistent Account & Contact CRUD
- Object describe and limited queries
- External-ID upsert & bearer authentication
- OpenAPI 3.2 REST contract & offline test lab
# run the compatibility laboratory
$ npm ci --prefix compat/clients/node --ignore-scripts
$ npm --prefix compat/clients/node run check
Who's next?
Every category on this board is a monthly invoice somewhere. The movement picks the next target in public — bring a spec, a use case, or a grudge.
Identity & Auth
ZeroAuthy — Auth0-compatible login, tokens and tenants.
CRM
SalesCompel — Salesforce-compatible records and REST API.
Docs & Wikis
Team knowledge bases that don't lock your writing behind a seat licence.
Issue Tracking
Tickets, sprints and boards with a compatible API for existing integrations.
Feature Flags
SDK-compatible flag evaluation you can run next to your own services.
Observability
Logs, metrics and traces without per-gigabyte ransom notes.
Customer Support

articles.title: OccupySaaS
articles.body:
Every hire, every intern, every contractor — another line item. Infrastructure shouldn't charge rent by the head.
They laid us off. We're rebuilding their SaaS.
OccupySaaS is a protest movement written in code. Laid-off engineers, armed with AI and public documentation, are building clean-room, open-source, drop-in replacements for the platforms that rent our own industry back to us — one seat at a time.
1,000,000
The software built
by the 99% belongs
to the 99%.
In 2011, Occupy Wall Street asked who the economy was really working for. In 2026 we're asking the same question about the cloud. The tools every company runs on are now toll booths — and the people who built them were shown the door.
Proprietary APIs, export walls and surprise price hikes keep customers captive. Compatible open alternatives set them free.
A million engineers were let go while the platforms kept growing. We still know how to ship. Now we ship it in the open.

AI rebuild.
Drop-in.

- Rebuild with AI AI agents implement from the spec alone — contracts first (openapi.yaml), then code, then tests — under human review at every merge.
- Prove compatibility A compatibility laboratory runs the vendors' own public client SDKs against our server. If your existing code doesn't work unchanged, it isn't done.
- Release it to everyone Apache-2.0. Self-hostable. Pluggable storage. No telemetry you didn't ask for, and no seat counter.

- Public SDK behaviour
- Black-box test results

- Leaked or proprietary source
- Decompiled binaries
- Former-employer confidential info
- Copied UI assets or trademarks

occupied.
Identity and CRM: the two subscriptions almost every company pays for and almost nobody loves. Both are early, both are public, and both welcome contributors today.
ZeroAuthy
Auth0
A self-hostable identity server that speaks the Auth0 Authentication API. Point an existing Auth0 SDK at a ZeroAuthy tenant domain and it works with no code changes.
- OIDC discovery, JWKS & multi-tenant domains
- Hosted login, authorization code + PKCE
- client_credentials, rotating refresh tokens, revoke & logout
- Verified with auth0-spa-js, auth0-react & nextjs-auth0

$ go build -o bin/zeroauthy ./cmd/zeroauthy

Salesforce
A free, open-source Salesforce replacement with a tenant-isolated Go/PostgreSQL core, a Vue record editor, and a compatibility laboratory that checks behaviour against Salesforce's public API contract.
- Persistent Account & Contact CRUD
- Object describe and limited queries
- External-ID upsert & bearer authentication
- OpenAPI 3.2 REST contract & offline test lab
# run the compatibility laboratory
$ npm ci --prefix compat/clients/node --ignore-scripts
$ npm --prefix compat/clients/node run check

Every category on this board is a monthly invoice somewhere. The movement picks the next target in public — bring a spec, a use case, or a grudge.

ZeroAuthy — Auth0-compatible login, tokens and tenants.

SalesCompel — Salesforce-compatible records and REST API.

Team knowledge bases that don't lock your writing behind a seat licence.

Tickets, sprints and boards with a compatible API for existing integrations.

SDK-compatible flag evaluation you can run next to your own services.

Logs, metrics and traces without per-gigabyte ransom notes.

articles.title: Sneaking into the auditorium for the Windows 2000 launch rehearsal
articles.body:
The Windows 2000 launch in San Francisco was accompanied by an expo, and a large number of Windows 2000 team members were dispatched to run the various booths and stations, give informal presentations on the new features of Windows 2000, and answer technical questions from the various attendees. And from among the people who were sent to the expo, a smaller group was selected to attend the launch event itself in person.
Related reading: A ticket to the Windows 95 launch.
After a few of us arrived early at the Civic Auditorium for the launch event, we had to entertain ourselves until the doors opened. There was some speculation as to who the celebrity host would be, since it hadn’t been announced. One of my colleagues tried to sneak into what looked like a VIP tent.¹ I, on the other hand, went exploring.
I found an unlocked door that took me into the empty upper level of the main auditorium.
I took a seat and tried not to be noticed.
The stage was set up with a 10-meter tall mock laptop, screens to the left and right of the stage for projecting slides, prerecorded videos, or to get a better look at on-stage close-ups, gray curtains unobtrusively hung to shield from view what would turn out to be various surprises throughout the event, and various other desks, demo areas, and even an airplane cabin set.²
While I sat and took in the complexity of the stage, there was an announcement that they would be rehearsing the opening in one minute. The lights dimmed in preparation. The lid of the giant laptop closed very slowly.
About ten minutes after the announcement, the rehearsal actually began.
The laptop lid opened, and on the laptop screen, it looked like someone was signing into Windows 2000, and then the mouse clicked the Start button. This led to a video montage, and when the montage was over, a voice announced, “Ladies and Gentlemen, please welcome Patrick Stewart!”
Oh my goodness, Patrick Stewart is going to be the presenter for the Windows 2000 launch!
Mere seconds later, onto the stage bounded… a crew member wearing a headset pretending to be Patrick Stewart so that the camera and lighting crew could make sure they were properly positioned.
Okay, that’s the end of the rehearsal. The lights come back on, and the auditorium once again buzzes with the sound of equipment being moved and people discussing things.
I left the auditorium and went back to join the crowd of people waiting to get in. I didn’t tell them who the host was.
The event itself seemed to go off pretty much as planned. With the real Patrick Stewart.
Patrick Stewart had such a commanding presence. If he had come out on stage and announced, “It is the dawn of a new era: The era of lime Jell-O”, people would say, “Yeah, lime Jell-O, I need to upgrade to lime Jell-O.” But instead of trying to spark a new dessert trend, he talked about Windows 2000, reading words from a teleprompter that he almost certainly didn’t understand, but he made them sound great.
¹ My colleague eventually returned with a Commemorative Edition boxed copy of Windows 2000.
² The airplane cabin was used for a sketch that demonstrated mobile business computing. The demoer took their laptop on a plane trip, where they happened to sit next to a character named William Wentworth, portrayed by actor John O’Hurley, president of William Wentworth Worldwide. (He gave his email address as www@www.com.) The sketch demonstrated infrared file sharing and other mobile scenarios. Remember infrared file sharing? Of course you don’t.

articles.title: Faceted Faces and Surreal Still Lifes Fill GaHee Park’s Dreamy Paintings
articles.body:
Faceted Faces and Surreal Still Lifes Fill GaHee Park’s Dreamy Paintings
An eye peers from a goblet. A disembodied finger creeps from beneath a curtain. A supine figure, lost in a dream, envisions an uncanny array of game and fruit. For GaHee Park, landscapes, figures, and still lifes merge into seamless, surreal tableaux. Her signature glassy-eyed female characters move through spaces where the boundary between reality and fantasy blurs.
Park’s new solo exhibition, Soft Shell at Jessica Silverman, delves into a realm where protection and a sense of security are nebulous. Although she nods to domestic spaces and symbols of comfort and sustenance, such as bowls laden with fruit, there is always something… else.
At first glance, many of the scenes in Park’s oil paintings appear relaxed and calm, but something soon feels “off.” A dark cloud moves in above “Woman on the Beach with a Bird,” and an interloping digit advances toward a flower arrangement in “Bouquet with a Visitor.” Sometimes the strangeness is apparent right away, such as in “Soft Shell,” in which Park juxtaposes hard, distinct lines with supple, fuzzy shapes, and the whole scene appears to both expand and shrink.
The inspiration for this new body of work, along with the show’s title, is inspired by what the artist describes as “the containers of life that we inhabit to feel safe, but which do not protect us completely.” The artist explores the nature of consciousness and relationships between landscapes and interiors, beauty and the grotesque, and strength and vulnerability. Through a prism of dark humor, Park also infuses her works with subtle, quirky narratives.
In “Eating Angel,” for example, a white t-shirt and halo have been cast onto the floor, and a gleaming wing appears to have been picked clean by the curious cat. The nude female form, plus numerous anatomical hints in the shapes of fruit—or in this case, the breast-like cover on a food platter being presented from out of frame—Park also nods to the Surrealists. She turns the table on the early 20th-century works made predominantly by men, positioning women in roles of empowerment and directness. “Refusing to be conquered, these heroines are sly exhibitionists who draw the viewer into a ‘ping pong’ of gazes,” the gallery says.
Soft Shell continues through December 19 in San Francisco. Keep up with updates on Park’s Instagram.
