articles.title: Jeffrey Gibson’s ‘A Real Love Thing’ Surveys a Decade of the Artist’s Multidisciplinary Practice
articles.body:
Jeffrey Gibson’s ‘A Real Love Thing’ Surveys a Decade of the Artist’s Multidisciplinary Practice
Through abstract, prismatic acrylic paintings to garment-like sculptures and textile collages, Jeffrey Gibson explores questions of identity, lineage, and cultural translation. Working across media, the artist intricately beads monumental works and incorporates a wide range of fabrics and materials.
Jeffrey Gibson: A Real Love Thing at Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg Center delves into the cross-disciplinary breadth of the artist’s practice throughout the past decade. Fifteen works amplify his interest in pattern, queer iconography, and his Indigenous Mississippi Choctaw and Cherokee heritage. Drawing on the early and continuing influence of music, the artist often integrates song lyrics into tapestry-like wall hangings and three-dimensional works.
Music also inspired the title of the exhibition, which Gibson drew from a 1971 interview with soul artist Marvin Gaye, who described his seminal album What’s Going On by saying, “I think I’ve got a real love thing going. I love people, I love life, and I love nature, and I can’t see why other people can’t be like that.”
Reflecting this sentiment, Gibson’s approach is a luminous celebration of Indigenous symbolism and traditional materials, such as jingle cones used in ceremonial garments, tipi poles, and glass beads that have coated bags, moccasins, and other apparel hand-crafted by Native Americans throughout the centuries. The artist also posits a future full of hope, joy, acceptance, and, like Gaye, a love-above-all ethos.
A Real Love Thing continues through March 13 at the Bloomberg Center in Washington, D.C., where Gibson will present a talk as part of the esteemed Sam Gilliam Lecture series on November 12. And if you’re near Eugene, Oregon, the artist’s traveling solo exhibition They Teach Love is also on view through through March 7 at the University of Oregon.

Our most popular exclusive dinner recipe so far is this new take on melting cabbage. Developed by Senior Culinary Producer Janette Zepeda, this cabbage dish totally transforms the vegetable into the cozy, comforting dish of your cold-weather dreams. The sauce is creamy and garlicky; you’ll want to just lick it up off of your plate!
Get the recipe: Bacon and White Bean Melting Cabbage
One-Pan Caprese Baked Chicken
Not sure what to make on a busy weeknight? Check out our one-pan caprese baked chicken. Add everything to the same dish and wait just 30 minutes as the chicken soaks up all the flavors of the bursting tomatoes, sweet balsamic glaze, and fresh mozzarella. I’m getting hungry just thinking about this Italian-inspired supper right now.
Get the recipe: One-Pan Caprese Baked Chicken
Simple-But-Brilliant Pork Stir-Fry
It’s just like the name says: This stir-fry recipe is so simple, but so incredibly brilliant. All you need is a bag of coleslaw mix, ground pork, and Thai chili sauce and you have a highly flavorful dinner that comes together in no time.
Get the recipe: Simple-But-Brilliant Pork Stir-Fry
Jennifer Garner’s Signature Fall Salad
I actually published a love letter to this fall salad recipe, so you know that I’m a fan. As I wrote in my recipe review, the salad dressing is the star of the show because of the slight sweetness from the maple syrup. The veggies also become so tender and flavorful in the oven, you can’t help but love it.
Get the recipe: Jennifer Garner’s Signature Fall Salad
One-Pan Chicken with Charred Corn and Zucchini
Food Editor Patty Catalano says that skillet dinners like this one save her life on busy days when she doesn’t have time to linger over the stove. While this recipe uses fresh corn, there’s nothing stopping you from grabbing a bag of frozen corn at the grocery store.
Get the recipe: One-Pan Chicken with Charred Corn and Zucchini
Mexican Lasagna
While this is not an authentic Mexican dish, it doesn’t make it any less delicious. Instead of your traditional Italian lasagna flavors, swap in taco seasoning, corn, green chiles, red enchilada, and refried beans. And don’t forget the corn tortillas instead of noodles!
Get the recipe: Mexican Lasagna
Sheet Pan Greek Chicken
Tired of boring, dry chicken? This sheet pan Greek chicken recipe will make those complaints a distant memory. Not only do you get juicy, flavorful chicken with a crispy skin, but the veggies cook at the same time in all the delicious schmaltzy fat. Our best tip for maximum dinner enjoyment: grab some crusty bread to soak up all the juices in the pan. Nothing goes to waste here.
Get the recipe: Sheet Pan Greek Chicken
Tuscan Beef Stew
Associate Recipe Producer Jan Valdez tested this recipe and described the beef as “melt-in-your-mouth tender.” There’s not a better compliment I can think of for a beef stew. She also said that it was incredible how delicious and flavorful this stew was for only using a few ingredients.
Get the recipe: Tuscan Beef Stew
Spicy Peanut Beef Noodles
These noodles are packed with flavor and come together so fast. There’s nothing quite like a saucy bowl of noodles to comfort you after a long day, and this bowl does that. Finish things off with some cooling cucumbers and a little spicy sriracha. Just like one commenter said, “So tasty! It’s the chili crisp that brings all the flavors together!”
Get the recipe: Spicy Peanut Beef Noodles
Italian Spinach and Ricotta Baked Chicken
Allow me to convince you to make this dinner in one sentence: There’s no chopping involved. This baked chicken recipe is smothered in the delicious filling you would normally add to ravioli (aka the best part). I bet this will go into your rotation once you make it.

articles.title: Ubuntu still has not released patch for Linux 0day RCE in almost 3 weeks
articles.body:
Ubuntu LTS kernels still unfixed for critical CVE-2026-98432
No patched kernels are available yet for 22.04, 24.04, or 26.04 despite a CVSS 9.8 rating.
Ubuntu has not shipped fixed kernels for CVE-2026-98432, a critical vulnerability scored CVSS 9.8, leaving the 22.04, 24.04, and 26.04 LTS releases without a vendor update.
Operators running those releases therefore have no official kernel package that closes the hole. The gap matters most for internet-facing and multi-tenant self-hosted systems that rely on Ubuntu’s LTS kernels for isolation and privilege boundaries; until packages appear, those hosts remain exposed to whatever remote or local attack the CVE enables.
Ubuntu has not announced an ETA for the fixes. In the interim, affected administrators are left to decide whether to stay on the stock kernel, apply out-of-tree mitigations if any exist, or move workloads onto releases or kernels that already carry the patch.

articles.title: Making Peace with the Projective Plane
articles.body:
In my newsletter I give an introduction to the latest few posts and occasionally give some additional commentary. In my latest newsletter I wrote
Projective space and homogeneous coordinates seemed like arbitrary abstractions when I was a student because they were presented without any motivation. Much later I came to realize that they’re natural, almost inevitable. Exceptional cases and hand-wavy references to objects “at infinity” go away when moving to projective space.
My mathematics education was very top-down: abstractions first, specifics later (if ever). I was OK with that for a while, until I hit my abstraction tolerance sometime in grad school. Now I would advocate more of a bottom-up approach, motivating abstractions first rather than presenting them as a fait acompli.
The first time I saw the projective plane was probably in a topology class where someone said you could construct the plane by starting with a square and gluing opposite edges in a physically impossible way. This seemed like a gimmick, a way to construct a non-orientable manifold but not anything practical. Another construction is to say the projective plane is an ordinary sphere with antipodal points identified. I found that a little more satisfying, but it still unmotivated.
What I would have appreciated was someone saying that the projective plane was invented to make geometry more elegant by eliminating exceptional cases and making rigorous the idea of things “at infinity.” For example, geometric calculations often have to treat vertical lines specially, but vertical lines are not special in projective geometry.
You could start by saying we’re going to represent points in the plane not simply as (x, y) but as (x, y, 1) and use (x, y, 0) for the point at infinity in the direction (x, y). That may seem like a hack, but it’s certainly motivated. It’s exactly the sort of thing a graphics programmer would do. In fact, I imagine many programmers have done just that, independently bumping into projective geometry.
After having introduced this extra coordinate, it’s natural to ask what would it mean if the last coordinate were something other than 0 or 1. You’ll quickly run into this when you start doing calculations on these extended coordinates. You could have a rule that you always normalize by dividing by the last coordinate, if it’s not zero, and then you have essentially discovered homogeneous coordinates.
You’ll see something like the approach above in elliptic curve cryptography. Programmers wanting to implement encryption algorithms are thinking concretely in terms of (x, y) points, until they have to worry about a mysterious “point at infinity” and handle it correctly. Then homogenous coordinates appear as a tool for getting out of a bind.
***
I thought about titling this post something like “Dr. Stragelove, or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and and Love the Projective Plane” but I wasn’t sure how well that would go over. I doubt many readers have seen the 1964 movie this is alluding to, but the trope “How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love …” is more widely known than the movie itself.

articles.title: Last night an AI agent performed brain surgery on a mouse
articles.body:
Gabriel Ocana-Santero on X: "Last night an AI agent performed brain surgery on a mouse.
We gave it 19 gene therapy vectors in a spreadsheet, a mouse model of epilepsy, access to a motorize surgery rig with cameras and one goal: reduce seizures.
It picked the drug. It picked the brain region. It d… / X
Gabriel Ocana-Santero on X: "Last night an AI agent performed brain surgery on a mouse.
We gave it 19 gene therapy vectors in a spreadsheet, a mouse model of epilepsy, access to a motorize surgery rig with cameras and one goal: reduce seizures.
It picked the drug. It picked the brain region. It derived the coordinates from three papers. Then it drove the stereotaxic arms into the brain and injected 250 nanolitres while watching the entry site through the rig camera for bleeding.
A licensed vet gated every irreversible step and held a physical kill switch to stop the AI agent.
Thread on what it decided, what it saw, and the moment it refused to let me override it.
[Writing this on the spot out of excitement, but I've been 18hrs in front of my laptop coding and coordinating this, so keeping it brief and descriptive, more cohesive thoughts on this soon...]"

articles.title: Valve "played capitalism so well they broke it" and now Steam can't be replaced
articles.body:

A former Epic Games developer is calling out Steam users, saying that they wouldn't move on from Valve's store even if a better alternative emerged.
Kiaran Ritchie, former principal animation engineer at Epic Games kicked off discussions surrounding Steam's 30% sales cut last week (with the assertion that "you could vibe code a Steam alternative in a week"). Which in-turn led noted Steam hater Epic CEO Tim Sweeney to assert that "Valve has held gaming back for years" – because the person whose company proudly asserted it had"vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher" knows what's holding gaming back!
Ritchie elaborated on their opinions on the 30% cut in a separate post, with the post saying that while developers are paying 30% in order to access Steam infrastructure, "in reality it is purely to get access to the massive Steam userbase." He adds "PC developers have no option but to distribute through Steam or lose the vast majority of sales."
As for that 30%, he says that it's "siphoned out of the PC games industry into a black hole," arguing that "Valve could easily lower the distribution fee while maintaining healthy margins." He later gives "Kudos" to Valve, saying "They played Capitalism so well they broke it."
And while a point can certainly be made that Steam is generally a better platform than the alternatives, and that it has the most to offer players in its library, Ritchie argues that it doesn't really matter, claiming "no avid Steam user wants other stores to succeed."
"Even if an alternative were objectively better, by whatever metric you care about, it would still be of no interest to Steam users," Ritchie says, adding, "Competition in this space is not only uninteresting to most Steam users, it's actively denigrated!" He then says that the Steam users "the very ones maintaining this unbreakable stalemate, would benefit the most from a better financed game development ecosystem." He concludes, "I don't think this is fixable. It's just sad."
Personally, I don't think Steam needs to charge as much either, but Ritchie hits the nail on the head, that it's "to get access to the massive Steam userbase." Because unfortunately, losing 30% to Valve is probably better than joining the list of games that flopped on PC because they were Epic Games Store exclusives.

Emmanuel Rosier, director of market intelligence at research and analyst firm Newzoo told GamesRadar+ that "As long as Valve is independent and not a publicly traded company," it looks impossible for Steam to be overthrown as the de-facto PC gaming marketplace.
Scott has been freelancing for over four years across a number of different gaming publications, first appearing on GamesRadar+ in 2024. He has also written for the likes of PC Gamer, Eurogamer, VG247, Play, TechRadar, and others. He's typically rambling about Metal Gear Solid, God Hand, or any other PS2-era titles that rarely (if ever) get sequels.

articles.title: Anthropic clamps down on Claude’s AI video game clones
articles.body:
Anthropic has updated Claude Code’s system prompt to prevent the AI tool from being used to recreate existing video games, as reported by Tom’s Hardware. Retro gaming is currently being overrun with AI-made decompilations, recompilations, and ports, but while Anthropic will still let people use Claude Code to make games, it doesn’t want people to use it for direct clones.
Anthropic clamps down on Claude’s AI video game clones
Anthropic is steering Claude away from re-creating specific titles, but users can still use it to make their own games.
Last week, a user on X posted a screenshot allegedly showing two new sentences added to Claude Code’s system prompt: “Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is named or called original.”
Anthropic’s Addy Osmani, in a reply, didn’t confirm that specific language but did say that the company had updated the prompt in Claude Code on Opus 5.5:
We added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.
Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working.
We’ll continue to iterate to ensure we’re striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that’s yours, send it my way.
We’ve asked Anthropic if it has or will be updating other Claude system prompts as well.
